# Chapter 5: Nobody Wins Alone On Monday there was a tube of Shoe Goo on the seat of the van where Deja usually sat. There was no note, just the tube, half used and rolled up from the bottom like toothpaste. Somebody had written *V.N.* on it in Sharpie. She glued the heel back on Sunday night at the kitchen table. Actually she did it Monday night, but she told herself Sunday, because Sunday meant she'd done it before she saw the tube. She clamped it overnight between two dictionaries and a bag of flour. In the morning it held, and it looked terrible. Clear glue had bubbled out along the seam and dried with a dog hair in it. She'd spent the whole weekend not believing it. It was easy, and it felt good. Coach was a lady from Scranton with a drinking problem, which everybody said, and a knee thing, and a Honda that smelled like soup. People said stuff. Coach had said a crazy thing on the side of the interstate in the sleet, and Deja had said a crazy thing back, and that was that. She told Kiara none of it. She told Priya none of it. She looked up "Nike goddess" on her phone at two in the morning and got four hundred pictures of a statue with no head and no arms. It was big and white and all wings, and it looked nothing like anyone she knew. She felt stupid. Then she looked at it for a long time. At practice on Tuesday she waited until everybody was doing core on the wet infield. Then she walked over to the fence where Coach was leaning. "Prove it," Deja said. Coach didn't look away from the girls doing planks. "Morgan, your butt's in the air. Put it down. Prove what." "You know." "I'm not doing tricks." "Then tell me something you couldn't know." Coach was quiet for a while. Deja thought she wouldn't answer and was already turning to go back to the planks. "Five twenty-one point three," Coach said. "Eighth grade. September, a Thursday, sixth period. You ran it on the middle school track in jeans. The boy who dared you said you couldn't break six, and you did it to shut him up. You didn't know the time. Nobody had a watch. You found out later from your gym teacher, who guessed five-thirty. He was wrong." Deja stood there. "You were leading the whole way," Coach said. "There wasn't anybody to beat. You made somebody up. That's how I noticed you, three years ago, from across town. I didn't know your name. I just felt somebody decide something." "That's creepy." "I know." "That's actually really creepy." "I *know*. Go do your planks." She went and did her planks. She didn't hear a thing anybody said for the rest of practice. --- The fight happened on Thursday, and it was her fault, mostly. They were in the van after a tempo run with everybody else gone, Coach in the driver's seat not starting it. "So why not," Deja said. "Just tell me why not." "Because then it's not yours." "It's not mine now." Deja counted on her fingers. "Kemper has a private coach. She has a nutritionist. She goes to Flagstaff every summer and runs up a mountain. She has spikes with a *spring* in them, you said so. Her dad drives her everywhere. She doesn't work. She's never worked. She's never smelled like a pretzel in her life." "So?" "So which part's hers? Tell me which part. Her legs? Fine. And then like forty grand of other people's stuff on top." Deja was talking too fast. "So she gets the dad and the mountain and the spring, and I get to be principled? That's cute. You want me to be principled. That's really cute." "It's not the same." "Why." Coach started to say something about Olympia. It was about athletes who got caught bribing judges, and statues of Zeus they paid for with the fines, lined up by the stadium entrance so every runner walked past them. Halfway through she stopped. Deja could see her hear herself. It sounded like somebody who'd won a lot of stuff explaining that the rules were fair. "I don't tip races," Coach said finally. "That's all. That's the one thing. I don't do it." "For me or for you?" Coach didn't answer. She started the van. --- On Friday, Priya asked her in the locker room if she thought Priya could break six by the end of the season. "Is that stupid? You can say it's stupid." "It's kind of stupid," Deja said. "You ran six-forty." Priya's face didn't fall. It just held very still. That was worse. She said "Okay, yeah, totally," and went and sat on the bench and tied her shoes with a lot of attention. Deja stood at her locker for a while. There were four yellow sticky notes on the inside of the door that Priya had put through the slot over the past month: *YOU GOT THIS!!* and *proud of u* and a drawing of a cheetah. She'd thrown out most of the others. She had kept the cheetah one in her left shoe, under the insole. She didn't know why. It was bad for the insole. She took a hair tie off her wrist and dropped it on the bench next to Priya. "Your ponytail's gonna come out," she said. "It always comes out on the backstretch." "Oh," Priya said. "Thanks." That was as far as Deja could get. --- Saturday was the late shift, four to close. It was dead, so she wiped the same counter five times. At eight-fifteen a guy came up in a quilted vest with no socks, in April. His sneakers looked like they'd been taken out of the box in the parking lot. They were black and red, with laces so white they hurt. "Four originals," he said. "And a lemonade. Actually two lemonades." She rang it up. She could feel him watching her, not in a creepy way, more like how Coach watched her at the fence. "You're Deja," he said. "It's on my name tag." "It is, isn't it." He smiled like that was the funniest thing he'd heard all week. "How's your sister? Kiara, right?" Deja stopped with the tongs in her hand. "Tell her Mercer says hey," he said. "She won't remember. That's fine." She bagged the four pretzels. He handed her a twenty and a fifty folded together and said keep it, and she said she couldn't. He was already walking backward toward the escalator, balancing the two lemonades, one of which he'd never drink. He didn't say anything about shoes. He didn't say anything about running, or Coach, or races, or anything. She stood there holding the fifty for a long time. Then she put it in the Band-Aid tin in her backpack with her dad's twenties, which she'd never spent either.

# Chapter 6: The Dumpster The practice was bad in the ordinary way, which was the worst way. It was a Wednesday at the end of April. It was fifty-two degrees, the first warm day, and every girl on the team ran like it had personally let them down. Morgan had cramps. The twins were back, and nobody knew why. Priya ran her 800 repeats in Deja's old hair tie and went out too fast, which she'd learned from watching, and she died on the backstretch every single time. Nike called her splits to the tenth and watched her die. Deja ran six of eight 600s and then walked off the track. She didn't quit. She just walked to the infield and sat down on the grass with her knees up and her arms around them, in the terrible glued Ghosts. She looked at the scoreboard, which had been broken since 2011. Nike went over. She should have waited. She knew she should have waited. She went over anyway. "You've got two more." "I know." "So get up." "My legs are fried. I worked till close. I'm doing two tomorrow." "Kemper's doing two today." Deja looked up at her. She had salt in white lines at her temples, and her eyes were very flat. "You know what's funny," Deja said. "You want this more than I do." "That's not—" "No, you do. It's fine. I'm just saying it. You stand at the fence and you look like you're gonna puke. I'm the one who pukes. You look like it." She stood up and brushed the grass off. "I'll do two tomorrow." She walked to the parking lot. Nike stood on the infield while eleven girls pretended not to have heard, and the pull in her chest turned slowly over, like something on a spit. --- The Dick's on Peach Street closed at nine. She got there at eight-forty. She didn't decide to go. She got in the Honda and drove, and the Honda went there. In the running aisle she stood in front of the Brooks wall under the lights, and there they were: Ghost 15s in grey and a green that was almost teal. They didn't match the old ones, but they were close enough. She knew the size without thinking about it. She'd been looking at the girl's feet for two months. A kid in a referee shirt asked if she needed help. She said no. He asked if she wanted to try them on, and she said they weren't for her. He said, "Oh, cool, for your daughter?" She said yes, because it was faster. They were a hundred and forty dollars. She paid in cash, and she'd rather not think about where the cash was from. At home she put the box on the kitchen table next to the Shoe Goo and the butter knife. She poured a bourbon and didn't drink it. The TV was on in the other room, on a poker tournament, men in sunglasses in Macau, and she could hear a dealer say *river*. She opened the box. The shoes were wrapped in tissue, and she took them out one at a time. They smelled like the inside of a new car, like chemicals and nothing. She put her hands on them. It wasn't a ritual. There had never been one. People had built altars and poured wine and sung things, and it had all been for them. On her end it was always this: a thing, and a wanting, and her hands. She thought about the backstretch on the bell lap. She thought about Hollis Kemper's pink spikes a stride ahead, and the gap closing, and closing, and the girl's shoulder coming level. Then she let go of what she'd been holding back for two hundred years. It took nothing. It was like opening a hand. The shoes didn't glow. They didn't do anything. They sat on the table under the light with the tissue paper around them. They were a hundred and forty dollars' worth of foam, and if you'd put them on your feet, you'd have won. She drank the bourbon then. She poured another and drank that too. For about half an hour she felt better than she had since Carter was president, warm all through, her knee quiet, like somebody had come into the room she'd been sitting in alone and turned on a lamp. That was how she knew it was bad. She'd been here before, in other centuries, with other things. At a quarter to midnight she put the shoes back in the box and the tissue paper back over the shoes. She put the lid on and taped it shut with packing tape, around and around, more than you'd need. She carried it down the back stairs past the dark vacuum repair shop to the dumpster in the alley. She lifted the lid, put the box in on top of somebody's broken lamp and a bag of what smelled like shrimp, and let the lid come down. It was loud. A dog two yards over started barking and didn't stop for a while. She went up and went to bed and didn't sleep, and then she did. --- Sometime near dawn she heard a truck, or thought she did. It was a big diesel sound in the alley and the hiss of brakes, and then it was gone. Pickup was Thursdays. It was Thursday. She was pretty sure it was Thursday. At six-thirty she went down in her sweatpants and bare feet and opened the dumpster. The lamp was there. The shrimp bag was there. There was a pizza box she didn't remember and a lot of wet cardboard. She moved it around with her arm up to the elbow, which she would think about later, and she didn't find the box. So the truck had come. Except the truck would have taken the lamp. She stood in the alley with her arm wet and smelling like shrimp. Then she went upstairs, washed it in the kitchen sink with dish soap, and called him. He picked up on the second ring. Behind him she could hear the organ, tinny through the phone, and a horse-pole creaking, and "Daisy Bell." It was six-forty in the morning. The mall wasn't open. The carousel was running anyway. "Vic," he said. "You're up early." "Where are they." "Where are what?" "You know what." A pause. The organ went *on the seat of a bicycle built for two*. "Gone where?" Mercer said. It was the voice he'd used on shepherds. He'd used it on the Pharaoh's grain clerks and on a customs man in Baltimore in 1804, and on her, many times, over a lot of years. It was gentle and interested and completely unhelpful. She hung up. She drove to school. First period she had study hall duty, and she sat at the front of the library with forty kids on their phones. At lunch she ate a gas-station hot dog in the van. At three-fifteen Deja came across the lot with her hands in her hoodie pocket and got on the line for her two 600s. She ran them well, better than well, in the old glued shoes. The cheetah note was probably still under the left insole. Nike called the splits. She didn't say anything else.

# Chapter 7: Bell Lap The box came on a Tuesday. It was on the porch when she got home from practice, wedged against the storm door. It was a plain brown box with her name printed on a label and a return address that was just a P.O. box in Pittsburgh. Inside were Brooks Ghosts, grey with a green that was almost teal, in a seven and a half. That was her real size, not Kiara's. He lifted the pretzel at her like a toast. She looked away. Coach was at the fence by the two-hundred mark. She hadn't said much all morning. She'd told Deja her socks were wrong, which they weren't, and told Priya her 800 was "fine, actually," which scared Priya more than yelling would have. Now she stood with her arms crossed high and her weight off the bad knee. She wasn't looking at the bleachers either. "Go out like an idiot," Coach said, when Deja jogged past. "On purpose." "I know." "Kemper sits. She'll sit till the bell." "I *know*." Coach's mouth did something. "Okay," she said. "Go." --- There were twelve of them on the waterfall start, curved across the track. Lane one in the first hundred meters was like a door everyone tried to go through at once. A McDowell girl caught her in the ribs. Somebody stepped on her heel and the shoe held, it didn't even move, and she was out and clear and in front by the first turn. Just like always, just like an idiot. The wind hit her on the home straight like a hand on her chest. "Seventy-three!" Coach, at the fence. "Seventy-three, you're fine, relax your hands!" Lap two she felt Kemper arrive. She didn't hear her so much as feel the space behind her right shoulder fill up. Then came that breathing, steady as a sewing machine. The wind was in Deja's face on the home straight and she knew, the way you know you've left the stove on, that Kemper was using her like a wall. "Two twenty-seven!" Coach yelled. "She's on you, let her be on you!" Lap three was the bad one. It always was, but this one was worse. Somewhere on the backstretch her legs turned to something heavy and wet, like sandbags. The penny taste came up, and her arms went tight up by her ears. She could feel her stride shortening and couldn't stop it. The McDowell girl pulled up on her left and Kemper was still right there on her right, and for about fifty meters Deja thought, very clearly and without drama, *okay, third again, that's fine*. It was the same voice Kiara used about everything. *It just felt like homework.* "You're sitting down!" From the fence. Coach was somehow at the top of the curve now, where the pace died. She was standing where she always stood. "Holloway! You're sitting in a chair! *Get out of the chair!*" She got out of the chair. She didn't know how. She just stood up in her own hips, and the McDowell girl slid back. The bell was ringing. Somebody was ringing it really hard. Coach had said Kemper would go at the bell, so Deja went before it. She went at about the three-fifty mark, stupidly early, three hundred and fifty meters from the line. It was a dumb, bad idea that no coach would tell you to try, and she tried it because it was hers. She went into the wind on the curve with her arms high and her mouth open and her whole chest scraped out. She heard Kemper say something, one short sound, surprised. The backstretch was silent. She didn't hear anything, not the crowd or Coach. She heard her own feet, *left* and *left* and *left*, and the shoe didn't slap. There was nothing broken in it to slap. She didn't know if that was good. She couldn't think about it. There wasn't room. Around the last curve Kemper came. Deja saw the pink first, at the edge of her eye, then the green-and-white shoulder, then the French braid. It came up level and stayed level, and Kemper's breathing wasn't a sewing machine anymore. She remembered the big orange numbers on the board going blank and then filling in, and her own name on top. *HOLLOWAY, PRESQUE TWP. 4:58.61.* Under it: *KEMPER, FAIRVIEW. 4:59.14.* She walked four steps onto the infield grass, put her hands on her knees, and threw up. The Kemper moment—reaching up a hand without looking, Deja pulling her up, neither saying anything—is earned. It doesn't redeem Kemper or make her a lesson. It's just two exhausted people. WEAKNESSES: "like a hand on her chest" for the wind is a bit flat. "Steady as a sewing machine" for Kemper's breathing is good the first time; the callback ("wasn't a sewing machine anymore") works but is slightly over-explained. The Priya screaming moment is fine but slightly convenient—she's there to provide the emotional release Deja can't perform herself, which is a legitimate choice, but it's the one beat that feels slightly functional rather than organic. The plan called for "Nike's reaction comes from the outside: she's gripping the fence and not cheering, pale, because it felt like every win she's ever had, and she cannot tell." DIALOGUE: Sparse and effective. Nike's fence-side coaching is the best dialogue in the chapter. The opening shoe-box exchange with the mom ("Did I what?") is quick and real. There's very little weak dialogue here. METAPHOR/POETRY: The chapter is largely restrained. The "door everyone tried to go through at once" is vivid. "Left and left and left" for the footfall rhythm is good. The wind "like a hand on her chest" is the one forced moment. Overall, the poetic gestures land more than they miss. FAITHFULNESS TO PLAN: Very high. The wind had his vest flapping. Still no socks. "Vic," Mercer said. "Congratulations." "Don't." "I'm allowed to say congratulations. It's a nice word. It's a Latin word. He shrugged, and it was a beautiful shrug, four thousand years in the making. "Or I did. Or the truck came and the box fell off the back in the alley and a kid found it and sold it on eBay to a lady in Pittsburgh who returned it because it was the wrong size, and the post office did something the post office does. Does it matter?" "Yes." "Why?" She opened her mouth. A gull came down on the roof of the Tahoe and the man threw a tent stake at it. "Because I'd know," she said. "Would you?" He said it gently. That was the worst part. "You were standing right there. Did you know?" She didn't answer. He reached into his vest, past the folded square of wax paper, and took out a twenty. He held it out between two fingers. "You won the bet," he said. She looked at it. "She ran four fifty-eight." "She did." "You bet she'd go under five. I bet she wouldn't. I lost." "Did you?" said Mercer, and tucked the twenty into the pocket of her windbreaker, and patted it once, and walked off across the lot toward nothing in particular with his hands in his vest. She had no way to tell, and he'd known that when he did it, and that was the whole gift. --- Deja came across the lot with her bag over her shoulder and her medal stuffed in the hoodie pocket like it was something she'd shoplifted. Deja looked where he'd gone. Then she looked at Nike, and then, very deliberately, down at her own feet. "So." Nike had the whole thing ready. The Dick's on Peach, the tissue paper, the bourbon, her hands. The lid of the dumpster coming down. It was right there, two sentences' worth, and all she had to do was open her mouth and let it out the way she'd let the other thing out on the kitchen table. "So," she said. "Could you tell?" Deja said. "Like, from the fence. Could you feel the difference?" The wind came across the lot. Somewhere a car alarm started and gave up. "No," Nike said. Deja waited for more. "It felt like every one I've ever had," Nike said. "That's all. That's all it feels like. It feels like someone won." Deja stood there a while. Then she drank the rest of the Gatorade and crushed the cup and said, "Okay," and got in the van. --- Priya fell asleep before Girard with her ribbon in her fist. The twins had headphones in. It was spitting rain, and the wipers sighed. "That guy in the quarter-zip," Nike said, somewhere past the Route 5 exit. "Fairview. Did you see him? At the end? He had the stopwatch up. He *timed* it. The board's right there. It's electronic. There's a man in a tent. He timed it anyway, like he didn't believe the board." "Mm," said Deja, from the back. "And he's got her going out in seventy-five. Seventy-five, with those legs. Into that wind. She could've been clear of you by the six hundred and he had her sitting like a—like a *hen*." "Mm-hm." "I'm just saying he's bad at it. He's a bad coach. Somebody should say it." "You said it," Deja said. "At the invitational. You got warned." "Well, he's still bad." In the mirror Deja had her head against the window and her eyes shut, and she was smiling a little, with the gap in her teeth showing, which she never let happen in pictures. She let Nike keep going. Nike kept going all the way to Pittsburgh Avenue. --- I ran four years at Slippery Rock. I was pretty good. I made nationals once and finished eleventh, which is the kind of place nobody remembers, including me, mostly. I do billing for an orthopedic practice now. My daughter's six and thinks running is something you do to get to the swings. I still have the Ghosts. They're in a shoebox on the top shelf of the hall closet behind the Christmas stuff. I could take them anywhere. I could cut the insoles out. Kiara says there's a guy on YouTube who X-rays sneakers for authenticity, and I could send them to him and he'd tell me they're just foam. I've never done it, and I've stopped pretending I'm going to. Anyway. It's true, what people didn't used to believe. Gods wore sneakers. Mine were ugly. The moment Deja goes before the bell because "it was hers" is the thematic payoff of the whole piece, and it lands. The epilogue (Deja's adult voice) is a risk that pays off. Occasionally the dialogue tips into being slightly too clever (Mercer's carousel scenes walk this line but mostly stay on the right side). # Brainstorming **Tone targets:** Darkly comic, British, YA. Think the gallows humour of *Skins* and *The End of the F***ing World*, the teenage voice of Louise Rennison sharpened with menace, and the small-town claustrophobia of Hollyoaks crossed with a true-crime podcast. It should be funny about awful things without being flippant about grief or fear. Voice matters most: first person, sardonic, self-aware, with specific British texture like Year 11, sixth form, Greggs, the Tesco Express, WhatsApp group chats, mocks, bus shelters and Mum's Prosecco. **Interpretations of the three blood-drop emojis:** 1. **A pact signal.** Years ago, a friend group agreed that 🩸🩸🩸 meant "I've done something terrible, come now, no questions." It was a joke rule from Year 7, and it has never been used until tonight. 2. **A period joke gone wrong.** The protagonist assumes it's a crude joke from her best friend about her period. It isn't. The comic misreading opens the story and then curdles. 3. **A murder-club game.** A school "Assassins" game (water pistols, fake kills) where the emoji means you've been "killed." Then someone actually dies, or goes missing. 4. **A wrong number / sender unknown.** The text comes from a dead girl's number. Someone has her phone. Is it a prank, or is it a message? 5. **A vampire LARP or theatre society.** The drama kids' production of *Dracula* uses fake blood. Then there's real blood. 6. **Sent by the protagonist's own phone** while she slept. Sleepwalking, a hacked phone, or a sibling messing about. 7. **The pet.** The blood is the family hamster's, or the text is about a neighbour's cat that everyone hated. The dark comedy comes from escalating overreaction to a small death. **Character ideas:** - **Narrator: Maya / Priya / Ellie / Josie.** Sixteen, doing GCSEs, anxious and funny, a self-appointed "sensible one" who is secretly desperate for drama. Maybe she wants to be a crime journalist or runs a failing true-crime TikTok. - **The sender: best friend Tash / Cassie / Bex.** Chaotic, charismatic, the kind of friend who gets you in trouble. Maybe the friendship is fraying because the narrator is pulling away toward sixth-form ambitions. - **Third friend: Dev / Ollie.** Deadpan, gentle, a pedant who keeps correcting people's grammar during crises. He carries a Nando's loyalty card like a badge. - **Adults:** a mum who is too online, a weary PCSO, a headteacher obsessed with Ofsted, a creepy-but-harmless neighbour, and an older brother who's useless but has a car (a Corsa, obviously). - **Antagonist or victim:** a popular girl, a teacher, Tash's awful stepdad, the school's PE teacher, an ex-boyfriend named something like Kieran. **Plot directions:** - **A:** The pact is invoked. The narrator sneaks out and finds Tash in a kitchen with a body: Tash's mum's boyfriend, who is dead, or seems dead. Comic body-disposal attempts follow (wheelie bins, a Sainsbury's trolley). The twist: he's not dead, just very drunk and concussed. The real crime is something else, and the friendship is tested. - **B:** The text comes from a girl who died last month. The narrator and friends investigate, uncovering that the dead girl's sister is sending messages to flush out who was responsible. It's darker, with grief at its core. - **C:** Assassins game spiral. Each "kill" is marked with 🩸, then real injuries start happening. Maybe it's too thriller-ish. - **D:** The pact, but the "terrible thing" is ambiguous. Tash has hit a badger (or a swan, which belongs to the King!) with her brother's car, while unlicensed. There's comedy in the escalating panic about treason. The dark undercurrent is that Tash was driving away from something at home. The comedy is the swan; the darkness is the home life. **Story beats (rough over 8 chapters):** 1. Midnight text. Establish the voice, the pact's origin (Year 7 sleepover, blood oath with a compass that got infected), and the narrator's decision to go. 2. Sneaking out, recruiting Dev, and the journey through the sleeping town, with comic obstacles. 3. Arrival and the reveal of the "terrible thing." Horror meets comedy. 4. Planning and disposal. Bad ideas, Google searches they'll regret ("how long does it take for a swan to"), and the first complication. 5. A midpoint twist that reframes things: the body isn't what they thought, or something is off with Tash's story. 6. Confrontation and truth. The real terrible thing emerges (the abuse at home, a secret, or guilt). 7. Climax at dawn: police, a parent, a chase, a reckoning. 8. Aftermath. Friendship redefined, one final darkly comic sting, maybe a new 🩸 text. **Pacing:** Around 1000 words per chapter means tight scenes, one or two per chapter. Open fast. Chapters should end on hooks. Humour should come through the voice rather than slapstick overload. # Reflection The pact idea is the strongest engine. It explains why a teenager would get out of bed at midnight for three emojis, it gives instant backstory and stakes (loyalty, "no questions"), and it's inherently comic because it was invented by eleven-year-olds and taken deadly seriously. It also lets the prompt's image, the three blood drops, carry both childish melodrama and real menace. The "dead girl's phone" idea is compelling but tips toward thriller and grief drama. It would be hard to keep comic without seeming callous, and at 8,000 words the mystery machinery could swamp the voice. The Assassins game has the same problem, plus it's a well-worn setup. The hamster/pet version is funny but too low-stakes to sustain eight chapters unless something darker is layered underneath. Blending A and D feels promising. The farcical surface, a body in the kitchen or a swan in the boot, gives set pieces for comedy. Underneath, the real "terrible thing" can be about Tash's life: why she was out, why she called the narrator and not anyone else, and the narrator's guilt at having drifted away. That gives the ending emotional weight without betraying the tone. The swan belonging to the King is very British and very funny, but a human "body" gives higher stakes and a better midpoint twist when he turns out to be alive. Perhaps both: a wrong-footing early reveal, then escalation. I should be careful not to overstuff; one central "body" problem is probably cleaner. The stepdad or mum's-boyfriend angle risks heaviness. Handled with restraint, though, it's authentic to YA and gives the dark in "darkly comic." It works best if the violence is implied and past, with Tash's action self-defence or accidental, so readers stay on her side. The comedy must never mock the victim, only the absurd logistics and the teenagers' incompetence. Dev as a deadpan third voice is useful for rhythm. Dialogue with three people bounces better than two, and he can be the moral compass who is also ridiculous. The older brother with the Corsa is a handy device for transport and complications, but might be one character too many. Structurally, the midpoint twist (he's alive, or it's not who they thought) is essential to stop the disposal comedy going stale. The dawn climax gives a natural time frame: one night, midnight to sunrise, which is tight and propulsive. The ending should circle back to the emoji. A final text, lighter or ominous, would give a satisfying bookend and a comic sting. Voice is the make-or-break element. A first-person narrator with a crime-podcast obsession could frame everything as "episodes," but that might get gimmicky. Better to use it sparingly, as a joke that pays off when reality proves unlike true crime.

# Intention **The core idea:** An old childhood pact, set off for the first time, pulls three sixteen-year-olds into one long night that begins as farce and ends as reckoning. The story runs from midnight to dawn. The comedy comes from the logistics: incompetent teenagers, bad Google searches, a supermarket trolley. The darkness comes from what is underneath: a friend in danger at home, and the narrator's guilt at having drifted away just when she was needed. **Plot choices:** - **The pact.** In Year 7, three friends swore a blood oath using a compass. Josie's finger went septic. The rule: 🩸🩸🩸 means "I've done something terrible. Come now. No questions." In five years, nobody has ever used it. - **The "body."** Gary is Tash's mum's boyfriend. Tash's mum is away on a hen do in Magaluf. Gary came home drunk and went for Tash, and she hit him with a knock-off Le Creuset casserole dish. He is on the kitchen lino, bleeding, and they believe he is dead. - **Midpoint twist.** Gary is alive. He groans mid-disposal, while wedged in a Morrisons trolley under a duvet. This kills the disposal farce before it goes stale and turns the question from "how do we hide this?" to "what do we do now?" - **The real terrible thing.** Tonight was not the first time Gary hurt Tash. She never told anyone, fearing care or her mum choosing him. Josie missed the signs because she has spent months ignoring Tash's messages for her shiny new sixth-form-application friends. - **Resolution.** Tash is legally and morally in the right. The violence is implied and past, and her act was self-defence. The ending is honest (police, an ambulance, an adult who listens) without being preachy. - **Bookend.** The story opens with Josie misreading the text as a period joke and closes with another midnight 🩸🩸🩸 that actually is one. The emoji is reclaimed as friendship rather than emergency. **Characters (kept deliberately tight):** - **Josie Pike (narrator), 16, Year 11.** She is anxious, sardonic and self-dramatising, and considers herself "the sensible one." She hosts a true-crime podcast with eleven listeners, four of whom are her nan. Her arc runs from treating life as content to showing up for real. - **Tash Doyle.** Chaotic and magnetic, she hides everything behind jokes. Her bravado cracks slowly across the night. - **Dev Mistry.** Deadpan and gentle, he pedantically corrects grammar in a crisis, carries a Nando's card like ID, and turns out to be the moral compass. He supplies the story's rhythm and its best lines. - **Gary.** He is never humanised as a joke; the jokes are about the situation, not his cruelty. He is mostly unconscious, and briefly menacing when awake. - **Supporting cast.** PCSO Barbara, weary and kind, and Josie's mum, too online and ultimately solid. The older brother is cut. **Setting:** Haverstoke, a fictional flat, grey commuter town on the Essex fringe. It has a canal, a 24-hour Tesco Express, a bus shelter with a cracked Perspex panel, and a Greggs that serves as the story's moral centre. **Voice and style:** - First person and past tense, with an immediate, confessional feel. - British texture throughout: mocks, WhatsApp, Year 11, "our Gary," nan, lino and Wotsits. I will avoid Americanisms entirely. - Humour will come mainly from the voice: specific, observational and self-deprecating. Short punchy paragraphs, with occasional one-line zingers at chapter ends. - The podcast gimmick is used sparingly, three or four times. Josie narrates "episode intros" in her head, and the final one is abandoned because real life isn't content. - Every chapter ends on a hook. **Aims:** Laugh-then-wince tonal shifts; genuine warmth in the friendship; the dark moments landing quietly. **Things to avoid:** - Mocking abuse, and gore beyond a comic-grim level. - Tash being wrong or punished for defending herself. - Too many characters, or thriller machinery. - A saccharine ending. - The pact feeling contrived. It must be seeded early and feel childish yet sacred. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1: 🩸🩸🩸 (00:04)** - Josie is awake revising, or rather watching murder documentaries, when the text arrives from Tash. - She first assumes it's a period joke and nearly replies "gross." Then she remembers the Year 7 pact: the compass, the septic finger, Dev insisting on an antiseptic wipe. - We establish that Josie and Tash have drifted. Scrolling up shows three weeks of Tash's unanswered messages ("u alive?", "need to talk", "nvm"). - She sends "??" and gets back only: "pact. now." - Hook: Josie's phone lights up with Dev: "Did you get it too?" **Chapter 2: The Sensible One (00:20)** - Josie sneaks out past her mum, who is asleep with an eye mask and Prosecco-scented breath. She climbs out over the conservatory roof and loses a slipper. - She meets Dev at the bus shelter. He is wearing a cagoule "in case of evidence." - They walk through sleeping Haverstoke, speculating about what Tash has done. Theories: arson, a stolen Deliveroo moped, a Bumble date gone wrong. Dev corrects Josie's "less" to "fewer." - Josie delivers a podcast intro in her head ("Episode One: The Summons"). - Hook: Tash opens the door in a Primark onesie spattered red, holding a casserole dish. "I think I've killed Gary." **Chapter 3: Lino (00:41)** - The kitchen: Gary on the floor, a head wound, a smashed dish and a spilled Chinese takeaway. - The horror and comedy tangle. Josie freezes. Dev checks for a pulse using a tutorial he remembers from Scouts, gets confused, and pronounces him "probably quite dead." - Tash's story comes out in fragments, with jokes deflecting the truth: "he was being a knob, I was being a knob, casserole happened." - Invoking "no questions," Tash refuses to call the police. Mum would never forgive her. - Hook: Josie realises she is already calculating what to do with him, and that frightens her more than the body. **Chapter 4: How Long Does It Take (01:30)** - The disposal farce, built from terrible ideas: the wheelie bin (it's bin day, and the bin men would notice), the canal, and Dev's grim knowledge of lime. - They trade search-history jokes ("how heavy is an average man," "can Google see incognito"). - They fetch an abandoned Morrisons trolley and wrestle Gary into it under a Frozen duvet. - The first complication: a passing drunk hen party of middle-aged women (a parallel to Tash's absent mum) cheers them on, thinking it's a stag prank. - Hook: on the canal towpath, the duvet groans. **Chapter 5: Not Dead (02:15)** - Gary is alive and semi-conscious, mumbling. - Relief comes first, then a new panic: now he'll know. There is a comic argument about whether it's "worse or better" that he's alive. Dev: "Objectively better. Legally better. Emotionally, I'm conflicted." - As Gary mumbles something vicious at Tash, Josie sees Tash flinch. It is an old flinch, not a new one. - Josie notices yellowed bruises on Tash's arm, the kind that aren't from tonight. - Hook: Josie finally asks the question the pact forbids: "Tash, how long?" **Chapter 6: No Questions (02:50)** - The emotional core. They park the trolley by a lock and sit on a bench while Gary snores and bleeds mildly. - Tash admits the truth: months of it. She messaged Josie, and Josie never answered. She didn't tell Dev because he'd tell an adult. - There is a raw argument. Josie is defensive about her new life, then shattered. - The humour thins but doesn't vanish; Tash's jokes become brave rather than evasive. Dev says the pact never said "no answers." - Josie abandons a podcast intro mid-sentence. - Hook: Gary is gone from the trolley. **Chapter 7: Dawn, Towpath (04:40)** - A tense, darkly comic chase. Gary staggers toward Tash's house, threatening to say she attacked him and to "tell your mum everything." - The confrontation happens on the towpath or at the lock gates. Gary lunges and slips. He ends up in the canal, which is only waist-deep, flailing in shopping trolleys and indignity. - Josie does the sensible thing at last: she calls 999, and then her own mum. - PCSO Barbara arrives on a bike, then the ambulance. Josie tells the truth for Tash, and Tash lets her. - Hook: Josie's mum arrives in a dressing gown and one Ugg, and Tash starts crying for the first time. **Chapter 8: 🩸 (Some Weeks Later)** - The aftermath. Gary has been charged. Tash's mum came home sunburnt and devastated, and chose Tash. For now, Tash is staying in Josie's box room. - Josie deletes the podcast episode draft. - The friendship is rebuilt imperfectly: Greggs sausage rolls, mock exams, the scar on Josie's finger. - The final beat comes after midnight: 🩸🩸🩸 from Tash, sent from the next room. Josie panics, then reads the follow-up: "not pact. actual period. u got any tampons x". Dev replies in the group chat: "This is a misuse of an emergency protocol." - Josie gets up and brings them anyway.

Model Output:
# How a Human Might Approach This A human writer given "The text came just after midnight: 🩸🩸🩸" with the brief "darkly comic British YA" would probably not start with a structure. They'd start with a voice, a line, or a memory: the actual feeling of your phone buzzing at midnight when you're sixteen, the specific dread and thrill of it. They'd probably draw on something real: a friend who went quiet, a group chat in-joke that outlived its meaning, the particular smell of a mate's kitchen. The emoji would stay concrete and a bit stupid, because teenagers use emojis stupidly. A human writing darkly comic British fiction also tends to be *meaner* than an LLM. They trust the reader to handle a character being unlikeable, a joke landing badly, or a situation staying unresolved. British comedy especially runs on understatement, awkwardness, class detail, and people failing to say what they mean. It rarely explains its own jokes and almost never lets characters articulate their emotional arcs out loud. A human would also be less tidy. They'd let the plot wobble. They might write a scene where nothing much happens because the characters are funny together. They'd pick one or two details and lean on them hard rather than scattering "British texture" like confetti. And they'd let the ending cost something. # Telltale LLM Tendencies (General) 1. **Safety and moral hygiene.** Protagonists are fundamentally good, wrongdoing is always justified, adults turn out reliable, and the "right" thing (call the police, tell an adult) is rewarded. The story becomes a PSA. 2. **Wrapping it up with a bow.** Every thread is resolved, every relationship repaired, the villain punished, and a closing image mirrors the opening "for resonance." 3. **Checklist texture.** Cultural markers are listed rather than lived: Greggs, Primark, Prosecco, Tesco Express, Nando's. It reads like a tourist's idea of Britain. 4. **Quirk-as-character.** Characters are defined by one gimmick (the pedant, the chaotic one, the podcast girl) rather than contradictions. 5. **Articulated emotions.** Characters explain their feelings in clean, therapised language ("I didn't tell you because I was scared you'd choose them"). Real teenagers deflect, get it wrong, or say something unrelated. 6. **Symmetrical structure.** Midpoint twist, dark night, climax at dawn, epilogue. It's competent but predictable, and readers feel the scaffolding. 7. **Jokes that are "quirky" rather than funny.** Zany similes, pop-culture name-drops, a character "correcting grammar during a crisis." These are joke *shapes* without actual punchlines. 8. **Overwriting.** Lyrical imagery at emotional peaks, triads, and sentences built to impress rather than move. 9. **Dialogue that's too good.** Every line is a quip, everyone is equally witty, and nobody mishears, trails off, or talks over each other. 10. **The sanitised darkness.** Abuse or violence is gestured at through "yellowed bruises" and "an old flinch," stock signifiers that let the story feel serious without being specific. 11. **The epiphany.** The narrator learns a Lesson and states it, or performs it symbolically (deleting the podcast). 12. **Ending on a cute callback line.** "This is a misuse of an emergency protocol." It's neat and applause-baiting. # Deep Dive: Critiquing the Intention & Plan ## 1. The story is morally *too* safe The plan explicitly states "Tash being wrong or punished for defending herself" as something to avoid, and makes her act clean self-defence against a clearly evil man. This is the classic LLM move: construct a scenario where the characters can do something shocking (try to dump a body) without any moral taint. It defuses the "dark" in darkly comic. - The funniest and darkest part of the premise is that three kids *genuinely decided to hide a body*. The plan hurries to exonerate them via "he's alive" and "he was abusive." A human writer might let that decision sit longer and be more uncomfortable. How quickly and how practically did they agree? Josie realising she's "already calculating" is a good seed, but it's resolved too cleanly. - Could Tash's account be less reliable? Not that she's lying about abuse, but the night might be messier: she was also drunk, she'd been winding him up, or she hit him twice. Moral mess doesn't have to mean victim-blaming; it means she's a person. ## 2. The abuse storyline risks being a Very Special Episode "Months of it," "yellowed bruises," "old flinch," "she messaged Josie and Josie never answered." It's the most generic possible version of this reveal, and it tips the story from dark comedy into issue novel at exactly the moment (Chapter 6) where the comedy should be earning its keep. - A human might keep Gary's awfulness more specific and less cartoonish: petty, controlling, pathetic rather than monstrous. He eats her food, reads her post, calls her "princess," and turns the Wi-Fi off. Those details are both funnier and more chilling. - The bruises are a stock signifier. What would Josie *actually* notice? Maybe something she'd already seen and explained away: Tash always wearing a hoodie at Josie's house, never wanting to go home, a lock on her bedroom door. - Would the reveal happen as a heartfelt bench confession? More likely it comes sideways, in a joke that isn't one, or Dev states it flatly because he figured it out months ago. ## 3. Josie's arc is an LLM-shaped Lesson "From treating life as content to showing up for real." "Deletes the podcast episode draft." "Abandons a podcast intro mid-sentence." This is very tidy symbolic growth. The podcast is a device installed to be removed. - Either make the podcast funnier and more embarrassing (her nan's reviews, a sponsorship from a local carpet shop), or drop it. As is, it's a thematic prop. - What if Josie doesn't fully learn? Perhaps she still, deep down, thinks it would make a great episode, and hates herself a bit. That's more human and more darkly comic. - Her guilt about ignoring Tash is valid, but "new sixth-form-application friends" is vague. Who are they? What did Josie get from them that Tash couldn't give? The drifting should be understandable, even sympathetic, not just a sin to atone for. ## 4. The ending is wrapped with a bow, twice Gary charged, Mum chooses Tash, Tash moves in, friendship rebuilt, podcast deleted, Greggs, and a cute callback text with a Dev punchline. It's a double bow. - Real outcomes are messier. Gary gets bail. Mum hasn't decided. Mum *does* choose Tash but blames her a bit too. Tash doesn't want to live with Josie and goes to her auntie in Chelmsford. The friendship is changed but not "rebuilt." - The period-emoji bookend is clever on paper but sitcom-neat. It also slightly undercuts the opening misread by making it the joke's destination. Consider whether the final beat should be quieter, or odder, or less on-the-nose. - "Josie gets up and brings them anyway" is a warm, safe closing gesture. Could the ending sting a bit more? Or end before the aftermath altogether, at dawn, with things unresolved? ## 5. The adults are too reliable PCSO Barbara, "weary and kind"; Mum, "too online and ultimately solid"; an ambulance; the system works. This is reassuring YA-PSA territory. - In darkly comic British fiction, adults are often useless, absent, or mortifying. The police might not believe them at first. Mum might be more concerned about the conservatory roof. The PCSO could be twenty-two and panicking. - Solid adults aren't wrong, but they shouldn't be the resolution. The kids should still be doing most of the work, and adult help should feel partial. ## 6. The British texture is a checklist Greggs, Morrisons, Tesco Express, Primark onesie, Prosecco, Magaluf hen do, Nando's card, Uggs, Wotsits, Corsa, lino, nan, "knob." That's a lot of branding, and together it reads like an AI proving it knows what Britain is. - Pick fewer and make them work harder. One brand used repeatedly and meaningfully (the knock-off Le Creuset is good because it's a status joke *and* the weapon) beats ten namechecks. - British humour is less about brands and more about tone: understatement ("bit of a situation"), class anxiety, politeness in absurd circumstances (apologising to a corpse), and passive aggression. - The dialect is generic. Where exactly is Haverstoke? "Essex fringe" is vague. Would these characters say "innit," "well bad," or "our Gary"? "Our Gary" is Northern, and that clashes with Essex. That's a small tell of assembled rather than lived detail. ## 7. Dev is a quirk, not a person A deadpan pedant who carries a Nando's card, corrects grammar mid-crisis, and wears a cagoule "in case of evidence." Every trait is a joke-delivery mechanism. His lines in the plan ("Objectively better. Legally better. Emotionally, I'm conflicted." "This is a misuse of an emergency protocol.") are AI-comedy: tidy, rhythmic, quotable. - What does Dev want? Why does he come? Maybe he's always been slightly in love with one of them, or he's desperate to be needed, or he has his own home stuff. - The grammar-correcting gag is overused in fiction generally. Replace it with something more particular. - Let him be wrong, cowardly, or annoying at some point. Maybe he wants to leave. Maybe he threatens to call his dad. Maybe *he's* the one most willing to hide the body, which would be a good dark joke. ## 8. The structure is textbook Midnight inciting incident, sneak out, reveal, farce, midpoint twist, dark night of the soul, climax at dawn, epilogue. Each chapter has a neat timestamp and a hook. It's efficient but feels engineered. - Timestamps in every chapter title are a tidy, clever-looking device. Maybe keep them, but let the chapters bleed and vary in shape. - Not every chapter needs a cliffhanger. Mandatory hooks create a relentless, thriller rhythm that fights the comedy. Some chapters could end on a flat, funny, or sad note. - The farce is compressed into one chapter (Ch 4) and resolved by a groan. A human might let the farce run longer and get more absurd, since that's the story's selling point, and compress the emotional stuff. ## 9. The set-pieces are stock The trolley, the Frozen duvet, the drunk hen party, the canal, Gary falling in the water. They're all fine but familiar: they could come from any British comedy. The hen party as a "parallel to Tash's absent mum" is a thematic rhyme that feels planned. - Look for stranger, more specific obstacles. A neighbour walking a dog at 1 a.m. who wants to chat. A Deliveroo driver who has definitely seen them. Tash's little brother waking up. Gary's phone ringing constantly with a name like "Big Steve." - Gary slipping into a waist-deep canal is a slapstick resolution to the climax: the villain is humiliated by gravity, not dealt with by the characters. It lets them off the hook. ## 10. The "no questions" rule is underused The pact's "no questions" clause is potentially the best thematic engine. It holds friendship as unconditional loyalty versus friendship as actually asking. The plan uses it once as a hook ("Tash, how long?"). That's the right idea, but it could thread through more: Dev asks questions constantly and gets told off, and Josie's failure over the months *was* a failure to ask. ## 11. Voice is described, not yet found "Anxious, sardonic, self-dramatising" is generic YA-narrator. What makes Josie's voice *hers*? Her specific obsessions, her verbal tics, what she notices that others wouldn't, what she lies to herself about. The plan hasn't pinned down anything distinctive about how she thinks. # Brainstorming Ideas to Make It More Human **On moral mess:** - Let them get further with the disposal before discovering he's alive. They make real, irreversible choices: they've wiped the kitchen, lied to a neighbour, and posted in a group chat. - Let one friend be genuinely, disturbingly good at it. The comedy is in how quickly competence arrives. - After Gary's alive, have a brief, awful moment where someone suggests, half-joking, that they could still put him in the canal. Nobody laughs, and nobody says no right away. - Tash hit him more than once. She doesn't feel sorry. Josie finds that frightening and understandable. **On Gary and the darkness:** - Make his menace domestic and specific: he renamed the Wi-Fi, he keeps the heating off, he has a mug that says "World's Best Stepdad" he bought himself. - Drop the bruises. Let Josie realise from accumulated small wrongnesses she can suddenly see. - Keep it ambiguous how far it went; the reader doesn't need a full inventory. - Let Gary awake be pathetic as well as scary. He cries, he wants his mum, and that's somehow worse. **On Josie:** - Give her one strange, specific obsession instead of the podcast, or make the podcast mortifying and keep it as flavour, not arc. - Let her guilt be complicated: she ignored Tash partly because Tash was exhausting, and she's allowed to have been a bit right about that. - Let her not quite get the redemptive moment. Maybe Tash doesn't forgive her by the end, or forgives her too easily, which is worse. - Find her verbal habits: lists, a way of rating things, thinking in exam-mark-scheme language because it's mock season. **On Dev:** - Give him a reason to be there that's not just loyalty: he's lonely, or he's the one who invented the pact and has quietly wanted it used for five years. - Let him be the practical, slightly frightening one. - Replace grammar pedantry with something personal, like narrating what his mum would say, or bringing snacks compulsively. - Let him have a moment of real anger at Josie for dropping Tash, because he didn't. **On the adults and ending:** - The police are slow, sceptical, or bureaucratic. The PCSO asks if they've "tried talking to him." - Mum isn't solid in a heroic way; she's solid in an annoying way, bringing a flask and a cardigan and saying the wrong thing. - Tash's mum's reaction is left unresolved or ambivalent. - End at dawn, or shortly after, without a neat epilogue. If there's a coda, keep it small and a bit sad-funny rather than warm. - Reconsider the period bookend. If kept, flatten it: no Dev zinger, and maybe Josie doesn't find it funny yet. **On texture and voice:** - Pare back brands to a handful that recur and mean something (the knock-off Le Creuset is a keeper). - Nail the geography and dialect: an Essex-ish town with estuary speech patterns, and no stray Northernisms. - Lean on British understatement and politeness in horror: apologising to Gary's unconscious body, offering a cup of tea at the crime scene, worrying about the neighbours. - Let dialogue be messier: interruptions, mishearing, people saying "what?" a lot, and jokes that don't land that the others ignore. **On structure:** - Let the farce breathe across two chapters; compress the confession. - Vary chapter endings: some hooks, some flat, and at least one that ends on a small, sad observation. - Consider an out-of-order element, such as opening with a flash-forward to the canal or a police interview, but only if it serves the voice. - Remove any thematic rhyme that feels designed (the hen party mirroring Tash's mum) unless it can be made genuinely surprising. **On prose:** - Keep sentences plain. Josie is funny, not lyrical. No sunrise-as-metaphor-for-hope at the climax. - Resist making every line a quip. Let silence and awkward pauses do work. - Avoid characters explaining their feelings in full sentences. Let the most important things go half-said.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **Core idea.** "The text came just after midnight: 🩸🩸🩸." The story lives and dies on that text: what it means, who sent it, and what three sixteen-year-olds are willing to do because of it. In Year 7 they made a pact. Three blood drops means *I've done something terrible. Come now. No questions.* Nobody has used it in five years. Tonight Tash does, and Josie and Dev spend the hours between midnight and dawn finding out what the pact actually asks of them. The comedy is in their incompetence and how quickly it turns into competence. The darkness is in that too. **What the story is really about.** The "no questions" clause. At eleven it sounded like loyalty. At sixteen it turns out to be the problem. Josie stopped asking Tash anything months ago, and the pact gives her permission to keep not asking even while she helps drag a man across a car park. The story's turn is Josie breaking the rule, and discovering that asking is harder and later than it should have been. **Plot choices (revised):** - **Gary.** Tash's mum's boyfriend of eighteen months. His menace is petty, domestic and specific. He renamed the Wi-Fi "GARYS HOUSE GARYS RULES". He put a padlock on the thermostat and keeps a shelf in the fridge labelled with his name. He calls Tash "madam." He has hurt her before, but the story never inventories it. We see the house, and that is enough. - **The act.** Tash's mum is away at her sister's in Clacton; it's an ordinary weekend, not a sitcom hen do. Gary came in drunk. Tash hit him with the knock-off Le Creuset (Dunelm, orange, her mum's pride), and she hit him twice. She says "once" at first. The second blow is the thing Josie can't stop thinking about. - **Moral mess.** The disposal runs across two chapters, and the kids make real choices. They bleach the lino. Josie lies to a neighbour's face. Dev turns out to be calmly, alarmingly good at it. When Gary turns out to be alive, Dev says quietly that the canal is still right there. Nobody laughs, and nobody says no for a few seconds too long. That silence is the darkest beat in the story, and it is not resolved with a speech. - **Tash is not a saint.** She's funny, exhausting and sometimes cruel to Josie. She isn't sorry about Gary. The story is on her side without laundering her. - **Adults are partial.** The police are slow. A young PC asks, not unkindly, whether Tash "could have just gone to her room." Josie's mum is useful in an annoying way: flask, cardigan, wrong things said, but she turns up. Tash's mum is ambivalent and unresolved: she's on the phone, crying, asking what Tash *did*. - **Ending.** No bow. Gary is arrested for the assault on Tash after her statement, but he's also a man with a head injury and a solicitor, and nothing is certain. Tash goes to her auntie's in Southend, not into Josie's box room. The friendship is changed, not repaired. The final beat returns to the emoji, quietly. **Characters:** - **Josie Pike (narrator).** Sixteen and mid-mocks, she thinks in mark schemes ("this would get a Level 2 at best: some awareness of consequences"). She's the "sensible one," which mostly means cowardly. She drifted from Tash not out of snobbery but because Tash was hard work and new friends were easy. That's a sympathetic reason and still a failure. She never gets a clean epiphany. At one point she thinks, and hates herself for thinking, that this will be a great story one day. - **Tash Doyle.** Loud, quick, a liar about small things, with jokes that are sometimes load-bearing. She refuses to be anyone's project. She is furious with Josie and doesn't say so until she does, badly. - **Dev Mistry.** He invented the pact and brought the compass. He has quietly wanted it used for five years because it means he's needed. He's a compulsive snack-bringer (his mum's influence) and very practical. He's the one who kept messaging Tash after Josie stopped, so he knew more than he let on. His anger at Josie is the story's sharpest confrontation. His quirk serves the character, not the other way round: he brings snacks because he doesn't know what else to do with love. - **Gary.** Mostly unconscious. When awake, he is pathetic and frightening at once. He cries and asks for Tash's mum, then calls Tash "madam" in the same breath. **Setting.** Stanbridge, a fictional Essex new town near Basildon: roundabouts, a retail park, a flood-relief channel (the "canal" everyone calls it) behind the Asda, and an underpass everyone avoids. The speech is estuary: "well," "innit" sparingly, "proper," "mental." There are no Northernisms. Brands are pared right back: the Dunelm casserole dish (recurring), an Asda trolley (recurring), and little else. **Voice and style:** - First person, past tense, plain sentences. Josie is funny through precision and understatement, not zany similes. - British comedy comes from politeness in horror: apologising to an unconscious man, Dev offering Gary a Frube, worrying the neighbours will hear the trolley wheels. - Dialogue is messy. People interrupt, mishear, say "what?", and make jokes that die and are ignored. Not everyone is witty all the time. - Feelings stay half-said. The confession comes out sideways and incomplete. - Chapter endings vary: some hooks, some flat, one sad. - Timestamps appear as chapter titles only; it's a light device. **Avoid:** - A PSA tone, stock abuse signifiers (bruises, flinches), and therapised dialogue. - A deleted-podcast-style symbolic Lesson, and a cute zinger ending. - Gravity resolving the climax for them. - A checklist of Britishness. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1: 00:03** - Open on the text itself. Josie is in bed, not revising, halfway through a YouTube video about Victorian arsenic. The phone buzzes: Tash, 🩸🩸🩸. - Her first thought is that it's a period joke, and she types "gross" before stopping. Her thumb hovers. - She remembers the pact in quick, funny, specific memory: Dev's compass, the "oath" scripted on a Pukka Pad, and Josie's finger going septic and needing antibiotics. Her mum still brings it up. - She scrolls up. Her last reply to Tash was in October. Below it sit Tash's messages: a TikTok, "u coming saturday", "josie", "ok". There's nothing heavy, which makes it worse. - She replies "??". The reply comes: "no questions. thats the rule." - End flat and wry. Josie gets dressed and puts on her school coat because it's the only dark one she owns: "Looking back, I'd dressed for a funeral or a detention, and I'd been to more detentions." **Chapter 2: 00:26** - Josie creeps out. It isn't a conservatory-roof caper; the back door just squeaks, and her mum shouts "Jose?" in her sleep. Josie freezes on one foot for a whole minute. - She meets Dev under the flickering light by the underpass. He's brought a carrier bag of snacks and a head torch. He's weirdly happy. "Five years," he says. She realises he's been waiting for this. - On the walk, their theories are Dev's grim ones against Josie's hopeful-stupid ones: she's broken her mum's telly, she's shaved her head. Dev mentions, too casually, that he still talks to Tash. Josie doesn't ask, and notices herself not asking. - They reach Tash's house on the close. The Wi-Fi network pops up on Josie's phone: GARYS HOUSE GARYS RULES. - Tash opens the door holding the orange casserole dish. She's in a Stanbridge Swimming Club hoodie with something dark down the front. "Right," she says. "Don't be weird about it." **Chapter 3: 00:40** - The kitchen. Gary is face-down on the lino between the fridge and the bin. There's a doner kebab everywhere and blood that looks wrong, too dark and too much. - Josie's body does stupid things: she apologises to Gary, and she notices the fridge labels. - Dev checks for a pulse at the wrist, then the neck, then gives up and says, "I don't know how, actually. I thought I'd know." That's funny and frightening together. - Tash tells it fast and jokey: "He was being a knob, I told him he was a knob, he did a thing, I did the casserole." Josie asks "How many times?" Tash says "Once." Later, in Chapter 6, it becomes "twice." - Tash won't call anyone. Her mum. Care. "No questions. You swore." Dev, very quietly: "We did swear." - End on dread. Josie realises she's already thinking about the neighbours, the bins and the CCTV on the Asda car park, and not about Gary at all. **Chapter 4: 01:15** - Farce, part one. Dev becomes horribly practical. He bleaches the lino using YouTube knowledge from a show his dad watches, and he puts the kebab in a bag "so it looks normal." - They discuss the options. The wheelie bin is out because it's bin day. Josie's contribution, "we could just leave?", gets ignored. - They search the internet on Tash's phone because "it's already ruined." The searches are grim and funny: how heavy is a man, and does the flood channel go to the sea. - Josie fetches an Asda trolley from the verge by the bus stop. - Getting Gary in is a long, clumsy, undignified set piece: an arm won't cooperate, and Dev says "sorry, Gary" and means it. They cover him with Tash's old Minions duvet. - End on a flat note. Tash sits on the back step and eats one of Dev's Frubes while the other two stand panting. She says it's the first time the kitchen's been quiet in a year. **Chapter 5: 01:50** - Farce, part two, darker. They push the trolley along the close. Every wheel sounds like a scream. - A neighbour, Mr Okafor, is out in slippers walking an ancient Staffie that won't wee. He wants to chat. Josie lies to his face ("it's for a Duke of Edinburgh thing") and is sickeningly good at it. The dog sniffs the duvet for a long time. - Along the path behind the Asda, the retail-park lights go off one by one. - At the flood channel, the duvet moves. Gary groans, then says Tash's mum's name. - Relief, then worse. Dev stands by the water and says, not joking, "It's still right there, though." Nobody laughs. Nobody says no. Josie counts four seconds. - Tash says "don't" at last, but to Dev or to herself isn't clear. End there. **Chapter 6: 02:30** - They sit on the concrete lip of the channel with the trolley braked against a bench. Gary drifts in and out, crying a bit. - The truth comes sideways. Dev starts it by snapping at Josie: "You don't get to look shocked. You stopped answering." It's the story's real fight. Josie defends herself. Tash was a lot, and she was allowed a life. Dev says, "Yeah. She was a lot. That was the point." - Tash, bored of being talked about, fills in pieces without a speech: the thermostat, the lock on her bedroom door that she fitted herself with a YouTube video, the fact that she was sleeping at Dev's on weekends and Josie never knew. "It was twice," she says. "The casserole. It was twice." She isn't sorry. - Josie breaks the pact. She asks a real question at last, "Why me? Why text me?", and Tash doesn't answer it properly. "You're the sensible one. And I wanted to see if you'd come." - End sad. Josie realises she'd have been more use in October. **Chapter 7: 04:10** - Gary gets out of the trolley while they aren't looking and staggers off towards the close, bleeding, shouting that Tash tried to kill him and he'll tell her mum everything. He's frightening and pathetic in equal measure: he falls over the kerb and gets up crying. - It isn't a slapstick canal fall. Tash goes after him, and Josie grabs her. Dev stands between them and Gary with his carrier bag like a shield. - Josie rings 999, and it's awful and ordinary. She's put on hold for eleven seconds. She rings her mum next. - A patrol car arrives first. The young PC is sceptical and asks the terrible question about going to her room. It's Josie who tells it, all of it, including the bleach, the trolley and the four seconds, while Tash stares at her. She's telling on all of them, and it's the first loyal thing she's done in months. - Josie's mum pulls up in her dressing gown with the car still in second gear, holding a flask of tea for no one. She says "I knew that finger was a bad sign," and hugs Tash first. **Chapter 8: 00:07, Three Weeks Later** - The aftermath is compressed and unresolved. Gary was arrested at the hospital, is out on bail, and has a solicitor. The bleach is a problem for the three of them; there were words like "caution" and a lot of parents in a lot of rooms. Tash's mum rang Tash every day for a week, then less. Tash is at her auntie's in Southend with a new school and no casserole dish. - Josie did her mocks and got a 6 in English Language. She hasn't told anyone that she wrote the whole night down in the back of her revision book, and that she's ashamed of how good it is. - Dev and Josie are fine, carefully. He still brings snacks. - It's just after midnight. Josie types 🩸🩸🩸 to Tash, deletes it, and types it again. She sends it, then adds: "not a pact. nothing happened. just checking it still works." - There's no reply. She falls asleep holding the phone. - Last lines: the morning message from Tash, 07:48, "was asleep you absolute weirdo". Then, after a gap, "it works". Josie doesn't reply straight away. She gets up, goes to school, and answers at break. That's the whole change: she answers.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Josie Pike **Background.** Josie is sixteen and in Year 11 at Stanbridge Academy (formerly Stanbridge Comprehensive; the sign still has the old name showing through the vinyl). She lives with her mum, Karen, in a two-bed semi on the Brookfield estate, a ten-minute walk from Tash's close. Her dad lives in Colchester with his girlfriend and a Cockapoo called Biscuit. She sees him every other Sunday and they go to the same Harvester. There's no drama there, just a slow politeness that she finds harder than a row would be. She met Tash on the first day of Year 7, when Tash stole her pencil case as a joke and then got so involved in the joke that she kept it for a week. Dev came as part of the package because he sat next to Tash in form. **Personality.** Josie calls herself "the sensible one." What that mostly means is that she's frightened of consequences and has turned the fear into a personality. She's clever in a revision-guide way, very good at knowing what the examiner wants and less good at knowing what she wants. She's funny, but privately. Her best jokes happen in her head, and she only says about a third of them out loud. She's an observer and a noticer of small things. She will clock that someone's lanyard is from a different school before she notices they're crying. The narrative voice depends on this: her precision is her comedy, and it's also how she avoids feeling things. **Idiosyncrasies:** - It's mock season, so she thinks in mark schemes. "Some awareness of consequences. Level 2." She grades her own decisions, other people's excuses, and once her dad's apology. - She has a quiet obsession with historical poisoners and Victorian murder. She's watched every YouTube video about Mary Ann Cotton. It isn't a podcast or a brand; she just likes it. She doesn't tell her new friends. - She picks at the scar on her left index finger from the pact, a small white pucker. She doesn't realise she does it when she's anxious. - She says "sorry" to furniture she bumps into, and to unconscious men. - She keeps a Notes app list titled "things I should have said," which is mostly comebacks from 2021. - She can't eat in front of people she doesn't know well, so she has a flapjack in her coat pocket at all times and rarely eats it. **Flaws.** Josie is a coward who dresses it up as reasonableness. She drifted from Tash in September because Tash was exhausting: always a crisis, always late, always turning up at 11pm wanting to go to the retail park. And Josie had found Ella, Maisie and Priyanka, sixth-form-application friends who talk about personal statements and have parents who own cafetières. Being with them felt like resting. She told herself she hadn't dropped Tash. She'd just "not replied yet," for three months. She's also, quietly, a bit of a snob, and would be mortified to be told so. She's judgemental about Tash's mum's fake tan and Gary's van, and ashamed of the judgement, which she then resents Tash for making her feel. Her worst habit is turning her own experience into a story while it's still happening. She's composing sentences about the night during the night. **Physicality.** She's medium height and holds herself as if she's trying to take up less room than she does. She has straight mousy-brown hair, always in a low ponytail with a Boots scrunchie. Her face is pale, with the kind of cheeks that go blotchy red rather than blushing prettily. She bites the skin on her lower lip. Her school coat is navy, a size too big because her mum bought it "to grow into" in Year 9. It's the only dark coat she owns. She walks fast, looking at the pavement, and hates being looked at. When she's nervous she goes very still, like a rabbit, rather than fidgeting. In company, she laughs a half-second after everyone else, checking the joke is safe first. **Motives, allegiances, relationships:** - **What she wants:** to get through Year 11 with good grades and no scenes, then get into the sixth form college in Chelmsford with Ella and Maisie and become someone slightly different, someone calm. - **Tash:** Josie loves Tash the way you love weather. Tash was the most exciting thing that ever happened to her, and also the most tiring. Underneath the drift is guilt, and under the guilt is a small, ugly relief that she got out. She doesn't know yet that she was needed. - **Dev:** She's taken him for granted for five years. She assumes he'll always be there, slightly behind, holding the snacks. She has never once wondered what he does on a Saturday. - **Her mum:** They're close in a bickering way. Karen overshares on Facebook and Josie is mortified. But Josie gets into her mum's bed when there's a thunderstorm, still, and would die if anyone knew. - **Gary:** She has met him four times. She thought he was "a bit much," a man who says "alright, trouble" to teenagers. She never thought any further than that, and that's the point. **Voice:** > "I'd like to say I knew straight away what it meant. I didn't. I thought she'd started her period and wanted me to know about it, which, to be fair, was something Tash would do. I'd typed 'gross' and a vomiting emoji before I remembered the compass." > "There's a specific kind of quiet you get in a kitchen where someone's lying on the floor. It's not silence. The fridge is still going. The clock on the oven still says 00:41. Everything's just carrying on, like it hasn't been told." > "Sensible, I decided, was just a word for people who'd never been asked to do anything." > *(internal, Ch 6)* "I wanted to say I'd been busy. I had been busy. That was the worst part: it was true, and it didn't matter." --- # Tash Doyle **Background.** Tash is sixteen and lives on Harrow Close in a three-bed ex-council house with her mum, Donna, and, for the last eighteen months, Gary. Her dad left when she was four and lives in Spain doing "property," which Tash suspects means painting apartments. He sends a birthday card every other year with £20 in it and her name spelt "Tasha." Donna had Tash at nineteen. They were more like sisters for years: Tash ran the house and Donna ran the fun. They did each other's nails, ate Chinese on the sofa, and slagged off the telly. Then Donna met Gary at a fortieth in Wickford, and the house became his. Tash swims, or used to. She was county level at twelve, and the hoodie still says so. She stopped in Year 10 when the early-morning lifts became Gary's job, and she didn't want to be in the van with him. **Personality.** Tash is loud, fast, funny and exhausting, and she knows all of that and uses it. She talks in bursts and fills silences before they can fill her. She's a brilliant mimic: she can do every teacher, every Love Island contestant, and Gary, cruelly accurately. She lies about small things constantly and for no reason. She'll tell you she had toast when she had cereal. It's reflexive, a way of keeping a bit of herself back. She never lies about big things, though. She just doesn't mention them. She's generous in chaotic ways: she'll spend her last fiver buying you a milkshake and then need you to lend her bus fare. She's fiercely loyal, and she expects the same back without ever having said so. She keeps a ledger in her head and pretends she doesn't. **Idiosyncrasies:** - She calls everyone by their surname when she's annoyed. "Pike." "Mistry." Josie hasn't been "Josie" to her since November. - She cuts her own fringe with kitchen scissors, badly, and defends every cut. - She eats Super Noodles dry, from the packet, with the flavouring sprinkled on. - She has a habit of saying "Anyway" loudly to end a topic she doesn't like. - She fitted a bolt on her bedroom door herself, watching a YouTube video on her phone propped on the radiator. It's slightly wonky and she's proud of it. - She never sits with her back to a door. Nobody's noticed except Dev. - She still knows the pact oath off by heart, including the bit Dev wrote in Latin that was wrong. **Flaws.** Tash can be cruel, especially to the people she loves, and especially when she feels abandoned. She tests people: she'll make plans and cancel them to see if you'll push back. She wanted Josie to notice without being told, and she's furious that she didn't. But she never gave her a proper chance to notice, either. She refuses help on principle. Being a "situation" to be managed by teachers or social workers is her nightmare, because she's watched it happen to her cousin. She'd rather handle it herself and fail than be rescued. She isn't sorry she hit Gary. She isn't sorry she hit him twice. Some part of her wanted to, for a long time. That frightens other people more than it frightens her. **Physicality.** Tash is small and wiry with a swimmer's shoulders going soft. Her hair is dark blonde, grown out, usually in a claw clip, with the famous uneven fringe. She's always cold because the thermostat is padlocked, so she lives in the swimming club hoodie with the sleeves over her hands. She has a chipped front tooth from diving at ten and a big laugh that seems too loud for her size. She moves all the time: jiggling a knee, spinning a ring, walking backwards in front of you to talk to your face. She stands too close. She touches people's arms when making a point. When she goes still, something's wrong. **Motives, allegiances, relationships:** - **What she wants:** tonight, for someone to come. More broadly, her mum back as she was, Gary gone, and to not be anyone's project. She'd like to swim again but would never say so. - **Donna, her mum:** Tash loves her mum fiercely and is terrified that if she's made to choose, Donna will choose Gary. This fear is the engine of all her secrecy. She protects her mum from the truth as much as from anything else. - **Josie:** Tash thinks of Josie as her person. She has done since Year 7. Josie's drift felt like a door shutting in a house full of shutting doors. She sent the text to Josie as much as to Dev as a test: *will you come?* She hasn't decided whether she'll forgive her. - **Dev:** He's her secret safe place. She has slept on his bedroom floor most weekends since the summer. His mum thinks it's a sleepover thing. Tash loves Dev, but not the way he might want. She takes him for granted and knows it. - **Gary:** She is scared of him and hates that. She also despises him, which helps.
