# 00:03 The text came just after midnight: 🩸🩸🩸 I was in bed, not revising. I had my English Language paper in nine days and a revision timetable on my wall with colour-coded boxes, and the box for that evening said *Q5 descriptive writing, practise 2 x plans*, and instead I was forty minutes into a video about a woman in Liverpool in 1884 who'd poisoned three husbands with flypaper. She'd soaked the flypaper in water to get the arsenic out. It was quite clever, actually. The man narrating it had a voice like a funeral director. The phone buzzed on my duvet and I thought it would be Maisie, because Maisie sent voice notes at midnight about her personal statement, and I'd started letting them build up and listening to them all at once on double speed. It wasn't Maisie. It was Tash. Three drops of blood. Nothing else. I'd like to say I knew straight away what it meant. I didn't. I thought she'd started her period and wanted me to know about it, which, to be fair, was something Tash would do. In Year 9 she'd announced hers to a whole Geography lesson because Mr Hendry wouldn't let her go to the toilet, and he'd gone the colour of corned beef and let everyone go early. So I typed *gross* and a vomiting face, and my thumb was actually on the arrow when I remembered the compass. It was Dev's dad's compass, the proper metal kind from a geometry set, with a little screw on the hinge. We were eleven. We were in Dev's bedroom because his was the only house with a lock on the bedroom door, and Dev had read a book about the Freemasons and got very into the idea of an oath. He'd written it out on the back page of a Pukka Pad in his best handwriting. There was a line in Latin at the bottom that he said meant *blood binds us forever* and which I found out in Year 10 actually meant something closer to *the blood is tied up*. The rule was simple, because we were eleven and we thought simple meant serious. If one of us ever did something terrible, *properly* terrible, not a detention, they'd send three blood drops, and the other two had to come. Straight away. Wherever. No questions. Dev had a packet of antiseptic wipes for afterwards. I wouldn't use one, because it stung, and Tash laughed at me and called me a baby, and then she didn't use hers either, so neither of us did. Dev did. By the Wednesday my finger was twice the size of the others and hot to touch, and by the Friday I was at the walk-in centre on antibiotics, and my mum was telling the nurse, the pharmacist, and later most of her Facebook friends, that that Tash Doyle had given me blood poisoning. Tash's finger was fine. Tash's finger was always fine. I still have the scar. It's a little white pucker on the pad of my left index finger, and I was rubbing it with my thumb while I held the phone, which I only noticed later. I deleted *gross*. I deleted the vomiting face. Then I did the thing I'd been not doing for about three months, which was scroll up. The last message I'd sent Tash was on the ninth of October. It said *haha yeah maybe*. I don't know what I'd been saying maybe to. Underneath it, going down the screen, was everything she'd sent since. A TikTok of a man falling off a paddleboard. *u coming saturday* A TikTok of a cat in a Tesco. *pike* *josie* *ok* Another TikTok, in November. Then nothing for a bit. Then, at Christmas, a picture of her mum's Christmas tree, which was pink, with the caption *look at the state of this*, and I remembered seeing it and thinking I'd reply when I'd thought of something funny, and then not thinking of anything. There was nothing heavy in there. That was what I kept looking at. No *I need to talk to you*. No *please*. If there'd been something like that, I think I'd have felt worse and also better, because at least then it would have been obvious. This was just someone knocking on a door every so often, and then not. Some awareness of consequences, I thought. Level 2. Limited development. I typed *??* and sent it. The two grey ticks went blue almost immediately. She'd been sitting there with the phone in her hand. The dots came up, and went away, and came up again. I watched them for so long my screen dimmed and I had to tap it. *no questions. thats the rule* I sat there. Downstairs the boiler clicked off. The funeral director on YouTube had frozen mid-sentence with his mouth open, and behind him was a photograph of the Liverpool woman, who looked about as bothered as someone waiting for a bus. I thought about going back to sleep. I want to be honest about that. I thought quite seriously about putting the phone face down and telling her in the morning that I'd been asleep, and I think there's a version of me who did that, and who is doing very well at sixth form college in Chelmsford, and who I'd quite like to punch. Then my phone buzzed again. Dev. *Did you get it too?* I typed *yes*. *I'm leaving now. Underpass in 15?* I didn't answer him. I got up and put my jeans on over my pyjama shorts, and my trainers without socks, and then I stood in the dark in front of the wardrobe trying to decide what you wear to something terrible, and ended up putting on my school coat because it was the only dark one I owned. Looking back, I'd dressed for a funeral or a detention, and I'd been to more detentions.

I thought: this is what burglars must feel like, all the time, and I felt a bit sorry for them. Then I went. It was cold in the way January is in Stanbridge, which is damp more than anything, like the air's been left in a bag. Every house on Brookfield had its curtains shut. Someone's security light came on when I passed and I nearly apologised to it. The only sound was the A127, which you can always hear if you listen, a sort of long breath that never finishes. The underpass goes under the ring road between our estate and the retail park, and nobody uses it if they can help it, because it smells of wee and someone once found a hedgehog down there that had been set on fire. There's one light halfway along that flickers. Dev was standing under it. He had his cagoule zipped up to his chin and a head torch on, switched off, strapped over his hair like a miner. In one hand he had a Sainsbury's carrier bag, the thick kind. He was smiling. Not a lot. Dev doesn't smile a lot. But the corners had gone. "You came," he said. "You said fifteen minutes." "I know. I've been here since ten past." He held up the bag. "I brought stuff." "What stuff?" "Just stuff. Frubes. Mini Cheddars. There's a banana. I brought the flask but I didn't have time to put anything in it, so it's just a flask." He looked at it. "I don't know why I brought the flask." "Why have you got a head torch on?" "It's an emergency," he said, like that answered it, and then, because I was still looking at him, "I've had it since Year 8. I bought it with my Christmas money. For this, basically." He switched it on and a white circle landed on my chest. "Five years. I honestly thought someone would've used it by now." "Can you turn that off?" He turned it off. We started walking. Tash lives on Harrow Close, which is about a mile, past the Asda and the Carpetright and the roundabout with the sculpture on it that's meant to be a heron and looks like a coat hanger. Dev walked slightly ahead, because his legs are longer now. He shot up in Year 10 and he still walks like he hasn't been told. "What do you reckon she's done?" I said. "Don't know." "Go on, though." He thought about it. You could see him thinking; he did it with his coat toggles. "Arson," he said. "Maybe. Or she's taken someone's car. Or she's hurt someone." "She hasn't hurt someone." "You asked." "She's probably broken her mum's telly," I said. "Or she's shaved her head. Remember when she did the fringe and made us come round to tell her it was fine?" "That wasn't three drops, though. That was a normal text." "It was a bad fringe." He didn't laugh. We went past the Asda, which was still lit up inside, and there was a man on his own in there stacking yoghurts, and I watched him for a bit and envied him more than anyone I've ever envied. "She's been all right, you know," Dev said. "Mostly." He said it too casually, to the pavement, the way you say something you've decided to say. "You still talk to her?" "Yeah." A pause. "Every day, pretty much." I knew there was a question there. I could feel the shape of it, like a step in the dark. *How is she? What's been going on? Why would you say mostly?* And I didn't ask any of them. I noticed myself not asking, which was worse than just not asking, because it meant I knew. I said, "Oh, right," and then I said something about how cold it was. Dev didn't say anything for a while after that. Harrow Close is one of the older bits, pebbledash semis round a bit of grass with a sign on it that says NO BALL GAMES that somebody has corrected to NO BALL GAMES ALLOWED, which isn't even funny, it's just longer. Number 14 had every light off except the kitchen, round the side. There was a white van on the drive. HOLLIS HEATING, it said, and underneath, NO JOB TOO SMALL, and a clip-art thumb. Then he leaned over, not touching the dark bit, and put his fingers on Gary's neck, under the ear, where the stubble started. He stayed there for ages. The fridge hummed. The clock on the oven said 00:41, and then 00:42. "I don't know how, actually," Dev said. He didn't look up. "I thought I'd know. You watch enough of it, you think you'd know." He took his fingers away and looked at them. "I can't tell if that's mine. My pulse. In my fingers. I think it might be mine." "Is he dead?" I said. "I don't know, Josie. I just said." Tash laughed. It was one short noise, like a hiccup, and then she put her sleeve over her mouth. "What happened?" I said. She took the sleeve away. "No questions." "Tash." "He was being a knob," she said, fast, like she'd practised it on the stairs while she waited for us. "I told him he was being a knob. He did a thing. I did the casserole." She shrugged, a big shrug, all the way up to her ears. "That's the whole story. Anyway." "What thing?" "A *thing*, Pike." She looked at the kebab on the cupboards instead of me. Her knee was going, under the hoodie, jigging. Tash never stood still unless something was really wrong, and she wasn't standing still, and I didn't know if that was better. "How many times?" I said. I don't know why that was the question. It was just the one that came out. "Once," she said. Dev looked up at her then. Just for a second. Then he looked back down. "Okay," I said. "Okay. She'd stopped jigging. "If you ring someone, they come, and then it's police, and then it's my mum getting a phone call at her sister's in Clacton at one in the morning, and then it's social workers, and then it's me in some flat in Harlow with a woman called Bev who does *check-ins*. I wanted him to say something sensible, because I'd always been the sensible one and I'd suddenly run out, like a pen. He was still kneeling on the lino with his cagoule sleeve rolled up. He had a bit of chilli sauce on his knee. He looked at Gary for a long time, and then at Tash, and then at me. "We did swear," he said, very quietly. That was all. It went into the kitchen and stayed there, with the fridge and the clock and the smell. And here's the thing I didn't tell the police, later, even when I told them everything else. It came out in bits, in between other things, while she picked at the concrete with her thumbnail. "You saw the thermostat," she said. Not a question. "Yeah." "Sixteen degrees. He goes out to work, he takes the key." She shrugged. "I sleep in this." She plucked at the hoodie. "Mum says it's to save money. It's not to save money." Then, a bit later: "I put a bolt on my door. Madam.* Like that's a word that means anything." Then, later again, not looking at either of us: "I've been at Dev's. Weekends. Since the summer, mostly. His mum thinks it's, like, a sleepover thing." She looked at Dev. "She makes me eggs. She does them in a little pan just for eggs." Dev didn't say anything. He was pulling at his coat toggle so hard I thought it would come off. Every weekend since the summer. Every weekend I'd been at Ella's, watching films with the big light off, eating those posh crisps her mum buys, thinking how nice it was that nothing ever happened there. "It was twice," Tash said. "What was?" "The casserole. I said once. It was twice." She looked at me properly for the first time since the door. Her face was very tired and very still. "He was on the floor after the first one, and I did it again. I'm not sorry, so don't wait for that bit." I didn't know what to say. There isn't a mark scheme for it. I sat there with my soft Mini Cheddars and thought about the chip in the enamel, the little white crescent, and whether it came from the first time or the second. Behind us, Gary breathed. "No questions," I said. "That's the rule, isn't it." "That's the rule." "Can I ask one anyway?" She didn't say yes. She didn't say no. "Why me?" I said. "You've got Dev. Dev's been... Dev's been everything. Why'd you send it to me?" Tash looked at the water for so long I thought she wasn't going to answer, and I'd have deserved that. "You're the sensible one," she said. Then she pulled her sleeves down over her hands and tucked them into her armpits. "And I wanted to see if you'd come." That was it. She didn't say anything else, and she didn't need to. I'd come. I'd climbed out of my own back door and walked a mile in the cold and cleaned a kitchen and lied to a man with a dog. I'd done everything the pact asked me to, and none of it was any use, because it was January, and the time to come had been October, when she'd sent me a TikTok of a cat in a Tesco and I'd been saving up something funny to say.

There are occasional moments where the writing reaches slightly too hard — "a sort of long breath that never finishes" for the A127 is fine but slightly familiar — but these are rare. The writing avoids purple prose almost entirely. PLOT AND COHERENCE: The plot is coherent and the escalation is believable. The decision not to call an ambulance, the cleaning, the trolley, the flood channel — each step follows from character and circumstance. The four seconds at the railing is the story's moral center, handled with admirable restraint. The story doesn't resolve neatly, which is correct. UNEARNED TRANSFORMATIONS: The ending is carefully managed. Josie doesn't have a redemption arc so much as a first step — she answers. The story is honest that things are "carefully fine" rather than fine. Tash's situation is not resolved. This is mature handling. WEAKNESSES: The Mr. Okafor scene, while charming and funny, is slightly convenient — the dog sniffing Gary and then wandering off is a little too perfectly timed. The final chapter's meta-moment (Josie writing the story in her revision book) risks being too clever, too self-aware, though it's handled with enough self-criticism ("I'd made Gary's sock with the hole in it into a sentence I was pleased with") to mostly work. The story is perhaps slightly long for what it is, and the final chapter could be tighter. FAITHFULNESS TO PROMPT: The prompt asked for darkly comic British YA fiction with the text "🩸🩸🩸" as the inciting incident. The story delivers on all counts with considerable skill. Overall, this is a genuinely impressive piece — specific, funny, dark, emotionally honest, and technically accomplished. It reads like the work of a writer who knows what they're doing. # Brainstorming **Genre blend:** Space Western means frontier justice, dusty outposts on asteroid belts, bounty hunters, homesteaders on terraformed rocks, and six-shooters swapped for pulse revolvers or kept as antiques. The tone could run gritty like *Firefly* or *The Mandalorian*, mythic like a Leone film, or wry and weary. Western archetypes to draw on: the reluctant gunslinger, the widow rancher, the corrupt railroad baron (a mining conglomerate), the sheriff past his prime, the orphan, the snake-oil salesman. **The crate: what's moving inside?** 1. A child: a stowaway, a smuggled heir, or a genetically engineered kid the Company wants back. 2. An alien creature: dangerous at first, then revealed as a sentient being, perhaps the last of its kind or a juvenile whose mother is coming. 3. A person in cryo waking up: an outlaw legend, the captain's thought-dead brother, or a witness to a massacre. 4. An AI or android: a "lawman" unit, or a synthetic built to be sold. 5. Livestock gone wrong: space cattle, a "longhorn" beast. Played comic, then turned into a plot engine. 6. Seeds or a living terraforming organism, which could make a dying colony viable. That puts it at the center of a water or land war. 7. Nothing alive: a bomb ticking, or a mechanical tracker. **Crew ideas:** - Captain: a former cavalry officer from a lost war (the Belt Secession), now hauling freight. Could be a woman in her fifties, Captain Ada Voss, or a gruff man named Jed Harlan. - The speaker of the prompt line: a young deckhand, an engineer named Pip, or a nervous kid mechanic. - A pilot who's quiet and deadly. - A ship with personality, e.g., *The Dry Gulch* or *Lucky Penny*, an old ore hauler. **Antagonists:** a Company enforcer or bounty hunter tracking the crate, a Marshal with a warrant, or the original buyer, a cattle baron of the rings. **Structure over 8 chapters (~8000 words):** 1. Salvage/pickup and the line "Captain, something's moving." Hook. 2. Opening the crate and the reveal. 3. Deciding what to do: moral conflict, the crew splits. 4. A frontier town stop where pursuers arrive. Saloon scene. 5. Chase or escape, with a cost. 6. Low point: betrayal or loss, and the truth about the cargo. 7. Showdown at high noon, e.g., the shadow line of a planet's terminator, or a standoff on a derelict station. 8. Resolution: riding off into the star-set. **Themes:** what we owe strangers, cargo vs. people (echoing slavery and indentured servitude on the frontier), redemption, the frontier closing as the Company arrives. **Twist possibilities:** the crate was meant for the captain. The thing inside is the captain's own clone. The creature is the "gold" everyone's mining (sentient ore). The pursuer is sympathetic, a mother or parent. # Reflection The child-in-a-crate idea is familiar (*Firefly*'s River, *Mandalorian*'s Grogu), so it risks feeling derivative unless given a fresh angle. The alien creature offers more tension and a creepy opening, but it needs sentience to carry emotional weight across 8000 words. The terraforming organism is the most thematically "Western," tying into land and water rights, homesteaders vs. barons, and the frontier closing. It's less viscerally frightening at the start, though. A hybrid might work best. The crate moves, there's genuine horror-tension early, and then the thing is revealed as a living seed-organism, maybe beastlike, that could make a dead colony bloom. The Company wants it destroyed or owned. That gives a real stake: the crew could sell it for a fortune or deliver it to struggling homesteaders. That's a classic Western moral choice, like Shane or The Magnificent Seven. For characters, a weary, older captain with a war past gives the story gravitas and a reason for a final stand. The young crew member who says the prompt line can serve as the point-of-view contrast and the emotional core, the one who bonds with the creature first. Pacing: 1000 words per chapter is tight, so the cast should stay small: three or four crew, one main antagonist, one town. The frontier town chapter is essential for Western flavor, but it can't bloat. A standoff showdown feels mandatory for the genre, and it should include a quiet, drawn-out tension beat rather than just laser fire. Tone should balance humor and grit. Dialect-flavored dialogue helps sell the Western without becoming parody. The ending could be bittersweet: the captain pays a price, and the organism takes root. The final image might be green spreading on red dust, a strong visual for a "sunset." A twist where the antagonist has a personal link to the captain, like an old war comrade, could deepen the showdown without adding characters. I want to avoid over-explaining the sci-fi and let the Western bones carry it.

# Intention **Premise and core choice:** An aging freight captain and her small crew take a salvage contract to pull an abandoned cargo pod from a wrecked Company hauler. The pod contains a living, semi-sentient terraforming organism: a "seedbeast," part plant and part animal, able to make dead soil fertile and draw water from rock. The Company engineered it and then marked it for destruction, because a world that feeds itself doesn't need Company water shipments. The crew must choose between a fortune in bounty and delivering it to a failing homestead colony. This is the Shane/Magnificent Seven moral spine in a sci-fi frame. **Characters (kept small for the word count):** - **Captain Ada Voss**, late fifties. She is a veteran of the lost Belt Secession, dry-humored and tired, and she hauls freight to stay out of trouble. Her arc is from "not my business" to a final stand. - **Pip Okonkwo-Hale**, nineteen, deckhand and mechanic. Pip speaks the prompt line and is the first to bond with the creature. Pip is the emotional core and the reader's eyes on wonder. - **Tobiah "Mute" Crane**, the pilot. He is quiet and competent, and he carries a debt to the Company that tempts him toward betrayal. - **The ship:** *Lucky Penny*, an old ore hauler with patched hull plates, a temperamental water reclaimer, and a brass bell the captain rings for luck. - **Antagonist: Marshal Elias Grant**, Company-deputized. He is Ada's old commanding officer from the war, who switched sides when the Secession collapsed. He is sympathetic, principled in his way, and believes order beats freedom that starves. - **The colony:** Redwater Flats on the moon Kessel's Reach. It is dying of drought under Company water tariffs, led by a widow homesteader, Maren Dray. **Voice and style:** Close third person, alternating mainly between Ada and Pip. The prose should be spare and dusty, with Western cadence and sensory grit: dust, rust, sweat, recycled air. Dialogue carries frontier idiom lightly ("reckon," "ain't," clipped sentences) but never tips into parody. Science stays soft and undeclared, with no technobabble. Western iconography gets translated: pulse revolvers alongside one antique six-gun, a saloon inside a hollowed asteroid, and a high-noon showdown on a moon's terminator line, where light and shadow meet. **Tone:** Tension and creeping horror early, then wonder, then grit and melancholy. Humor comes from character, not jokes. **Aim for:** - A genuinely eerie opening before the reveal. - A real temptation, so the money matters. - A showdown that is mostly stillness and talk before a short burst of violence. - A bittersweet ending with a strong final image: green spreading across red dust at star-set. **Avoid:** - Cute-creature syndrome. The seedbeast should be strange and alien. - A cartoon villain. - Over-explained lore. - Bloated side characters. - A tidy, costless ending. **Themes:** What we owe strangers. The line between cargo and life. Redemption for a soldier who lost her war. The frontier closing under corporate order. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 – "Salvage"** The *Lucky Penny* pulls a sealed Company pod from a gutted hauler drifting in the Tethys debris field. The contract is anonymous and the pay is too good, which Ada notes and ignores. During the night shift, Pip hears scratching and a slow pulse. They find frost melting on the pod's seals, the temperature inside rising, and the metal warping. Pip wakes Ada on comms: "Captain, something's… moving in that crate we picked up." The chapter ends with Ada loading her antique six-gun. **Chapter 2 – "What's in the Box"** The three crew open the pod, tense and armed. Vines like pale muscle, roots, and a slow-breathing body the size of a calf spill out and cling to the deck. The creature is frightening: tendrils seek water and crack a coolant line. Chaos follows until Pip realizes it's thirsty, not hostile, and gives it water. Where it touches, rust blooms into moss. A Company data slate reads "PROJECT GENESIS — TERMINATE ASSET." A bounty notice appears on the band: an enormous reward for the pod, returned intact. **Chapter 3 – "The Price of Things"** The crew argues in the galley. The bounty would clear the ship's debts and Crane's indenture. Pip names the creature "Sprout," to Ada's disgust. Ada insists it's cargo and they'll sell it. That night Pip shows her the moss spreading across the hydroponics bay, and the reclaimer produces clean water for the first time in years. Ada remembers the Secession farms burning. Crane quietly sends a ping to the Company. Ada agrees to one stop at Deadwood Rock to find a buyer, telling herself it's business. **Chapter 4 – "Deadwood Rock"** At the hollowed-asteroid trading post, Ada enters a saloon full of miners, gamblers, and a piano player running on a battery. A fence tells her the Company has quietly doubled the bounty, and why: Genesis would end their water monopoly across the Reach. Marshal Elias Grant walks in. He and Ada recognize each other from the war, and their conversation is civil and loaded. He offers her a clean deal: the pod handed over, and her record wiped. She says she'll think on it. Leaving, she meets Maren Dray, a homesteader selling her last water rights to buy passage off Redwater Flats. **Chapter 5 – "Running Dry"** Grant's men try to seize the ship in dock, and a short firefight breaks out. The *Penny* blasts free, damaged. Crane is revealed as the one who sent the ping, and he confesses. Ada doesn't shoot him, but the trust is broken. Sprout, stressed, begins to wilt as the damaged reclaimer fails. Pip nearly dies in a vacuum-breach repair, and Sprout grows over the breach to seal it, saving them. The act of sacrifice is a turning point. Ada sets course for Redwater Flats. **Chapter 6 – "Redwater"** The colony is cracked red earth, empty cisterns, and families packing up. Maren Dray is wary, then stunned. They plant Sprout in the dead creek bed, and it roots and begins to spread, but it needs days. Grant's ship is tracking them, with a gunship and deputies. The colonists are not fighters. Ada gives a quiet speech that is not heroic: "I lost a war once. Ain't in a hurry to lose another." Crane chooses to stay, handing Ada the Company codes he'd been given. That night Ada and Pip talk about what she did in the war and why she runs. **Chapter 7 – "Terminator Line"** Grant lands at the edge of the moon's day/night line. He wants to talk before any shooting. The long standoff is the heart of the chapter: two old soldiers on the boundary of light and dark arguing order versus freedom, with debts, dead friends, and who betrayed whom. Grant nearly wavers. Then his deputies move on the creek bed. Violence comes in a sudden burst. Crane uses the codes to ground the gunship. Ada draws the antique six-gun. Grant falls, and so does Crane, who dies protecting Pip. Ada is wounded. **Chapter 8 – "Star-Set"** Some days later, Grant's final words and his mixed legacy linger. Company lawyers will come eventually, and Ada knows the frontier is closing, but Redwater has water now. Green creeps across the red flats. Crane is buried under the first tree. Ada, limping, is offered land by Maren and declines. The *Lucky Penny* is still hers. Pip chooses to stay with Sprout and the colony, and their goodbye is understated. Ada rings the brass bell and lifts off alone. The final image is the setting star and a spreading line of green on a red moon, seen from orbit as she heads out.

Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
# How a Human Might Approach This A human writer given "Captain, something's… moving in that crate we picked up" would probably notice that the prompt is a bit pulpy and a bit funny. The ellipsis is doing comic-horror work: someone nervous is reporting something they'd rather not be responsible for. A human might grab that tone and run with it before deciding what's in the crate. They'd ask: - Who says this line, and why are they the one on shift? - What's the captain doing when they hear it? Asleep, drunk, in the head, losing at cards? - How does the captain respond? Probably not with gravitas. Something like "Is it paying rent?" A human would also treat "Space Western" as a set of feelings as much as a set of props: boredom, long distances, the economics of being poor and far from help, work that grinds you, law that's for sale, loneliness. The real Western texture is labor and debt, and saloons and six-guns are the costume. Humans also write from obsession and specificity. They'd have a weird pet detail they can't let go of: - the captain's bad knee - a ship that smells like cabbage because the reclaimer is fed with it - a crewmember who keeps a ledger of what everyone owes the coffee fund They'd be willing to let the story be a little lopsided, a little funny when it "should" be serious, and a little unresolved. They'd let characters be wrong and stay wrong. They'd likely not know the ending when they started, and the plan would show some unevenness because of it. # Telltale LLM Tendencies (General) **1. Structural safety.** LLM plots march through the hero's-journey checklist: hook, reveal, moral dilemma, betrayal, low point, sacrifice, showdown, bittersweet coda. Every beat lands where expected. Nothing surprises because nothing is allowed to go sideways. **2. Moral clarity dressed as nuance.** There's a "sympathetic villain" who gets a speech about order versus freedom. Structurally, though, the story has already decided he's wrong, and he dies. The nuance is ornamental. **3. Tidy, bittersweet bow.** The mentor limps off alone and the kid stays with the found family. The green spreads. Someone dies nobly so there's a cost, but the cost is exactly the size the story can absorb. This is the "sad ribbon" version of wrapping it up. **4. Redemptive death for the betrayer.** The character who betrays dies saving someone to balance the ledger. It's so common it's invisible. **5. Thematic statements in dialogue.** Characters announce the theme: "I lost a war once. Ain't in a hurry to lose another." It's quotable, trailer-ready, and not how people talk. **6. Generic names.** Voss, Grant, Elias, Maren, Ada, Pip, Crane, Genesis. These come out of an LLM like water from a tap. **7. Prose tics.** - Tricolons ("dust, rust, and sweat") - Portentous one-line paragraph endings - "Something shifted" - "The weight of..." - Breath they didn't know they were holding - Constant sensory lists - Every chapter ending on a hook or a resonant image - Metaphor density that trades readability for impressiveness - Characters' feelings named right after they're shown **8. Convenient magic.** The MacGuffin conveniently solves problems (seals breaches, cleans water) exactly when the plot needs it. **9. Cute-creature slide.** The plan says "avoid cute-creature syndrome" and then names it Sprout and has it heroically save the kid. **10. Even pacing.** Each chapter gets one beat, one set piece, one emotional turn. Real stories bunch up and stretch out. **11. Caution about offending anyone or anything.** The Company is purely bad, and the homesteaders are purely deserving and helpless. No one on the "good" side is petty, greedy, or cruel. # Deep Dive: Critiquing the Intention and Plan ## The premise A terraforming seed-creature that breaks a corporate water monopoly is thematically neat. It's *too* neat. It's the Western land/water war mapped one-to-one onto a sci-fi object, with the moral answer pre-loaded. The reader knows from Chapter 2 that the crew will deliver it to the homesteaders. The "temptation" of the bounty is structurally fake. "PROJECT GENESIS — TERMINATE ASSET" on a data slate is an exposition dump in a single prop. It also names the thing in the most generic sci-fi way possible. ## The creature The plan says "strange and alien," but everything it does is benevolent and useful: - It turns rust to moss. - It fixes the reclaimer. - It seals a hull breach to save Pip. That's a magic healing plant with a personality. There's no real danger after the first scene. The early "thirsty, not hostile" realization defuses the horror in one move, which wastes the best tension the prompt offers. The name "Sprout" is the cute-creature slide in action, however ironically Ada groans at it. ## Ada Voss She's the Weary Veteran With a Past, which is fine as an archetype, but she has no quirks, no pettiness, and no specific texture. "Late fifties, dry-humored, tired" is a character-sheet description, not a person. Her arc ("not my business" to final stand) is the Han Solo/Shane arc played absolutely straight. The war-guilt reveal in a late-night talk with Pip is a scheduled confession scene. The antique six-gun is doubly cliché: introduced in Chapter 1 and fired in the climax. It's Chekhov's gun, literally. ## Pip Pip is the wonder-eyed kid who bonds with the creature and nearly dies. Pip speaks the prompt line but has no flaws in the plan. They're pure reader-surrogate. The name "Okonkwo-Hale" feels like a diversity checkbox rather than a character with a history. Pip's gender is left vague, which reads as hedging rather than a choice. ## Crane The nickname "Mute" is attached to a man who apparently talks, and to whom nothing about muteness matters. Then comes the full trope: secret debt, betrayal, confession, choosing to stay, handing over codes, dying to protect Pip, and being buried under the first tree. That's the redemptive-death package verbatim. The codes are also a convenient plot tool that grounds the gunship. ## Grant The old commanding officer turned Company marshal is extremely expected. The "sympathetic antagonist" debate on the terminator line is a Theme Scene. Grant "nearly wavering" before his deputies force the violence is an old trick. It lets the hero off the hook, because she didn't choose to escalate. Then he dies, removing the moral problem he represented. ## Maren Dray The widow homesteader is a pure archetype. She's wary, then stunned, and then offers Ada land at the end. She has no agenda of her own. ## Setting pieces The saloon with a battery piano and the fence who explains the stakes is Western cosplay plus exposition delivery. The terminator-line showdown is a clever image, but it's also exactly the kind of "high concept visual metaphor" an LLM reaches for. Light and dark, order and freedom: the symbolism is spelled out. ## Structure and pacing The plan has one beat per chapter, evenly spaced. Chapter 7 is overloaded: a long standoff, a debate, a gunship grounding, Grant's death, Crane's death, and Ada's wound, all in 1,000 words. Chapter 6 also crams in planting, a speech, Crane's turn, and a confession. Meanwhile the plan has no scenes of ordinary life aboard ship. That's where humans put character, and where Westerns breathe. ## The ending Ada declines land, rings the bell, and flies off alone. The kid stays. Green spreads on red at star-set, seen from orbit. It's the textbook bittersweet bow. The cost (Crane) was pre-assigned to the most expendable character. The Company threat is waved at ("lawyers will come eventually") but not felt. ## Tone statements "Humor comes from character, not jokes" and "never tips into parody" are sensible, but they signal a risk-averse, earnest register. The prompt has an inherent comic nervousness that the plan drops entirely after Chapter 1. # Brainstorming: Ways to Make It More Human ## Lean into the prompt's voice - Let the opening be funny and small. Ada is trying to sleep, or she's in the middle of cutting her own hair, or she's arguing with the ship's reclaimer. - Have Pip say the line and then add something worse ("...and it's warm"). - Play a scene of two people who don't want to deal with it trying to find reasons not to. Humor can coexist with dread, and it makes the dread land harder. - Consider giving the whole thing a narrative voice with some personality. Options include first person from Ada, or a slightly folksy close third that editorializes. ## Make the creature genuinely ambiguous, or costly - **It drinks first.** It needs water to root, and the colony's last reserves go into it with no guarantee. - **It's invasive.** The Company killed it partly because it's dangerous. It spreads uncontrollably, choking out other crops. Grant is actually right about something. - **It changes people.** Pip's hands develop green in the knuckles, or the moss grows in someone's lungs. It's unclear whether that's bad. - **Its sentience stays unclear.** Pip insists it's a person, and Ada thinks Pip is lonely. The story never settles it. - **Cut the heroic hull-breach rescue,** or invert it: the creature causes the breach while seeking water. - **Rename it,** or have Pip give it a dumb, specific name like "Deacon" or "Mrs. Pruitt" after someone Pip knew. Better, let it go unnamed, just "the crate" long after it's out of the crate. ## Make the money matter - The bounty should nearly win. Maybe Ada actually sells part of it, a cutting. - She takes the Company's money *and* delivers it, and has to live as a cheat. - The homesteaders can't pay, and she resents them for it. Humans are grudging about charity. - Show the debt concretely: a specific creditor, a missed payment, the ship's reclaimer she can't afford to fix. ## Give characters edges and specific textures **Ada** - Give her a petty vice, like chewing nicotine gum, cheating at solitaire, or a grudge against a specific brand of ration. - Make her war not heroic. Maybe she was on the losing side and did something shabby, like deserting or informing. - Don't let the confession come in a neat late-night talk. Let it slip out sideways in an argument, or never be told at all. **Pip** - Give Pip flaws: a liar, a petty thief, someone who ran away from Redwater Flats. - That last one is a twist with teeth. Pip is going *home*, and home doesn't want them back. - Pip's attachment to the creature might be partly selfish. - Decide Pip's gender and background and let it be ordinary. **Crane** - Drop the "Mute" nickname, or make it an ironic one for a man who never shuts up. - Let him betray them and *not* die. He just leaves, or he's forgiven badly and stays awkwardly. - Or don't make him the betrayer at all. Make it someone else, like Maren or a colonist who sells them out to the Company for a ticket off-world. **Grant** - Maybe he's not Ada's old commander. Just a tired company lawman who's good at his job and has never met her. - Or keep the history but make it trivial and embarrassing. He's someone she owes money to, or dated once. - Let him survive, and let him have a point. **Maren** - Give her an agenda. She wants the creature to sell it herself, or she doesn't trust it and wants to burn it. - Or she's already signed with the Company and the crew's arrival ruins her deal. ## Undercut the set pieces **The showdown** - The six-gun misfires, or Ada misses. - Someone unheroic, a scared colonist kid, shoots Grant. - Or there's no gunfight at all. The standoff dissolves because the Company recalculates the costs and pulls out, which is chillingly corporate. - Or Ada wins by being sneaky and ugly, not by a quick draw. **The terminator line** - Keep it if it's used for practical reasons: the dark side is cold enough to freeze engines, so it's tactical, not symbolic. - Or ditch it for something grubbier, like a stock pen or a dry creek. **The saloon** - Keep it short and weird, with a specific detail nobody explains. - Get the exposition out of the fence's mouth. Let Ada figure out the stakes by noticing things, like the price of water on a chalkboard doubling. ## Pacing and structure - Add quiet, "useless" scenes: meals, chores, a card game, an argument about music. That's where the Western feel and the character live. - Let one chapter be almost entirely a single long conversation, and let another cover days in a paragraph. - Spread out Chapter 7's crush of events, or cut events rather than compress them. - Don't end every chapter on a hook or an image. Some can end mid-thought or on a flat joke. ## The ending Alternatives to the bow: - **Uncertain growth.** The creature roots, but nobody knows if it'll take. Ada leaves before finding out. - **Mercenary exit.** Ada doesn't fly off alone with dignity. She flies off because she's broke and has a job. - **Pip doesn't stay.** Or Pip stays because they're not welcome aboard anymore, not because it's beautiful. - **Real cost.** The cost falls on the ship, Ada's livelihood, or her reputation, not just a sacrificial NPC. - **An anticlimactic last line,** a small joke or a mundane action, instead of the green-on-red vista from orbit. - **A time-jump coda.** Years later, Ada hears a rumor of green on Kessel's Reach, or that it's all gone to weed and the colony regrets it. ## Prose-level guardrails - Cut tricolons and sensory lists. Use one precise detail rather than three. - Avoid "something shifted," "the weight of," and held breaths. - Let dialogue be oblique. People answer the wrong question, deflect, and repeat themselves. - Don't name feelings after showing them. - Keep metaphors rare and plain, drawn from the characters' own world: engines, livestock, debt, weather. - Vary sentence rhythm naturally, not in a pattern of long, long, short-punch. - Allow a few unexplained things to stay unexplained. ## Names Replace the generic set with names that feel found rather than generated. Consider: - **Captain:** Hester Lusk, Dolores "Dee" Pruett, Winnie Carbo - **Kid:** Jubal, Tansy, Arlo Nkemdirim with a nickname that means something - **Pilot:** Faro - **Lawman:** Deputy Ottis Fry - **Ship:** *Lucky Penny* is fine, but something odder might be better, like *Mrs. Abernathy's Regret* or *Second Mortgage*. - **Colony/moon:** something that sounds like a failed real-estate pitch, like "Paradise Wells." - **Project name:** drop "Genesis" entirely, or use a dull corporate code, like "Item 7-Hydro."

# Intention **The core idea.** The prompt is nervous, a little funny, and a little dreadful. The story keeps that register all the way through rather than dropping it after the first scene. It is about poor people doing a bad job for bad money and finding something they can't afford to care about. The Western feel comes from debt, distance, labor, and law-for-hire. Saloons and six-guns are set dressing, used sparingly. **Premise.** Captain Dolores "Dee" Pruett runs the *Second Mortgage*, a cranky ore hauler she co-owns with a bank. She takes an anonymous salvage job: retrieve a sealed pod from a wrecked hauler, half paid up front. Something inside the pod wakes up. It is a Company-engineered water-finder, filed in the paperwork only as "Item 7-Hydro." It is part root and part animal. It pulls water out of rock and makes dead ground grow. It is also greedy, invasive, and possibly impossible to kill once rooted. The Company wants it back or destroyed. Some of that is about protecting its water-tariff business on the frontier. Some of it is because the thing is dangerous. Both are true, and the story never picks one. **Voice.** Close third person, anchored on Dee. The narration is wry and lightly editorial, with a folksy dryness ("which was the kind of money that ought to have warned her, and did, and she took it anyway"). Dialogue is oblique. People deflect, bicker, and answer the wrong question. Frontier idiom stays light. **Prose rules:** - One precise detail instead of a list. - No tricolons, no held breaths, no "something shifted," no "the weight of." - Metaphors stay rare and drawn from the characters' world: engines, livestock, debt, weather. - Feelings are not named after being shown. - Some chapters end flat, mid-conversation, or on a small joke instead of a hook. **Cast (kept to what 8,000 words can hold):** - **Dee Pruett**, fifty-eight. She has a bad hip, chews nicotine gum she's been "quitting" for eleven years, and cheats at solitaire and knows it. Her war was not heroic: she was a supply clerk for the losing side and deserted before the end. This comes out sideways, once, in an argument, and is never dwelt on. She is not noble. She is decent when it doesn't cost too much, and the story keeps raising the price. - **Tansy Mull**, nineteen. The deckhand and mechanic, and the one who says the prompt line. She is a liar and a petty thief, very good with engines. She ran away from Paradise Wells, the drought colony the story ends up at, and didn't leave on good terms. She bonds with the creature, but partly selfishly: it's a way to go home as somebody instead of a runaway who stole the co-op's battery money. - **Faro Delacroix**, the pilot. He never shuts up: horse-racing results from planets he's never visited, opinions about music. He is loyal, not a traitor, and he survives. He provides much of the humor and is the ship's ordinary life. - **Deputy Ottis Fry**. A Company-contracted lawman, tired, good at his job, with a ledger for everything. He has never met Dee, and there is no war history between them. He is the voice of the thing's real danger, and he has a point. He survives. - **Wendell Mull**. Tansy's uncle, who runs what's left of Paradise Wells. He's pragmatic and grudging, and he is the one who sells them out: he tips the Company hoping for a relocation bonus. He is not punished dramatically. He just has to keep living next to his niece. - **The creature** goes unnamed by the narration ("the crate," long after it's out of the crate). Tansy calls it "Mr. Haskett," after her old schoolteacher, and nobody else will. **The creature's rules:** - It is thirsty. Everything it gives, it takes first. - It cracks lines, drinks the ship's reserves, and grows where it isn't wanted. - The green that starts showing in Tansy's knuckles is never explained or resolved. - Whether it thinks stays unclear. Tansy says yes. Dee thinks Tansy is lonely. Neither is proven right. - It never performs a heroic rescue. **The money matters.** The ship is two payments behind, and the reclaimer is dying. Dee sells a cutting of the creature to a fence to pay for repairs. That act is her cheat, and it makes her complicit. The Company's half-payment is already spent. **The showdown is undercut.** It happens at the dry creek bed, in the ugly middle of the afternoon. It is mostly talk. Dee's antique six-gun misfires. There is a burst of violence: Faro takes a graze and a deputy breaks his arm on the rocks. But the confrontation is ended by paperwork, not a draw. The thing has already reached the aquifer, and ripping it out would cost more than it's worth. Fry recalculates, writes it off, and bills Dee for it. **The cost is real and unglamorous.** Dee loses her salvage license and gets a fine that puts a third mortgage on the *Mortgage*. Nobody dies. The colony does not throw a party. Tansy stays, partly by choice and partly because the ship can't afford her anymore. Nobody knows whether the green will be a miracle or a weed. **Avoid:** - Redemptive death. - A sympathetic villain who exists only to lose a debate. - Theme speeches. - Chekhov's gun paying off heroically. - A green-from-orbit final vista. - Evenly paced beats. **Aim for:** - Genuine creeping dread in the opening. - Real temptation. - Quiet, useless scenes where the characters live. - An ending that stops rather than resolves. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 – "Half Up Front"** - Dee is in the galley at 0300, losing at solitaire to herself, gum going stale. She thinks over the job: tow a pod out of a wreck and drop it at a relay buoy for an unnamed buyer, half paid up front. She reflects on what "half up front" usually means. - Faro is asleep. The reclaimer makes its usual sick noise. - Tansy calls on comms from the hold: "Captain, something's… moving in that crate we picked up." A pause. "And it's warm. Is it supposed to be warm?" - Dee spends a good while trying to find reasons this isn't her problem: thermal expansion, a loose shipping strap, rats. She goes down in her socks. - In the hold: frost sweating off the seals, a slow knocking like a heartbeat heard through a mattress. The metal lid has bowed upward half an inch. - End flat, not on a cocked gun. Dee says, "Well, don't *touch* it," and Tansy admits she already has. **Chapter 2 – "Thirsty"** - They don't open it. It opens itself, splitting a seam in the middle of an argument about whether to vent it into space. - Pale root-stuff comes out, muscled and slow, and goes straight for the coolant line. Real fear follows: Faro with a fire axe, Dee pulling Tansy back by her collar, the ship alarm going off. - The thing punctures the coolant line and drinks. When it has drunk, it goes still. - Afterward: a crust of moss on rusted deck plates, and a tangled body the size of a calf wedged in a corner, pulsing. - Tansy finds the pod's manifest tag: "ITEM 7-HYDRO — DO NOT THAW — DESTROY ON BREACH." No explanation. - Faro, shaking, asks whether they'll still get the other half. It's a real question. - End mid-conversation on the problem of the water reserves, which just dropped by a third. **Chapter 3 – "The Books"** - A quiet, "useless" chapter: two days of living with it. Tansy names it Mr. Haskett, and Dee refuses to use the name. Faro plays one song repeatedly until Dee threatens him. They eat bad ration hash. - The creature takes the drain in the hydroponics bay and turns the dead lettuce trays green. The reclaimer runs clean for the first time in a year. That is because the creature is in the pipes, which is unsettling. - Dee does the books at the table. The ship is two payments behind, the reclaimer rebuild is quoted at more than the ship is worth, and the half-payment is already spent. - Dee and Tansy argue. Tansy reveals the relay buoy coordinates put them a day from Paradise Wells, where she's from, and where "they'd kill for this." - Dee says, "They'd kill for anything wet," and that's not an answer. - Dee's war slips out here, sideways: "I carried the Secession's water ledgers for four years and then I walked off in the night. Don't tell me what people deserve." - Dee decides to go to Deadwood Rock first, to "see what it's worth." She tells herself it's business. **Chapter 4 – "Deadwood Rock"** - A short, weird stop at a trading post in a hollowed asteroid. The saloon has a mechanical dog behind the bar that nobody explains. Water prices are chalked on a board, and Dee watches a man rub one out and write it higher. - No fence explains the stakes. Dee works it out from the chalkboard and from who's nervous. - Dee cuts a length of the creature and sells it to a fence named Oyelaran for reclaimer parts and a month's payment. She does it without telling Tansy. - Deputy Ottis Fry is at the bar, filling out forms. They share a table because it's the only open one. He's polite and asks about her tonnage. - Neither says anything about crates. Dee knows exactly what he is. - She leaves fast. On the way out, Faro mentions he's been telling people in the saloon about their "weird cargo." He's cheerful about it. - End on Tansy discovering the cut stump in the hold and not speaking to Dee. **Chapter 5 – "Paradise Wells"** - They land at the drought colony on Kessel's Reach: cracked red flats, one functioning cistern, a store selling off-world tickets on credit. - Tansy's homecoming is bad. Uncle Wendell Mull remembers the battery money, and other colonists don't look at her. - The creature is shown in a stock trailer, and the reaction is suspicion, not wonder. One woman wants to burn it. Wendell wants to know what it costs. - They plant it in the dead creek bed anyway, with the colony's last cistern water poured in and no guarantee. That is the colony's real gamble. - Tansy's knuckles are faintly green, and Dee notices. Tansy sees her notice and pulls her sleeves down. - Wendell sends a message off-world that night. We see him do it, without comment. **Chapter 6 – "Roots"** - Days pass in a paragraph or two: the creek bed damp, then muddy, then sprouting pale shoots that are not quite grass. It spreads faster than anyone likes. It gets into a colonist's bean rows and chokes them, and there is an argument about that. - Dee should leave. She keeps finding reasons not to: the parts need fitting, and her hip is bad. - Tansy and Dee fight about the cutting Dee sold. Tansy hits her where it hurts: "You'd have sold all of it if the price was right." - Dee says yes. They are both right. - Faro finds Fry's ship on long-range scan. He tells a racing story instead of panicking, then panics. - End flat: Dee cleaning an old six-gun she knows hasn't been test-fired in a decade, and Faro asking her to please not. **Chapter 7 – "The Creek Bed"** - Fry lands at midday with two deputies and a clipboard. He wants to talk first. - The long stretch of the chapter is the conversation at the creek bed. Fry is reasonable and has a point: the thing is invasive, the Company lost a whole research station to one, and "you've just handed your grandkids a weed they can't pull." - Dee has no good answer. She doesn't make a speech. She just stays standing there. - Wendell is watching from the porch. Fry thanks him for the tip, in front of everyone. - Violence comes in a clumsy burst. A deputy moves on the creek with a burner. Dee draws, and the six-gun misfires. Faro tackles the deputy, gets grazed by a shot, and the deputy breaks his arm on the rocks. - It's embarrassing and fast, and nobody is dead. - Fry stops it by raising his hand. He walks the creek and pushes a probe into the ground. The roots have already reached the aquifer, much deeper than anyone guessed. - He does sums on his clipboard, out loud. Removing it would cost the Company more than letting it be. - End on him writing, not on anyone's face. **Chapter 8 – "Third Mortgage"** - Fry's resolution is bureaucratic and chilling. Item 7-Hydro is written off as a loss. The Company will "revisit" Paradise Wells. Dee's salvage license is revoked, and she's fined for the breach and the destroyed contract. The fine is enough that the bank now owns a larger share of her ship than she does. - He shakes her hand. He means it. He leaves. - The colony doesn't celebrate. Some people are glad. Some are packing anyway, because they don't trust a weed they can't pull. - Wendell has to keep living next to Tansy. - Faro's arm is bandaged. He's telling the graze story bigger already. - Dee can't afford a deckhand now. Tansy is staying, and the two things are both true, so neither of them has to say which one is the reason. - Their goodbye is understated. Tansy returns something she stole from the ship months ago, and Dee pretends she never noticed it was missing. - Dee takes the only job she can get: hauling fertilizer to a mining camp, which she notes is funny, and doesn't laugh. - Last beat: in the cockpit, Faro asks if the thing will take, or if it'll eat the whole moon. Dee says she doesn't know. She puts in a fresh piece of gum, the first in eleven years that she's decided to actually enjoy. - No view from orbit. They lift, and it stops.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Dolores "Dee" Pruett **Background.** Dee was born on a hydroponics barge in the Tethys Belt to a mother who repaired air scrubbers and a father who drank. She learned arithmetic from ration inventories. At twenty-two she enlisted in the Belt Secession, not from conviction but because the Secession paid in water chits and her mother's barge was on quarter rations. She was never a soldier. She was a supply clerk at Harrow Depot, and for four years she kept the water ledgers: who got it, who didn't, which outposts were written off. Near the end, when the ledgers stopped balancing and she understood that certain columns were towns being left to die, she walked out of the depot at night with a duffel and a stolen requisition stamp. She's never told anyone about the stamp. She still has it, in a coffee tin. After the war she crewed freighters for twenty years, saved badly, and at fifty-one bought the *Second Mortgage* with a bank loan that owns 60 percent of it. The name was a joke when she registered it. It has stopped being a joke. **Personality.** Dee is practical to the point of rudeness and funny in a way that sounds like complaining. She is decent in small, cheap increments: she'll give you her last coffee but not her last water. She mistrusts enthusiasm, speeches, and anyone who uses the word "destiny." She does sums in her head constantly, what things cost and what they'd sell for, and can't turn it off. It's the ledger habit, and she knows exactly where she got it. **Idiosyncrasies:** - She chews nicotine gum she's been "quitting" for eleven years. She keeps a count of pieces on the galley wall in grease pencil and cheats the count. - She plays solitaire and cheats, moving a card when she's losing. She says it's "not cheating if nobody's harmed," then adds, "I'm harmed. I know." - She calls the ship "she" when it's working and "that thing" when it isn't. - She keeps her boots by the hatch and goes everywhere else in socks, which are always mismatched. - She talks to the reclaimer. Not kindly. - She can't sleep past 0300 and won't admit it's the war. She says it's her hip. **Flaws.** She is cowardly in a specific way: she runs from anything that asks her to take a side, and calls it being sensible. She makes decisions by delay, letting circumstances choose so she doesn't have to. She's stingy with praise and never apologizes directly. She lies to herself about money, telling herself a thing is "just business" right up until it isn't. Selling the cutting is the most honest thing she does in the story: an act of pure self-interest she doesn't pretend otherwise about. **Physicality.** She is short and thick through the middle, with forearms like a dockworker's. Her grey hair is cut with engine shears in the galley mirror, uneven at the back where she can't see. She has a bad left hip, and she walks with a slight roll and lowers herself into chairs in two stages. Her face is sun-damaged from a childhood under grow-lamps, the lines deep around her mouth from chewing. Her hands are always doing something: working gum wrappers into tiny squares, tapping a stylus. When she's angry she gets very still and very quiet, and people who know her find that worse than shouting. **Motives and allegiances.** Dee wants to keep the ship. That's most of it. Under that, she wants never again to be the person deciding who gets water, and the story puts her exactly there. She has no political loyalty left. She's loyal to Faro in a long-married, irritated way; they've flown together six years. She took Tansy on eighteen months ago because Tansy fixed the drive coupling for free at a dock and then tried to steal Dee's wallet. Dee liked her immediately, which she has never said. **Voice:** > "Half up front is a sentence you should listen to all the way to the end. Half up front means somebody's already decided you might not be alive for the back half." > "No. Don't name it. You name a thing, next you're buying it a collar, next you're crying over it. I have a budget." > *Internal:* She told herself she was going down to the hold because Tansy was nineteen and couldn't be trusted with a wrench near anything pressurized. That was true. It was also true she wanted to see it, which was the kind of wanting that had cost her before. # Tansy Mull **Background.** Tansy grew up in Paradise Wells on Kessel's Reach, a drought colony named by a land company that sold plots off a brochure. Her mother died of a lung complaint when Tansy was nine. Her father went off-world for contract work and sent money for two years, then stopped. She was raised by her uncle Wendell, who fed her, never hit her, and made clear every day that she was an expense. She was very good with machines: at thirteen she rebuilt the co-op's well pump from parts of two broken ones. The colony praised her and still treated her like Wendell's charity. At seventeen she took the co-op's battery fund, 340 credits in a lockbox meant for replacing the solar array's storage cells, and bought passage off-moon. The colony ran dark for a winter because of it. She tells herself it was her pump money, that she'd earned it. She half believes it. **Personality.** Tansy is quick, sly, and funny, and much more sentimental than she'll allow. She lies reflexively: about her age, where she's from, whether she ate the last ration bar. Most lies are pointless, a habit of keeping herself unfixed. She wants badly to matter and hides it under being flip. She attaches fast and hard to things that can't reject her: engines, a stray cat at a dock once, and now the creature. **Idiosyncrasies:** - She steals small things from the ship and hides them in a sock in the vent above her bunk: a brass hex key, a photo of Faro's sister, one of Dee's gum packets. She doesn't know why. - She hums while she works, always the same four bars of a hymn from the colony chapel, and gets annoyed when anyone points it out. - She names every tool. The torque wrench is "Mrs. Bannerman." - She eats standing up. - She can hear a bearing going bad two decks away. This is why she's the one on shift and hears the crate. - She keeps her hair tied with electrical wire. **Flaws.** She's a thief who resents being called one. She's reckless and touches things she shouldn't (the crate, in chapter one) because not knowing feels worse than danger. Her love for the creature is real, and it is also a plan: arriving home with a miracle means she won't have to apologize for the batteries. She never admits this, even to herself, until Dee says it for her in chapter six. She can be cruel when cornered, and her aim is good. **Physicality.** Tall and bony, with elbows and knees everywhere. Dark freckled skin, burn scars across the backs of both hands from solder and hot manifolds, nails always black. She sits on counters, on crates, and on the back of the galley bench with her feet on the seat. When she's lying she gets very eye-contacty; when she's telling the truth she looks at something mechanical nearby. The green in her knuckles starts as a faint tint under the skin, like a vein, and she keeps her sleeves pulled down over it. **Motives and allegiances.** She wants to go home and she dreads it. She wants to be forgiven without having to ask. She's loyal to Dee in a prickly way; Dee is the first adult who wanted her around, and Tansy tests it constantly, including the wallet. She likes Faro and treats him like an idiot older brother. Her relationship with Wendell is the sore at the center: she wants him to be proud, and she wants to punish him for never having been. She believes the creature is a person because she needs it to be. **Voice:** > "Captain, something's… moving in that crate we picked up. And it's warm. Is it supposed to be warm?" *(Pause.)* "I didn't touch it." *(Pause.)* "I touched it a little." > "His name is Mr. Haskett. He taught me long division and he smelled like the inside of a pipe. It suits him. Look how serious he is." > *Internal:* She'd pictured it a hundred ways, landing at the Wells. In most of them she was taller. # Faro Delacroix **Background.** Faro is forty-four and from a big, loud family of ferry pilots on Delacroix Station, a place named after a great-grandfather nobody liked. He has five sisters and calls each of them every month, which eats a painful share of his pay. He flew passenger shuttles until he clipped a docking arm; nobody was hurt, but his commercial rating was pulled. He's been with Dee six years. He's a very good pilot who flies like he's bored, which he usually is. **Personality.** Warm, talkative, unbothered, and allergic to silence. He fills every quiet with something: racing results, theories about music, gossip about people he's never met. The talking is how he stays calm, and the crew can read his fear by when he goes quiet, which is rare and alarming. He's generous, a bad gambler, and incapable of keeping a secret, not out of malice but because it simply doesn't occur to him that a thing might be secret. **Idiosyncrasies:** - He follows horse racing on three planets he's never visited, by delayed feed, and bets on races whose results arrived weeks ago. He loses anyway. - He's obsessed with one song, "Lonesome Water" by a dead country singer named Ruby Vale, and plays it on loop during long burns. He has opinions about which of the four recordings is best. - He cooks. He's the only one who can make ration hash tolerable, using a spice blend his sister mails him. - He talks to the ship during maneuvers, sweetly: "Come on, darling, come on." - He never sits in the co-pilot's chair; it's "for guests." **Flaws.** He blabs, and does so to half of Deadwood Rock in chapter four, cheerfully. He avoids conflict by joking until it goes away, and will not take a side between Dee and Tansy, which frustrates both. He's physically brave in a panic and cowardly about feelings. He owes money to at least two people he hasn't mentioned. **Physicality.** Big, soft-bellied, broad-shouldered, going bald and wearing it with a flat cap indoors. He has a deep laugh that comes out before the joke ends. He's surprisingly graceful in the cockpit, all small precise movements, and clumsy everywhere else, banging his head on the galley hatch daily. He has reading glasses he's embarrassed by and keeps pushed up on his forehead. **Motives and allegiances.** He wants a quiet life, a steady paycheck, and one day a win at the track. He loves Dee in the steady way of long partnership and would never say it. He's protective of Tansy. The tackle in chapter seven is not heroism he chose; it's his body moving before his mouth could talk it out. He doesn't care about the creature one way or another. He cares whether they get paid. **Voice:** > "Do we still get the other half? No, I'm asking. I'm asking genuinely. Is there a clause for this?" > "Now the '61 recording, the bootleg one, she's got a cold in that. You can hear it. That's why it's the best one. You can hear she didn't want to be there." > *After being grazed:* "I'd like it noted I was very brave. I'd like it noted by somebody official." # Deputy Ottis Fry **Background.** Fry is sixty-one, a contract lawman licensed through the Harlan Reach Mining Consortium, which the colonists just call the Company. He's been doing this twenty-six years. Before that he was an insurance adjuster, and he still thinks like one: the world is liabilities and exposures, and his job is to minimize both. He has a wife on Harlan Prime he's been married to thirty-four years, and a daughter who's a veterinarian and doesn't speak to him much. He was at the Karrow Station research outpost after the first 7-Hydro specimen got loose. It rooted into the station's water system and cracked the foundations in eleven weeks. Three technicians drowned when a hab flooded from below. He saw that, and he isn't lying about it. **Personality.** Polite, tired, methodical, never in a hurry. He doesn't enjoy violence, but he doesn't flinch from ordering it. He believes, sincerely, that the Company is the only thing standing between the frontier and a lot of people dying messily, and he's seen enough messy deaths to mean it. He isn't cruel. He's indifferent in a way that's worse than cruelty: he'd destroy a colony or spare it depending on which column came out larger, and would lose no sleep either way. **Idiosyncrasies:** - He keeps a paper ledger, real paper, in a waterproof sleeve. He says screens lie and paper just gets wet. - He fills out forms at bars. He likes the noise. - He drinks milk. Reconstituted, at great expense. People stare. He doesn't care. - He addresses everyone by rank or title, "Captain," "Mister Mull," even while arresting them. - He does arithmetic aloud when thinking, under his breath. - He carries a sidearm he's fired four times in his career and keeps a record of each. **Flaws.** He's incurious about anything that isn't a cost. He takes the Company's framing as simply how the world is. He's vain about his fairness; he believes he's a reasonable man, and would be deeply offended to hear otherwise, which makes him easy to flatter, though no one in the story tries. **Physicality.** Long and thin and slightly stooped, like a coat on a hook. Grey moustache kept neat, clean cuffs, a wide-brimmed hat he removes indoors without fail. Moves slowly and with economy. His hands are always clean. He has very pale eyes, and he looks at you for exactly as long as is polite. **Motives and allegiances.** He wants to close the file cleanly, with minimum loss. He's loyal to the Company the way a man is loyal to a mortgage: it's what he's built his life on and he can't imagine it otherwise. He has no personal feeling about Dee. By the end he mildly respects her, in the way you respect a stubborn stain. **Voice:** > "I'm not here to take anything from you, Captain. I'm here to find out what it costs for you to keep it. Usually more than folks guess." > "I buried three men at Karrow because somebody thought this thing was a miracle. You've handed your grandkids a weed they can't pull. I'm just the one who has to write it down." > *At the creek bed, pencil moving:* "Excavation, forty days minimum. Aquifer remediation, call it... no. No, that's not worth it. That's not worth it at all." # Wendell Mull **Background.** Wendell is fifty-three and one of the original Paradise Wells homesteaders. He bought three plots off the brochure twenty-two years ago with his late brother's money and his own. He's watched the colony dwindle from sixty families to nineteen. He runs the co-op store, the cistern schedule, and anything else nobody else will. He raised Tansy after his sister died and his brother-in-law left, and did it dutifully and without warmth. He is not a villain. He is a man who has done arithmetic about survival every day for two decades and can't stop. **Personality.** Pragmatic, grudging, and exhausted. He has a dry wit that has curdled into bitterness. He is fair by the strictest definition and never generous. He resents dreamers because dreamers left him holding the bill. He sees clearly and hopes for nothing. **Idiosyncrasies:** - He measures the cistern level himself every morning with a knotted rope, even though there's a gauge. He doesn't trust gauges. - He keeps the ledger of who owes the co-op on the store wall where everyone can see. Tansy's line, "battery fund, 340," is still up, two years later. - He sweeps the porch constantly. The dust always wins. He sweeps anyway. - He says "well" before every sentence, like he's weighing it. **Flaws.** He holds grudges for years and considers that justice. He's never told Tansy she was good at anything, though he told other people. He sells them out to the Company not out of malice but because the relocation bonus would get the last families off-moon, and he genuinely thinks that's the kinder thing. He is probably wrong. He might be right. **Physicality.** Medium height, wiry, sun-browned to leather, with a permanent squint. Wears the same canvas coat year round. Walks like his feet hurt, which they do. Rarely looks directly at people; looks at the ground, the sky, the cistern. **Motives and allegiances.** He wants the colony's remaining people to survive, even if it means Paradise Wells doesn't. He's loyal to the dirt and the people on it, not the idea of the place. He loves Tansy in a way he never learned to show and is furious at her for leaving, mostly because he wanted to. He'll never admit any of that. **Voice:** > "Well. You brought a weed and a bill. Which one am I paying first?" > "Well, I didn't expect you'd come back. I expected you'd come back if you needed something. Here you are." > *To Fry, on the porch, quietly:* "They'll hate me for it. I'm used to that. They can hate me off-world where there's water." # Item 7-Hydro ("Mr. Haskett") Not a character in the usual sense. It needs consistent rules so it doesn't turn into a plot convenience. **What it is.** A Company-engineered organism meant to find and draw water from deep rock for mining operations. It has pale, muscular roots that move slowly, like something thinking. The core body is a dense tangle about the size of a calf, faintly warm, with a pulse you can feel through the deck plates. It smells like wet stone and cut stems. It makes no sound except a creak, like rope under load. **How it behaves:** - It moves toward water, always. Coolant, reserves, pipes, people's sweat. - It takes before it gives. The moss and the clean reclaimer water come after it has drunk the reserves down. - It spreads without restraint. It will choke a bean row as happily as it greens a creek bed. - It doesn't respond to being named, spoken to, or loved, but it does sometimes go still when Tansy is near, which could be anything. - It isn't hostile. It isn't friendly. It is hungry and patient. **The ambiguity.** Tansy's green knuckles, its stillness around her, the way it grows faster at night: none of it is explained. Fry thinks it's a machine made of plants. Tansy thinks it's lonely. Dee thinks it doesn't matter what it is, only what it costs. The story never decides.
