Constance Vance-Whitlock chose the Port Calder Yacht Club, which has a dining room shaped like the inside of a boat and salads that cost thirty-one dollars. She was there before me. She was always going to be there before me. "Mr. Kasprzak," she said. She said all of it, every consonant in the right place, which almost nobody does. It felt like being handed my own coat by someone who'd checked the pockets. She ordered the Cobb. When it came she looked at it for a moment, then lifted a strip of bacon off the top with her fork and set it on the bread plate, and then another, until the bread plate had a small neat pile and the salad had none. The waiter didn't blink. I got the impression this happened every Tuesday. "You've met him," she said. "I've interviewed Mr. Sorrell, yes." "Twice, I'm told." I have been in this job fifteen years, and I know the difference between someone guessing and someone knowing. She was knowing. I drank some water. "I'm not going to pretend I liked him," she said. "I'm sure he's told you I'm a snob. I am. It doesn't make me wrong." She had a watch on her left wrist, a heavy steel diver's thing, far too big for her, the band on the last hole and still loose. She turned it around so the face was on the inside. "Arthur taught me to sail when I was twelve. He was nine. He was unbearable about knots. He used to make me tie a bowline with my eyes shut and then check it with his teeth, like a dog. He cried at my wedding so hard the priest stopped." She looked at me. "I'd like you to know that about him, since you seem to be spending your time with people who only knew the ending." "I'm sorry," I said. I meant it, and she could tell, and she didn't like it. "He makes you feel chosen," she said. "It isn't the same thing. My brother made the same mistake, and he was cleverer than you." Then she told me about Mrs. Okafor, the neighbor, the retired pharmacist whose kitchen window looks straight into the Vance kitchen across twenty feet of lawn and two walls of glass. How Mrs. Okafor had been up that night because she doesn't sleep, and had seen a cigarette burning in the kitchen doorway. Not moving. For ages, she'd said. And Arthur on the floor behind it. "She told the police," Constance said. "They wrote it down and did nothing, because a cigarette is not a crime. But I'm told it matters to you." I had stopped eating somewhere in there. I'd ordered the halibut. I don't remember what it tasted like. I remember the napkin in her lap, and her hand smoothing it, flat, and flat again, the only part of her that moved. --- The pharmacy records came through that afternoon. Arthur Vance had a standing prescription for a beta blocker and an anticoagulant, refilled monthly at the Rexall on Delancey, regular as a mortgage, for six years. Then, eight weeks before he died, the refills stopped. No new pharmacy. No change in prescription. He just didn't go. I read it four times. It was good news for the claim, in the narrow way I'm paid to think. A man with a bad heart who stops his heart medication is a man who died of his heart. It was also the kind of thing you don't know what to do with, the way you don't know what to do with a letter addressed to someone who used to live at your house. I didn't call Jude. I told myself that was professionalism. He called me at eleven-forty that night. "I need my music," he said. No hello. "It's in Arthur's study. The lawyers locked it on Friday, the whole room, like there's treasure. There isn't treasure. There's his desk and a globe and my sheet music, which is mine. I bought it." "Then you should ask the estate's attorney." "I did. He said Monday. He says everything is Monday." A pause. Smoke, I could hear it. "Come with me." "Absolutely not." "I have a key to the house. It's my house. I just don't have a key to the room." "Then how—" "It's a very old lock, Kasprzak. It's mostly decorative. Like Arthur." I'd like to say I thought about it. I put my shoes back on. --- The study was on the top floor, at the back, the one room in the house with real walls. The lock was, as promised, mostly decorative. He opened it with a butter knife and a credit card that wasn't his, while I held my phone flashlight and felt my whole career standing behind me, clearing its throat. Inside it smelled like leather and dust and, faintly, a cologne I didn't know but could guess. Jude went straight to a cabinet by the window and started pulling out folders, humming under his breath, bass notes, left hand. I stood by the desk because I didn't know where else to stand. The top drawer wasn't locked. I don't know why I opened it. I know exactly why I opened it. Three orange bottles, lined up. The Rexall labels. Full. The foil seals still on. The dates on them went back two months. I photographed them. I put them back exactly as they'd been, labels facing out. Jude was sitting cross-legged on the floor with a book of Gershwin open on his knees, and he didn't look up, and I didn't tell him. Then headlights came across the glass. They swept the hall below us, white, slow, and threw our shadows up the wall, and Jude was up off the floor and had me by the shirt and back behind the door before I'd finished understanding what I was looking at. We stood there. The light swung through the room and over the desk and the globe and stopped, and then a car door didn't open, and an engine idled, and somewhere out on the Point a dog barked twice. He was pressed against me from the knee up. His hair smelled like smoke and rain. I could feel him breathing, fast, and then I could feel him start to laugh, silently, his whole chest shaking. "It's a neighbor," he whispered. "Turning around. It's always a neighbor turning around." "Then why are we—" He kissed me. It wasn't good. My glasses went sideways across my face and the doorknob was in my kidney and he laughed into my mouth, actually laughed, and I thought, very clearly, *well, that's that*, the way you think it when you miss a step on the stairs. The headlights went away. We didn't.

These are not decorative details but character-revealing ones. The watch is particularly good — it's mentioned in the character profile and deployed here without comment, letting the reader understand she's wearing Arthur's watch without being told. The line "It felt like being handed my own coat by someone who'd checked the pockets" is a strong metaphor that earns its place — it captures the particular social aggression of Constance's courtesy without overreaching. Her dialogue is excellent. "He makes you feel chosen. It isn't the same thing. My brother made the same mistake, and he was cleverer than you." He didn't take me back to the glass house. He said he couldn't sleep there, hadn't slept there since the funeral, and gave the address of a place on Marsh Street, a laundromat called Suds City with a pink sign and a hand-lettered card in the window that said NO DYEING IN MACHINES, WE MEAN IT. "You live above a laundromat," I said. "I kept it. When Arthur moved me in with him, I kept paying the rent. Five years." He was getting his keys out, dropping them, getting them out again. "Don't look at me like that. You'd have kept it too." I wouldn't have. That was the difference between us, and I already knew it wasn't the kind of difference that was going to help. The stairs went up the side of the building, outside, metal, slick with mist. Inside it was one room and a kitchen the size of a phone booth, a mattress on a low frame, a keyboard on a stand with a sheet thrown over it, and more ashtrays than one person needs. It was warm from the dryers downstairs. You could feel them through the floor, a big slow thump like a heart. Somebody down there was playing Fleetwood Mac, and not quietly. "She runs the place at night," he said. "Mrs. Tran. It's always *Rumours*. She told me once it's the only album where everybody's miserable and it still sounds good." He turned on one lamp and stood in the middle of the room with his coat still on. For the first time since I'd met him he didn't seem to know what to do with his hands. "Stay," he said. He said it like a dare, like he expected me to laugh. "Okay," I said. --- I want to be accurate about this, because I'm accurate about everything else. I was nervous. I hadn't done this in a year and a half, and before that not often, and before that not with anyone I was supposed to be investigating. I took my glasses off and then didn't know where to put them and put them in my shirt pocket, which I was about to take off. I apologized for that. Then I apologized for apologizing, and he put his forehead against my collarbone and laughed until he had to sit down on the bed. "You're allowed to be bad at this," he said. "I've been bad at this with much better-looking men." "Thank you." "That was a compliment. Sort of. Come here." He was gentler than I'd expected. He went slowly, and he watched my face the whole time like he was reading music he didn't know yet, and when I got my breath caught somewhere it shouldn't have been he stopped and waited and put his hand flat on my chest until it came back. Then he said something filthy and ridiculous about my good cuticles, and I laughed out loud, the real laugh I don't let out, and he looked so pleased with himself that I had to kiss him to make it stop. Somewhere in there my elbow caught an ashtray on the windowsill and sent it across the floor, a gray fan of ash over the boards. Neither of us got up. Downstairs "Dreams" came on for the second time, then, later, the third. Afterward I got up and folded my trousers over the back of the only chair. I did it without thinking. I fold them every night. He watched me from the bed, propped on one elbow, and when I turned around he had both hands over his face. "What." "You *folded* them." "They'll crease." "Miles," he said, and it was the first time he'd used my name, and he was laughing so hard he could barely get it out. "Miles, come back to bed before I fall in love with you. It'd be so embarrassing for both of us." I came back to bed. --- In the morning he made eggs. He made them the way you'd make eggs if you'd only ever heard them described: too high, too fast, with the shells mostly out. There was ketchup. We ate them standing up in the kitchen because there was nowhere to sit, and they were terrible, and I finished mine. Out the kitchen window you could see the laundromat's back lot and the side door where people came out to smoke. He knew all of them. The woman in the purple tracksuit, who came in Tuesdays and Fridays and was, he was certain, having an affair with the man who washed only work shirts. The college kid who brought his mother's laundry and read Dostoevsky on the folding table, for show, always the same page. "You can't know it's the same page." "I checked. I went over and checked. Page two-twelve. A man's feeling guilty about something." "That's all of Dostoevsky." "See, you're funny," he said, pointing a fork at me. "You hide it. Why do you hide it?" I told him about Karen. Not much. That we'd been married nine years, that she'd been funny too, that we were still friendly, that I sent her a text on her birthday and she sent me a thumbs up. "Did she know?" he said. "Before you told her?" "Before I did, probably." He didn't say anything to that. He just nodded, and reached over, and took a piece of eggshell off my sleeve. We didn't talk about the case. We didn't talk about Arthur. I was aware, standing in that small kitchen with the dryers going, of the exact shape of everything we weren't saying, the way you're aware of a step in the dark. The pill bottles were on my phone, in my pocket, in my trousers, folded over the chair. When he went to shower I rinsed the plates, because I'm the kind of person who rinses the plates, and I went to put them on the counter by the door. The gold lighter was there, and next to it, face up, a copy of his statement to the Port Calder police, three pages, stapled, his signature at the bottom in a big careless loop. I didn't mean to read it. I'm trained to read things. My eyes went down it the way water goes downhill. *Found my husband on the kitchen floor at approximately 10:15 p.m. and called 911 immediately.* Downstairs, Stevie Nicks was telling somebody that thunder only happens when it's raining. The shower ran. I put the plates down very carefully, so they wouldn't make a sound.

A week of that. I'd like to say I spent it agonizing. I spent it at work until five, then at Suds City until seven the next morning, then at work again, in the same three shirts in rotation, which Pruitt's assistant noticed and was too polite to mention. I went to the deli on Harbor Street and ordered turkey on rye, no tomato, and ate it at my desk with the Vance file open in front of me, not reading it. The photograph of the pill bottles was on my phone. The statement was on his counter. Every morning I walked past both. He was easy to be with, that week, which surprised me. He slept like somebody had turned him off at the wall. He stole my socks. He played the keyboard with the sound off at two in the morning, just the click of the keys, working out something in the left hand, and when I asked what it was he said, "Nothing. Not yet." He tried to teach me to blow smoke rings with his cigarette and I coughed until Mrs. Tran knocked on the ceiling with a broom. On the Thursday there was sun. It came out around three and stayed, a thin hard yellow that made everything in Port Calder look like a photograph of itself. Nobody knew what to do. People stood outside the bank squinting. Jude called me at work and said, "Come outside. It's an emergency," and I went. We walked down to the old waterfront, past the fish processing plant that closed in the nineties and the pier where the ferry used to go before they built the bridge. The pier's still there. Nobody's fixed it, so nobody's closed it. There were two men fishing at the end with a bucket between them and a radio playing a Mariners game, and the water was a color I hadn't seen it before, almost green. He was in a good mood. He was telling me that the purple-tracksuit woman had come in that morning without the work-shirts man and sat alone reading a magazine, and he was building a whole theory out of it, a breakup, a reconciliation, possibly a death. "I talked to Constance," I said. It wasn't what I'd meant to say. I'd meant to say something about the weather. He kept walking. "Great. How's her Cobb salad." "She told me about the neighbor. Mrs. Okafor." He stopped then. The two fishermen were maybe forty feet away and one of them looked round and looked back. "Right," Jude said. "And?" "She says she saw someone in the kitchen doorway that night. Smoking. For a long time. While Arthur was on the floor." "Is that a question?" "Your statement says you called immediately." "You read my statement." He laughed, one short breath. "Of course you did. It was on the counter. You read the back of cereal boxes." He put his hands in his coat pockets. "Are you asking as my boyfriend or as the insurance company?" I should have had an answer. I'd had a week. "I don't know," I said. I watched it land. I watched him decide something about me, quickly, the way he'd decided I was a Virgo. "Okay," he said. "Okay. You want it? Here." He took out a cigarette and didn't light it, just held it. "I came home. He was on the floor. He was making this noise. And I was halfway through a cigarette, and I stood in the doorway and I finished it. Four minutes. Maybe five, I don't know, I didn't time it, I wasn't thinking *oh, let me get an accurate figure for the insurance man*." His voice had gone high and fast. "I stood there and I thought, I could just let this be over. That's what I thought. Clear as anything. Like reading a sign. And then I put it out on the doorframe and I called." The mark. Shoulder height, the size of a fingernail. I'd stood right in front of it. "Jude—" "Is that murder? Come on. You're the expert. Price it." He was almost smiling, which was the worst part. "What's four minutes worth, Mister Claims? You've got tables for this. You must. What does a heart do in four minutes? Run the numbers." "I don't know," I said again, because apparently it was the only sentence I had left. "No, you don't. Nobody does. The paramedics don't. I asked one, at the hospital, I said, would it have made a difference if I'd been faster, and she looked at me like—" He stopped. He looked down at the lighter in his other hand, the gold one, like he'd forgotten he was holding it. *Click.* Open. *Click.* Shut. Then he threw it. Not hard. Just a flick, sidearm, the way you'd skip a stone. It went up and caught the sun once and came down about twenty feet out and was gone without much of a splash. One of the fishermen said, "Hey," mildly, like we'd littered. Neither of us looked at where it went in. Neither of us said anything about it. It was just gone. "I'm going to go," Jude said. "I'll drive you." "You won't." He put the unlit cigarette behind his ear. "Go back to work, Miles. Write it down. That's what you're for." He walked off down the pier toward the road, not fast, his coat open, and didn't look back, and I stood there with the Mariners losing on the radio and the sun going in behind a cloud like somebody had finally remembered to turn it off. --- He didn't answer his phone that night. Or the next. On the third day it went straight to voicemail, his voice saying, *It's Jude, you know what to do, and if you don't I can't help you*, and I listened to that more times than I need to tell you. I went back to my apartment. I checked the smoke detector. I ate every night at the taco truck by the container yard, the one called El Güero, two al pastor and a Jarritos, sitting on an overturned crate while the cranes moved boxes around in the dark like they were trying to solve something. On the sixth night I scrolled to *Karen Lindqvist* and pressed call and hung up before it rang. Then I sat there for a while holding the phone, as if she might call back to ask what I'd wanted. She didn't. There was no reason she would.

Dennis Pruitt called me into his office on Monday at ten, which is when he calls people in for things that aren't emergencies but that he doesn't want to do after lunch. He was doing the crossword. He didn't look up. He had his mug, WORLD'S OKAYEST GRANDPA, and his red pen, which he held over the paper like a conductor and never used. "Sit down, kid. Six letters, 'loses one's nerve.'" "Quails," I said. "Quails." He wrote it in, in ink. Then he put the paper down and took his reading glasses off and let them hang on the cord against his tie. "Where are we on Vance?" "Close. I'm waiting on a couple of things." "Constance Whitlock's attorney called me Friday. Very pleasant man. Golfs." He rubbed his eyes. "He mentioned somebody on Alder Point saw your car up at the house around midnight a couple weeks back. I told him that couldn't be right. I told him my people don't make house calls at midnight." He looked at me then, finally, with the tired, patient face he's had for as long as I've known him, the face of a man who has heard every version of every story and is mostly hoping for a short one. "I'm sure there's a boring reason. I'd love to hear a boring reason, kid." "Sorrell called about some documents," I said. "Personal papers. He was worried about the estate lawyers removing them. I went up to confirm they were there and to tell him not to touch anything until probate. Twenty minutes. I should have logged it. I didn't. That's on me." It came out whole. The pause in the right place, the small admission at the end to make the rest of it sound true. I've listened to people lie to me for fifteen years and I've learned what the good ones do, and it turns out I learned it better than I knew. Pruitt looked at me for a second longer than I liked. "Log it," he said, and put his glasses back on. "Seven letters. 'Hidden, as a fault.'" I didn't know that one. I went back to my desk and sat with my hands flat on either side of the keyboard until they stopped feeling like somebody else's. --- Mrs. Okafor lives in a low brick house on the Point that must have been there before anyone thought to build out of glass. She had a proper teapot, brown, in a knitted cosy, and she poured for both of us before she'd let me open my notebook. "You're younger than I pictured," she said. "On the phone you sounded like a man who irons his socks." "I don't iron my socks." "Mm," she said. Her kitchen window looked straight across the lawn into the Vance kitchen. You could see the steel counters from where I sat. You could see the doorway. "I was a pharmacist forty-one years," she said. "I don't sleep. I sit here with the radio. That night I looked up and there was a cigarette in that door. You know how it glows when someone breathes in. It glowed and it faded and it glowed. For ages. And he was on the floor, Arthur. I could see his feet." She turned her cup a quarter turn on its saucer. "I thought he was lying down. People do strange things in their own houses. I didn't know until the ambulance." "How long would you say? Ages." "I'm old, Mr. Kasprzak, not blind. I know what a cigarette looks like at night. It looks like someone waiting." She sighed. "Arthur brought my paper up the drive every morning. Every morning, eleven years, in his dressing gown. Nobody asked him to." "And Mr. Sorrell?" She thought about it honestly, which was worse than if she hadn't. "He waved at me once," she said. "Like a boy. I felt sorry for him. I don't know why." She pushed the sugar toward me. "You haven't touched your tea." --- That night I drove to Rudy's and didn't go in. I parked across Fourth, under the streetlight that flickers, with the burned-out martini glass pink in my windshield, and sat. The mist came down and beaded on the glass and I didn't run the wipers. People went in. People came out and smoked under the awning and went back in. The man with the gray ponytail came out, looked straight at my car, and went back in without doing anything about it. I didn't have a plan. I want to be honest about that. I didn't think he'd be there, or I thought he might, and I didn't know which I wanted. I sat for an hour and ten minutes. I know because I kept checking. Nothing happened. Nothing kept happening. Then somebody knocked on the passenger window. He was wet through, hair flat, no coat, just one of Arthur's sweaters gone dark at the shoulders. I unlocked the door and he got in and shut it and sat there dripping on my upholstery, and neither of us said sorry. I'd thought I would. I found I didn't want to, and he didn't look like he was going to either, and that seemed about right. He got a cigarette out and lit it with a pink plastic Bic, the kind they sell in a bucket by the register. It took him three tries. He rolled the window down an inch. Then he took another cigarette out of the pack and held it out to me, unlit, very solemn, like a man offering a rose. I took it. I held it the way you'd hold a pencil. "Oh, God," he said. "No. Here." He reached over and moved my fingers, first and second, and put the filter between them, and tilted my wrist down. His hand was cold. "There. Now you look like a man with a past." We sat. The wipers weren't going. Rudy's got blurry. "I don't know if it mattered," he said, to the windshield. Quiet. Not the pier voice. "I think about it every day. Every single day, I stand in that door again." He tapped ash out the gap in the window. "And I'm not going to stop being the kind of person who stood there. I can't take it back by being sorry enough. I'm telling you so you can't say later you didn't know." I looked at the unlit cigarette between my fingers. I thought about Mrs. Okafor's teapot, and Arthur's feet, and the newspaper coming up the drive every morning for eleven years. I didn't tell him it was okay. It wasn't, and he'd have known I was lying, and I was out of lies for the day. "Okay," I said. He breathed out. He leaned his wet head against the window. "Okay," he said.

I wrote it at my kitchen table over two nights, which is about four hours longer than a report like that should take. The first night I just laid everything out. The policy. The death certificate, cardiac arrest, which is what they write when a heart stops and nobody is paid to be more specific. The pharmacy records from the Rexall on Delancey. The autopsy, which found what you'd expect in a fifty-eight-year-old man who ate steak like it was a moral position and had stopped taking the pills that let him. The police report, two pages, closed. Constance's letter, on heavy cream paper, which I set a little apart from the others, the way you'd move a glass away from the edge of a table. And my notes from Mrs. Okafor's kitchen. Three pages in pencil. *A cigarette in that door. It glowed and it faded. For ages. I could see his feet.* I'd written it all down exactly, because that's what I do. I'd even written *turned cup quarter turn on saucer* in the margin, as if anyone would ever need that. I put those on top and went to bed and didn't sleep, and at about three in the morning I got up and checked the smoke detector. It was the twenty-sixth. I didn't tick the calendar. There didn't seem to be a box for it. --- The second night I wrote the report. Most of it was true. That's the thing I keep coming back to. Decedent had a documented cardiac history. Decedent discontinued prescribed medication approximately eight weeks prior to death, confirmed by pharmacy records and unopened containers observed at the residence. I didn't say how I'd observed them. Medical examiner found no evidence of foul play. Police inquiry closed. All true. You could have sworn to every word. Then the paragraph about the neighbor. I wrote it six times. The first version was just her words, and when I read it back it sounded like what it was: a decent woman at her window who'd seen a man wait. So I tried again. By the sixth version it said: *Witness statement from adjacent resident, recalled at night through two glass walls at a distance of approximately twenty feet, is unclear as to duration and identity and is not corroborated by physical evidence or other testimony.* Every clause of that is technically true. It is also a lie, the way a photograph with the edges cut off is a lie. I recommended payment in full. Somewhere around one in the morning, reading it over, I thought about the crossword. Seven letters, hidden as a fault. *Papered.* It came to me just like that, three weeks late, the way answers do when they're no use to anyone. I've spent fifteen years working out what people are worth dead. That's the job, when you take the nice words off it. It turns out that the first time it really mattered, I cooked the number for someone who was still alive. I'd like to say I felt worse about that than I did. In the morning I put Mrs. Okafor's three pencil pages in a manila folder, labeled it *Vance – Correspondence (Misc.)*, and filed it in the archive room in a box of 2019 auto claims, where nobody has looked for anything since 2019. Then I went to the deli and got turkey on rye, no tomato, and ate all of it. --- Pruitt read it on a Wednesday. He read it slowly, the whole thing, holding his red pen over each page and never putting it down. It took him twenty-two minutes. I sat across from him the entire time and watched the steam come off WORLD'S OKAYEST GRANDPA and stop. When he got to the neighbor paragraph he stopped. I watched him read it. I watched him read it again. He had his glasses on the end of his nose and his face didn't do anything at all. Then he turned the page, and signed the last one, and closed the folder, and slid it back across to me. "I hope he's worth the paperwork," he said. That was all. He picked up the crossword. I stood there a moment longer, in case there was more, and there wasn't, and I went back to my desk. I still don't know what he meant. I've decided both versions, depending on the day. --- Constance called on Friday, at four, on my desk line. "Mr. Kasprzak." Every consonant. "I've been told the claim was approved." "Yes, ma'am." There was a pause long enough for me to hear her breathing, and behind it, faintly, wind. She was outside somewhere. The garden, I thought, with the camellias. Or a boat. "You'll find out," she said, very calmly, and hung up. I sat with the receiver in my hand until the dial tone went to that loud off-the-hook noise. She didn't call again. I never saw her after that. She didn't get punished for anything, because she hadn't done anything. She'd just been right, and lost, and I was the reason, and I think she knew that better than I did. --- I went to Marsh Street after work. I hadn't told Jude the report was done. I'd wanted to tell him in person. I'd pictured it in the car, the whole drive over, and I hadn't pictured it very well. Mrs. Tran was downstairs folding towels. "Dreams" was on. She looked up at me and then at the ceiling and shook her head once, not unkindly. The door at the top of the metal stairs wasn't locked. The room was empty. Not tidy, just empty: mattress stripped, keyboard gone from its stand, the sheet that had covered it folded on the floor, which was the only thing I'd ever seen him fold. The ashtrays were still there. Somebody had emptied them. No note. I looked. I looked in the kitchen and under the mattress and, I'm embarrassed to say, in the freezer. On the windowsill, where I'd knocked the ashtray off, there was a pink Bic lighter. The one from the car, or one just like it. It's impossible to tell those apart. That's the point of them. I left it there. I went down the stairs and across the lot and got in my car and put my hands on the wheel. Downstairs, through the laundromat window, Stevie Nicks was still going. Then I went back up and took it.

They moved me to auto claims in March. Nobody called it anything. Pruitt's assistant came by my desk with a box and a list of files and said, "Dennis thought you might like a change of pace," and smiled the smile people use at the vet. Auto is fender benders, mostly. A man in Oyster Bay claimed a deer had backed into his Silverado. I spent a week on it. I'm fairly sure he was telling the truth, and I found that disappointing in a way I don't want to look at too closely. I didn't ask why I'd been moved. I think if I'd asked, Pruitt would have told me, and then we'd both have had to know. The probate went on without me. I heard about it in pieces, the way you hear about weather in another state. Constance had contested the estate, privately, through three lawyers, over the house and the trust and a painting I'd never seen. The claim itself was paid in April. Four million dollars went into an account in Jude Sorrell's name, and I don't know what happened to it after that, because it wasn't my business anymore, and because he didn't call. In May I started smoking. Not really. One cigarette, on Thursdays, on the little balcony off my kitchen that's too narrow for a chair. I bought a pack of Chesterfields at the Chevron on Highway 9 because I didn't know any other brand. The kid at the counter asked for ID, which I've decided to take as a compliment. I light it with the pink Bic. I hold it the way I was shown, filter between the first two fingers, wrist down. I don't inhale much. I mostly just stand there and let it burn and feel like an idiot, and then I put it out in a saucer and wash the saucer. It's the most regular thing I do that isn't in the calendar. In June the weather turned nice for the second time that year, and this time it stayed. Two weeks of it. Port Calder lost its mind. People ate lunch outside on the courthouse steps. The mist burned off by ten every morning and the channel went blue and the cranes stood around in the sun looking embarrassed, like men caught in their underwear. I found it unsettling. I kept expecting it to be taken back. On the nineteenth I texted Karen happy birthday. She sent back a thumbs up and, a minute later, a second message: *Phil says hi.* I read that more times than was reasonable. I texted back *Hi Phil*, which I think was the first thing I'd ever said to Phil directly. It felt like a real development. --- He turned up on a Tuesday, a little after eight, which was wrong. It should have been a Thursday. He's never once done anything on the right day. I opened the door and he was standing on the mat with a green duffel bag over one shoulder, sunburnt across the nose and the backs of his hands, peeling a little, hair gone lighter at the ends. He had on a T-shirt that said PORT ANGELES MARINA and one of Arthur's cashmere sweaters tied around his waist, which in June was insane. "Hi," he said. I didn't say anything. I'd pictured this. I'd pictured it more than I'm going to put down here, and in none of the versions had I just stood there holding the door. "Can I come in? I've been sleeping on a boat. It's worse than it sounds, and it sounds bad." I stepped back. He came in and dropped the duffel in the hall and looked around my apartment, the whole thing, in one sweep, the way he'd looked at me across the dining table on Alder Point, like he was reading the menu. His eyes stopped on the kitchen counter. "You kept the Bic," he said. "It's a lighter. It lights things." "Mm," he said, which he must have learned from Mrs. Okafor, except he'd never met her. He told me about the money while I made coffee, because it was eight at night and I didn't know what else to make. Most of it had gone to the lawyers. Constance's lawyers, then his own, then the estate's, then some other lawyers whose purpose he'd never fully understood. "It's like a lawn," he said. "You just keep paying people to stand on it." What was left, he'd spent on a boat. "What kind of boat?" "A 1974 Chris-Craft. Twenty-six feet. Mahogany. It's called the *Second Wind*, which is either very good or very bad luck, I can't decide." "Can you drive a boat?" "I've driven it into a dock. Once. It was a very forgiving dock." He took the mug and wrapped both hands around it. "It's fine. It's mostly fine. The man at the marina says the hull is only cosmetic." "The hull is the part that keeps the water out." "See, this is why I came back," he said. "Nobody else knows these things." He didn't apologize for leaving. I didn't ask him to. I thought about it, standing at the counter with my coffee, what I'd say, and then I thought about the laundromat apartment with the sheet folded on the floor, and I found I didn't want him to say sorry, because then I'd have to decide whether I believed it. "I have an idea," he said. "No." "You haven't heard it." "I don't have to hear it." "Mexico," he said. "We take the boat down the coast. All the way. Ensenada. Further. There are towns down there with bars that have pianos in them nobody plays. I checked." He was leaning forward now, the sunburn going pink across his cheeks. "Two months. Three. You've got leave. You've never taken leave in your life, I'd bet money." "Neither of us can sail." "It's a motorboat, Miles, you don't sail it, you point it." "Neither of us can point it." He thought about that. Then he grinned, the chipped tooth, the whole awful thing. "Constance could teach us," he said. "She's very good with knots." I laughed. I didn't mean to. It was a terrible thing to say, and it was funny, and I hated that it was funny, and he watched me laugh with the pleased, satisfied face of a man who has knocked something off a shelf on purpose. I know what this costs. I want that on the record too. I've done the numbers. I did them without meaning to, standing in my own kitchen, the way you add up a restaurant bill in your head while someone's still talking: the leave I'd have to fight Pruitt for, the boat that has already met a dock, the money that's mostly gone, the four minutes in a doorway that aren't ever going to be gone. A man who leaves without a note. A man who comes back on a Tuesday. I got an answer. It wasn't a good one. He'd got up while I was thinking and gone to the window over the sink. He was working the latch. It sticks. You have to lift it and push at the same time, and nobody knows that, and he'd figured it out. He shoved it open, and the warm air came in off the street, and he got a Chesterfield out of my pack on the counter without asking. He'd opened the window first. Before I'd said a word about the smoke. In all the time I'd known him, it was the first considerate thing I'd ever seen him do. It was small. It was a window. I decided it counted for something, and I didn't check.

It's not quite a masterpiece because some of the metaphorical moments are slightly over-worked, the ending is a touch over-explained, and Constance is somewhat schematic. # Brainstorming **Core premise:** A bounty hunter (or mercenary, or reluctant courier) is hauling a captive tiefling across dangerous country to Irongate, where someone powerful will pay dearly for her. She is sharp-tongued, relentless, and clearly trying to get under his skin. The prompt's energy is banter-driven: a slow burn wrapped in a road trip. The tension comes from the countdown ("three days out"), the power imbalance, and the question of whether she's as guilty as the bounty claims. **Consent and the captivity dynamic:** Because this is erotica, the intimate content needs to be unambiguously mutual and desired. The captivity is the source of friction and flirtation, but it can't be the context for sex. The romance should only become physical once she is free, or once the power has shifted so fully that she holds as much control as he does. That shift can be a major story beat in itself. When she chooses him while she could walk away, it becomes the emotional and erotic payoff. **Character ideas — the captor:** - *Garrick Vane*, a weathered human bounty hunter in his forties. Taciturn and practical, he is saving for something specific: buying back his family's land, paying off a debt, or quitting the trade. - A half-orc ex-soldier working off a blood-debt to the lord of Irongate. - A disgraced knight who took the job because it was the only work left to him. - Common thread: he is laconic, which makes him the perfect foil for a talker. His flaw is that he doesn't ask questions about his bounties, and this job forces him to. **Character ideas — the tiefling:** - *Seraphine "Sera" Ashgrove*: crimson hair, curling horns, a restless tail, gold eyes. A con artist, thief, or runaway. - Possible secrets: - She stole something from the Irongate lord: a ledger, a relic, or proof of his crimes. - She is the lord's runaway betrothed, or a bargaining chip in a political deal. - She has infernal-pact magic, bound by the manacles, that she could use if freed. - She is innocent of the crime on the bounty sheet but guilty of something else. - She was his mark years ago in some forgotten way, and she remembers him when he doesn't remember her. - Her talking is strategic. It's how she probes for weakness, fights fear, and stays human (so to speak) to a man trying to see her as cargo. **Tone options:** - Witty and romantic-comedic, with heat, in the vein of "enemies to lovers on the road." - Grittier, grim-fantasy noir with moral weight. - A blend: banter on the surface, genuine stakes underneath. **Plot beats and possible complications:** - Rival hunters want her too, so the bounty is bigger than he was told. - A river crossing, a storm, or a ruined inn forces close quarters. - She saves his life while bound, or could have escaped and didn't. - He learns what the lord actually wants her for (execution, a ritual, marriage by force). - The countdown: Day 3, Day 2, Day 1, then Irongate's walls. - Climax: he must choose between the payout and her. Possibly he delivers her as part of a con they plan together. - Ending options: they ride off together; she robs him and leaves a note, then returns; they con the lord and split the ransom. **Pacing across 8 chapters (~1000 words each):** 1. Wagon or horseback, day three out. Establish voice, banter, the bounty, his stubborn silence, and her relentless needling. Hint that something is off about the job. 2. Camp that night. Small humanizing details: food, her tail, his old wounds. Rivals are glimpsed. 3. Ambush. She helps, or at least doesn't flee when she could. Trust cracks open. 4. Shelter in a storm or ruined inn. Honest conversation; he learns her story. Charged tension, but he refuses to act while she's bound. She notices that refusal, and it matters. 5. Revelation of the lord's true intent. He unbinds her. She has every chance to leave. 6. She stays. The first consensual intimacy, framed around her choice and her initiative. The erotic centerpiece. 7. They plan together, then arrive at Irongate. The con or confrontation unfolds, with the ransom in play. 8. Resolution and escape, and a final bit of banter. Possibly a second, more tender intimate scene or an afterglow epilogue. **Alternative structures:** - Alternate POV between them each chapter. - Frame each chapter with a "days remaining" header. - Tell it entirely from his POV, so her secrets stay mysterious. **Motifs:** her voice versus his silence; the manacles (removed as a turning point, perhaps given to her afterward as a symbol); fire and warmth, drawing on her infernal heritage; ledger and coin as measures of worth versus the ransom's cheapening of a person. # Reflection The banter-driven slow burn is the strongest angle. It matches the prompt's wry tone ("talk him into an early grave") and gives each chapter natural momentum. A grimdark take risks souring the erotic payoff, while pure comedy undercuts the stakes of a hunter delivering someone to her death. The blend feels right: jokes that mask fear, silence that masks conscience. The biggest structural concern is consent. Any physical intimacy while she's restrained and in his custody would muddy things, so I'm drawn to making her release the hinge of the story. Chapters 1–5 can crackle with tension, attraction, and near-moments, with his refusal to cross that line becoming a character beat she respects. Then chapter 6 is her decision, freely made, which makes the heat feel earned rather than coerced. It also gives her agency, which suits a character defined by her voice. Her secret works best if it's something that indicts the lord, like stolen proof of his crimes. That turns the climax into a partnership and a con rather than a simple rescue. It also neatly subverts "king's ransom": they could collect it by tricking the lord. The "we met before" idea is charming but may crowd 8,000 words, so it's worth keeping only as an optional grace note. Single POV from the hunter probably serves the mystery best, though a single chapter from her side (perhaps chapter 6) could deepen intimacy. Pacing is tight: the ambush and the storm shelter might combine to leave room for the Irongate con. The countdown headers are a cheap but effective way to keep urgency alive. For the erotic content, it should grow out of the dialogue. Her talking is foreplay, and his quiet attentiveness is his answer. Focusing on sensory specifics (horns, tail, heat, rough hands) and emotional vulnerability over mechanics will keep it character-driven. Two scenes, one urgent and one tender, likely suit the length without overwhelming the plot.
