# Two Days to Irongate The rain came in off the moor at about four in the afternoon. It came like someone had been saving it. By then they were three miles on from Callow, him in the back of the cart with his leg out straight and her up front on the bench. He'd moved her there because he couldn't drive and couldn't let go of her, and that was the only arrangement that solved both. Her wrists were chained to the bench rail. He had the long chain from her ankle round his fist. Parson went where Parson liked, which was mostly the road. "I could steer," she said, "if you gave me the reins." "No." "I'm steering now. With my mind. He's very receptive." Then the rain hit and she stopped talking, which was how he knew it was bad. The road ahead went under. It didn't flood exactly. It dissolved, a brown sheet sliding off the slope into the valley, with the Irongate bridge somewhere beyond it that he could no longer see. They weren't getting to the bridge tonight. They probably weren't getting to it tomorrow. He did the sum and didn't like it. There was a tollhouse at the valley head, burnt out in some quarrel about the tolls before he'd ever ridden this way. Two walls and half a roof and a hearth. Getting into it took most of an hour. She had to climb down and lead Parson by the cheekstrap, with Cobb hobbling behind on a cart-stave, the chain between them. At one point he fell and she stood in the rain looking at him with no expression at all. Then she held out both chained hands and he took them and she pulled. He got a fire going with the dry wood someone had left stacked in the chimney corner, some drover who'd known what this road did. He blessed the man silently. He chained her to the iron firedog, and she didn't even complain about it. The knee wouldn't bend. He bound it with a wet shirt and sat against the wall with it out in front of him like a log. For a long time neither of them said anything. The rain came through the gap in the roof in a thin cord and hissed on the stones. Parson stood in the dry corner with his head down and steamed. "You're going to ask again," she said eventually. "Yes." "Go on then." "What did you take from Prye?" She pulled her knees up and put her chin on them. "Drafts," she said. "Working papers. Two hundred and six land deeds and transfer records, and the practice sheets I did first to get the hands right. The old hands, the dead clerks. You've got to learn how a man made his *e*s forty years ago before you can make him sell his house." He waited. "Tanner's Ward. By the river. You'll have heard they're pulling it down." "Warehouses." "Warehouses. And every family in it turns out to have sold up to the House decades ago. Grandfathers signing over the roof. Very sad. Very legal. There's paper for all of it, and I made the paper." She said it flatly, looking at the fire. "Four hundred crowns. Prye's man came and found me in Brannock and told me I was the best in the south, and I was, and I am, and I said yes before he'd finished the sentence." "Then why's he paying three thousand for you." "Because I kept the drafts. Everyone burns the drafts. I didn't. And then I went and walked through the ward when they started knocking it down, and I—" She stopped. "And I thought, I've been underpaid. So I wrote him a letter." "Blackmail." "Correspondence." He reached across, slowly, as far as he could without moving the leg, and put two fingers on her wrist above the iron. She let him. She knew why he was doing it now, he thought. Or she'd guessed. Cool. Cool as the stones. He took his hand back. "I grew up there," she said, to the fire. "In the ward. I'm not doing a speech about it, I can see you bracing. They threw offal at me on feast days. I've since forged the deeds to their houses. It's called balance." "Is it." "No." She laughed, badly. "I don't know what it's called." The rain came down. The fire got into the good wood and settled. She shifted closer to it, and that brought her closer to him, near enough that he could feel the heat coming off her. It was real heat. She ran hot all the time; she'd said so. Only the lying made it worse. "Long night," she said. "Yes." "We could lose tomorrow too, with that road. Lose a whole day." She wasn't looking at him. Her voice was very light. "A lot of hours, a day and a night. Cold, in a place like this. A man with a bad leg who needs looking after. A woman might get very grateful, if someone was, for example, looking the other way about a key. People have got a great deal warmer on less." The tail stirred under its cord. He looked at her for a while. "No," he said. "I didn't ask anything." "No." Then, because she was still looking at the fire in that careful way: "I'm not stupid." He turned onto his side, awkwardly, the leg dragging, his back to her and the fire. He didn't much care if she heard him grunt. He felt her looking at the back of his head. She laughed at him. It was a quick, sharp sound, not much in it, and he waited for the rest: the book, the song, the bishop, what his mother would think. It didn't come. It went on not coming. The fire ticked. Parson shifted. Cobb lay with his face to the burnt wall and listened to the rain and to her breathing, which wasn't the breathing of someone asleep, and to the silence. It was the longest he'd heard from her in twelve days. He couldn't tell what sort of silence it was, and he found he wanted to, and he didn't like that either. He did the sums instead. Three thousand. Two thousand one hundred and twelve. *Prye pays twice.* An address in the Counting House for delivery, not the magistrate's court, not the gaol. He'd noticed that in Brannock too and hadn't stopped for it. A knee that wouldn't bend. Pell out there somewhere downriver with a hole in his wrist and a dead nephew, or a living one, telling someone. Once for her. Once for whoever brings her in. Behind him, very quietly, so low it was nearly under the rain, she began to hum something. It wasn't the bishop. It was one line of a tune over and over, the kind you'd sing to a child, and it didn't go anywhere. He didn't turn round. He lay there and counted it, and lost count, and started again.

# One Day to Irongate The rain had stopped some time before dawn. He knew because he'd been awake for it. The cord of water through the roof thinned to a drip, and the drip went on for an hour, and then there was only the river down in the valley, loud and full of itself. When the light came it was the colour of dishwater. The knee had stiffened overnight into something that wasn't really a joint any more. He got his hands under him and his back to the wall and stood up in stages, the way he'd seen old men do in alehouses, and didn't make any noise about it that he could help. Fenn was asleep. Actually asleep, curled round the firedog with her chained hands tucked under her chin and her mouth a bit open. Her hair had dried in a red snarl round the horns. She snored. He hadn't known that. Parson was not in the corner. Cobb found him outside, standing in the wet bracken with his nose to the nose of a strange horse. It was a bay gelding, saddled, its reins broken off short and trailing, mud to the girth. It had come up out of the valley in the night, probably following the only other animal it could smell, which was Parson. It did that thing horses do with a mule, somewhere between respect and pity. He knew the horse. He'd last seen it standing in the ford at Callow with nobody on it. He took it by the cheekstrap. It let him. There was a saddlebag, and in the saddlebag a heel of bread, a flask with nothing in it, a pair of wool socks somebody's mother had knitted, and an oilcloth packet. In the oilcloth there was a card. It was a delivery chit. He'd carried a hundred of them. Good stiff paper, the Counting House seal pressed into the corner, and in that lovely sloping clerk's hand, an address. Not the House itself. Not the front steps with the brass rail where a man could stand in daylight and be seen collecting his money. *Cellar entrance, Weigh Lane, by the east wall. Knock twice. Ask for the Second Assessor's clerk. After dark.* At the bottom, smaller, a second line. *Remit on delivery, both parties.* He read it three times. He turned it over and there was nothing on the back. Then he stood in the bracken for a while with the card in one hand and the bay's reins in the other and looked at nothing in particular. He could still take her in. He could go to the front steps instead of Weigh Lane, make a noise about it, get his money in front of witnesses. Prye would pay, because Prye would have to, and then Prye would have a very long time and a great deal of money in which to find a man with a bad knee and no friends. Cobb had seen what the House did to people it merely disliked. It wrote to them quarterly. Or he could walk her down Weigh Lane after dark and knock twice, and find out what *both parties* meant. He thought about the boy's hand going under. He thought, and didn't want to, about Aysh, who'd been nineteen too, and who'd asked Cobb all the way to the gaol at Scarrow whether it would be a rope or an axe, and Cobb had said he didn't know, which had been true for about another four days. "Well," he said to Parson. "That's that, then." Parson looked at him with no sympathy at all. When he went back in, she was sitting up. She saw the bay behind him through the gap in the wall and her face went very still. "Dace's," she said. "Yes." "Is he—" "Don't know. Horse doesn't know either." He got the keys off his belt. There were three: the ring, the wrists, the ankles. He'd had them eleven years. They were cut by a smith in Harl's Cross who'd charged him double because he'd said no man should need keys like that. He knelt, badly, on his good knee, and undid the ankles first. She didn't move. She watched his hands. He did the wrists. The iron had rubbed her raw underneath in a red band, and he looked at it, and didn't say anything. He cut the cord on her tail with his mother's peeling knife, the only blade he had within reach, and it took a while because the knife was useless. When it came free her tail went straight up and then round, fast, and wrapped itself three times round her own forearm like it was checking she was still there. He put her knife in her lap, the long thin one he'd taken off her in Brannock. Then his purse. It had forty-one crowns in it and some silver. "Take the bay," he said. "South road, over the top. Don't go by Callow. Don't go to Brannock, either. Somebody sold you there." She looked at the purse. She looked at him. "You're a terrible bounty hunter," she said. "Yes." "This is the worst thing I've ever seen a man do. For money. Against money. Whatever this is." "Go on." She got up. She was unsteady for a moment on her feet and put one hand on the wall, and then she wasn't. She tucked the knife into her boot and the purse into her shirt, and walked out past him into the grey morning without looking back. She got up on the bay, clumsily, because she hated horses and had told him so on four separate occasions. She turned its head south. It walked ten yards. Then it stopped, because she'd stopped it. She sat up there with her back to him and her tail lashing. "You haven't thought about this at all, have you," she said. "I've thought about it." "You've thought about *me*. You haven't thought about you." She turned the horse round. It didn't want to, and she swore at it until it did. "You owe the House two thousand one hundred and twelve crowns. You've got no purse, because I've got it. You can't walk. Pell's out there. And when I don't turn up in Weigh Lane tonight, who do you think Prye writes to next? Very politely?" He didn't answer. "You're going to die without me," she said, "and then who will I complain to?" "Anybody. You'll complain to anybody." "It's not the same. They answer." She rode back the ten yards and looked down at him. Her eyes in that light were the colour of weak tea with the sun in it. "He wants his drafts. He's paying three thousand for them. So we give him drafts." "You've got the drafts?" "I know where they are. That's not what I said." She smiled, and it wasn't a nice smile. It was the smile of somebody who'd spent a long time learning how a dead man made his *e*s. "I said we give him drafts." Cobb stood in the doorway of the burnt tollhouse on one leg. "That's mad," he said. "Yes," said Fenn. She held out a hand, palm up, for the keys. "I'm keeping these, by the way."

# One Day to Irongate (Night) The hayloft belonged to a man called Tobe who kept geese at Hollins End, four miles short of the Irongate walls. Tobe asked no questions for six crowns of Cobb's own money, which Fenn paid him out of Cobb's own purse, with a flourish, as if it had been her idea to be generous. Getting up the ladder took Cobb about as long as the ford had. She went up first and hauled on his collar. At the top he lay in the hay on his back like something landed. "Graceful," she said. "Go away." She didn't go away. She sat cross-legged under the lamp with a board across her knees and the things she'd bought in Hollins End spread round her: a quire of old paper from the chandler, soft with age, and ink she'd mixed herself out of oak galls, rust, and something from Tobe's kitchen she wouldn't name. She had three pens and a little knife, and a bottle of cold tea she was using to stain the edges. Then she stopped talking. He'd thought he'd like it. He'd thought about it for twelve days. She bent over the board and her tail went still in the hay behind her, and her face went still too, like a pond with the wind off it. The only sound was the pen and the geese complaining below. She did a whole sheet like that, a deed of transfer in a dead clerk's hand, *e*s and all. When she held it to the lamp to dry he couldn't have told it from real, and he'd handled a lot of paper with the House's seal on it. It unnerved him more than the bishop had. "How many does he need?" he said. "All of them, but he won't count. He'll check the top four and the bottom four and one from the middle, because he's a man who's tired and thinks he's thorough." She blew on the ink. "Nine good ones and a stack of rubbish. I'll be done by midnight." "And you walk in chained." "I walk in chained, you hand me over, he gives you the money, he gives me the cellar." She said it lightly. "Then I slip the pins and we leave before anyone's counted to four." "No." "*No*," she said, in a voice a good deal deeper than his. "Very persuasive. What's the other plan?" "I go in alone. Tell him you're held somewhere. Trade the papers for the money." "And he has you killed on the stairs and sends men to find out where somewhere is. You can't lie, Cobb. You go red at the ears. I've watched you tell Parson he's a good boy." She put the pen down. "I can make the chains work. I can make *him* work. I'm the only one here who can." "I'm not walking you into a cellar." "You were going to. Three days ago you were going to do it for two thousand one hundred and twelve crowns and never think about me again." "Yes." "So what's changed?" He didn't have an answer he wanted to give. She looked at him. Then she put the board aside, very carefully so the ink wouldn't smudge, and came across the hay on her knees, and took his face in both her ink-stained hands, and kissed him. It wasn't gentle. Her mouth was hot and she tasted of cold tea, and she kissed like she argued, too much and all at once. When she pulled back she didn't go far. "That's my choice," she said. "Same as the chains. Are you going to argue with that as well?" "No," he said, and put his hand in her hair, and pulled her back down. It was not graceful either. He tried to roll her under him and his knee informed him that was not happening, and he made a noise, and she laughed into his neck and pushed him flat. "Stay there. Honestly. Lie still and think of your debts." She pulled her shirt over her head and her left horn caught him above the eye, hard, and he swore. "Oh, *sorry*—" "Keep going." "Are you bleeding? You're bleeding a bit." "Keep *going*." She did. She was all hard lines and heat, ribs he could count, small breasts with nipples gone dark and tight. When he put his mouth to one she made a sound he'd never heard her make, not a word at all. She got his belt open and his breeches down over the bad knee with more care than he'd expected, then very little care after that. She wrapped her hand round his cock and told him in some detail what she intended to do with it, and she was filthier about it than the bishop song. "You could stop talking," he said. "I could," she agreed, and lowered herself onto him, and for a moment didn't. Then she started again, breathless. *There*, and *slower*, and *no, like that, you stubborn—*, and his name, which she'd never said like that. He held her hips and let her set the pace, because she was going to anyway. Somewhere in it her tail came round his thigh, and then round his wrist, tight, as though it had made its own mind up about him. The tuft brushed his palm. She didn't seem to know it was doing it. "Shut up," he said, when she began to tell him, mid-stroke, that the hay was going somewhere she'd rather it didn't. She laughed, loud enough that the geese below went off like a bagpipe. And then she did shut up. She bent over him with her hair falling round both their faces and her horns black against the lamp, and moved, and he stopped counting anything at all. After, she lay half across him with her cheek on his chest. The hay itched and his eyebrow had stopped bleeding. Below them the geese were still arguing. "You've got a very kind face," she said into his shirt. "Under all that. It's deeply irritating." He put his hand on her arm. The inside of her wrist, the raw band from the iron. Cool. He left his hand there and didn't say anything. The lamp was burning low, and there were eight deeds still to do, and she'd said midnight. "I'll get up in a minute," she said. In a minute, she was snoring.

# Irongate Irongate smelled of the tanneries before you could see it. It was a sour brown stink that came up the valley road on the wind and got into your teeth. Then the walls came out of the murk, grey and tall and streaked black where the rain ran down them, with the river going under the east gate in a culvert. He'd left Parson with Tobe. He'd told the mule it was temporary. Parson had bitten him. They came in at dusk through the Tanner's Gate, which was the cheapest and the least watched. On the far side of it half the ward was gone. There were whole streets of rubble with the chimneys still standing, and at the end of one of them the new warehouse frames were going up in pale timber, lamps hung on the scaffolds. Fenn walked through it in front of him with her wrists chained and her head down and didn't look left or right. Once, passing a gap where a row of houses had been, her step went short. Then it didn't. The manacles were his, with the pins drawn and filed and pushed back in so they'd hold for show and come apart for a twist. The key pin for the wrists was in her mouth, tucked in her cheek. She'd practised in the hayloft until she could do it without her jaw moving. The false drafts were in a satchel on his shoulder. The real ones were wherever she'd said they were, which was not somewhere she'd said. Weigh Lane ran along the inside of the east wall. It was narrow, and it stank of coal because the House had its coal delivered there. He found the door. He knocked twice. A clerk opened it. He was young, with inky cuffs, and he looked at Fenn the way you'd look at a delivery of fish, then at Cobb's leg, then stood aside. There were stairs going down, white marble, worn in the middle. At the bottom was a long low room with a good fire and a table and four men along the walls who weren't clerks. Behind the table sat Master Ottlin Prye, small and grey and clean, pouring tea. "Master Cobb," he said. "Two thousand one hundred and twelve, as of the quarter-day. Sit, please. Milk?" "No." "You've hurt your leg." He said it as if noting a figure. "And Mistress Fenn. You look tired." "I've been listening to him," Fenn said. "It's exhausting." Prye smiled politely at that, the way you'd smile at a child. He didn't look at her again. "The papers?" Cobb put the satchel on the table. The clerk opened it and began to lay the sheets out. Prye took up the top one and held it to the lamp and read it through. Then the next, and the next. Fourth. Then the bottom four, one at a time, turned over and back. Then he reached into the middle of the stack, drew one out, and read that. Cobb watched him do exactly what she'd said he would. He watched Fenn not watch it. "Good," Prye said. He nodded to one of the men on the wall, who brought two canvas sacks from a strongbox and set one of them on the table in front of Cobb. It clinked heavily when it landed. "Fifteen hundred," Prye said. "The balance on verification. You understand. My clerk will want the evening with these." "That wasn't the terms." "No." Prye sipped his tea. "I'm afraid terms are something I set, Master Cobb. You've been in debt. You know." Cobb put his hand on the sack. Nobody stopped him. He understood then that nobody was going to stop him taking it, because he wasn't going to be leaving with it. The clerk was still at the papers, squaring them into a stack. He licked his thumb to turn one over, the way clerks do, and looked at his thumb, and stopped. It was brown. Oak gall and rust and whatever she'd got out of Tobe's kitchen, not quite dry at the thick of the letters. It had been drying twenty hours, not forty years. "Master Prye," the clerk said. Fenn spat the pin into her palm. He'd seen a lot of fights and most of them were like this, short and stupid and hard to tell afterwards. A man came off the wall at him and Cobb hit him in the mouth with the sack of gold, which was the best thing he'd ever done with money. The manacles fell off Fenn's wrists onto the flags. She had her long knife out of her boot, and another man went back from her holding his forearm. Prye hadn't moved. He sat with his cup in his hand and said, quite mildly, "Not the papers, please, mind the papers." Someone knocked the lamp over, and the forgeries caught at once. Of course they did, because she'd used old paper. "Stairs," Fenn said. "Cobb. *Stairs.*" He got to the stairs. He got four up. The fifth was worn smooth in the middle like a cupped hand, and his right foot went into the hollow and turned. The knee didn't go the way it had in the river. It went like a branch. He heard it. He went down on the marble on his face with the sack under him, and for a moment there was no cellar and no Prye, only white. Then she had him by the collar. Nobody was holding the door at the top because they were all at the bottom putting out the drafts, and she didn't go up. She went sideways, dragging him, along a passage by the stairs that stank of coal. There was a hatch at the end and a chute beyond it, a steep black slope of iron going up to a square of dark sky with rain in it. "I can't," he said. "You can't do anything. It's very well established." She got under his arm. "Push with the good one. *Push.*" He'd never know how long it took. Coal slid under him and he slid with it. She swore the whole way, steadily, in the low voice from the ford. The sack of gold banged against his ribs where he'd tied it to his belt, because he'd be damned if he'd leave it. At the top she went out first and turned and hauled. He came out through the coal hole into Weigh Lane on his belly like something being born, and lay in the wet with the rain on his face. She was black to the elbows. So was he. Her horns were black. She sat on the cobbles next to him breathing hard. Below them, through the grating, somebody was shouting for water, and somebody else was saying *the stairs, the stairs*, and underneath it Prye's voice, not raised, asking whether anything could be saved. Fenn looked at the sack. "That's not three thousand," she said. "No." "That's not even half of three thousand. That's barely the debt." She wiped her face and made it worse. "He cheated us. The bastard *cheated* us." "Yes," said Cobb, and started, for the first time in about a year, to laugh.

She was talking to Parson. She sat up on the bench with the reins slack in one hand, because Parson went where Parson liked and she'd stopped pretending otherwise, and her tail hung down over the side-boards and swung with the cart. Cobb lay in the back on the good blanket with his leg in a splint made of two lath strips and most of Tobe's bedsheet. It stuck out in front of him like a fence post. The bonesetter at Hollins End had felt the knee for a long time with cold fingers and said *stick*. Cobb had asked for how long, and the man had looked at him with something like kindness and hadn't answered. The iron ring was still bolted to the bed of the cart by his hip. He'd put his hand on it a few times, the first day. He'd stopped doing that. They'd been five days on the south road. The moor had gone behind them and the country had flattened out into hedges and wet stubble and the occasional church, and she'd stopped outside every one of them to sing the bishop song at it. "How much," he said. She didn't turn round. "How much what." "The Exchange." "Enough." "How much is enough?" "That's my line." Her tail flicked. "Six hundred. And a letter of credit I'm not telling you about, and a promise from a very old man named Ferrant that the House will spend the next two years in front of the Guild Court explaining how the grandfathers of Tanner's Ward all signed their deeds in the same ink. Which they did. I'm good, but I'm not a *miracle*." "Will it do anything?" "For the ward?" She was quiet for a bit. "It's rubble, Cobb. They've already pulled it down. Ferrant wants to hurt Prye, he doesn't want to build anybody a house." She shrugged, and the whole bench creaked. "Maybe somebody gets some money. Maybe Prye doesn't get his Assessorship. Maybe nothing happens at all and everyone gets richer except the people who lived there. That's usually how it goes." He didn't say anything. There wasn't anything useful to say. His share had been sorted out on the second night, by her, on the lid of a flour barrel at an inn. Fifteen hundred from Prye, which she'd weighed three times in her hands and called an insult. Half the six hundred, which she'd pushed across the barrel at him before he'd opened his mouth, and then looked annoyed with herself for about an hour. Eighteen hundred, less Tobe, less the bonesetter, less the inn. He'd done the sum on the flat of his hand with a finger. It came to about three hundred short of the House, and whatever interest they'd put on the quarter-day, and he'd never be going back to Irongate to pay it anyway. Somebody would write to him. They'd write to him very politely for the rest of his life. They'd stopped the night before at a waystation near Corry, a barn with a loft that the carriers used, dry and nearly clean. It had not gone well, in the sense that he couldn't kneel, couldn't turn over, and at one point had needed her to lift the splinted leg out of the way like the tail of a cart. She had laughed until she cried. He had told her to shut up. She hadn't. It had been, all the same, better than the hayloft. It had been slower, and she'd known where the horns were this time, and his eyebrow had come through it intact. This morning she'd woken first and was sitting up in the straw picking it out of her hair, cursing it strand by strand, with the grey light from the door coming across her shoulders. The raw band from the manacles had gone brown and was starting to heal. He'd lain there looking at it. "What's your name," he'd said. She'd gone on picking at the straw. "Hesk," she'd said, after a while. "It's awful. It's a name for a goat. My mother named me after her mother, who by all accounts was also a goat. Don't you dare use it." He'd reached over, and she'd let him, and he'd put two fingers to the inside of her wrist. It was warm. But the sun had just come in through the door and was lying right across her arm, and she ran hot anyway, she always had. He'd held it a moment longer and found he couldn't tell, and then found he didn't much mind. "Well?" she'd said, not looking at him. "Cold." "Liar," she'd said, and got up. Now she flicked the reins at Parson, who ignored her. "We need to decide." "Decide what." "Where. South is Harl's Cross, and your friend at the alehouse, the one you don't talk about, and Pell's cousins, probably, and the House's letters. West is the coast. There's a town called Senna where they don't care about horns because everyone's half sea-monster anyway. East is Brannock, and I've got money in Brannock, and I want very much to find Oskar and ask him some questions with a knife." "Not Brannock." "No. Fine. Not Brannock." "Somewhere flat," he said. She turned round on the bench and looked at him, and at the leg, and he thought she'd laugh. She didn't. "Somewhere flat," she said. "All right." He lay back on the blanket. There was a lark going up somewhere over the stubble. He thought about the ford at Callow, the brown water going over his face, and the fifth step on Prye's stairs worn smooth like a cupped hand. He'd come close enough to both that he could still feel them. He thought he'd probably die of her eventually, one way or another. He thought it might take a while. "I've redone the book," she said. Me—" Parson stopped to look at a thistle. Cobb let him. "—well. Me, I'm still not allowed to bet on. It's unsporting. But if I were—"

The piece demonstrates real craft in dialogue, pacing, and the management of tone — balancing comedy, tension, and genuine feeling without letting any one register overwhelm the others. # Brainstorming **Tone anchors: "Cozy-Horror."** The blend is the whole challenge. Cozy means warmth, found family, cooking, small domestic rituals, a hearth against the dark. Horror means body dread, the uncanny, the ethical wrongness of eating something that might once have been human, and spores getting inside you. The best version lets them bleed into each other: a recipe card that is also a confession, a kitchen that smells wonderful and is terrifying for exactly that reason. **Premise variations:** - A fungal outbreak turned people and animals into "spore mutants," or "bloomers." The survivors are starving. One desperate night they cook a bloomer, and it tastes like the best mushroom risotto imaginable, like umami made flesh. - The mutants aren't transformed humans at all. They're a new organism that mimics shapes: deer, dogs, sometimes people. That makes the eating morally murky rather than outright cannibalism. - The mutants were human. The story leans into the taboo. Too dark for cozy, perhaps, unless the fungus has fully replaced the tissue: "there's nothing of them left, it's all mycelium." - Eating them changes you. The spores colonize the eaters slowly. Is it a curse or a symbiosis? Maybe it makes the eaters invisible to the mutants, since the mutants recognize them as kin. That gives a survival advantage with a creeping cost. - The mutants are delicious *on purpose*. The fungus wants to be eaten, because that's how it spreads. The deliciousness is a lure, a horror twist. **Characters:** - **Protagonist options:** - A former line cook or diner owner, which makes the cooking central. - A grandmother figure running a shelter in an old bakery. - A teenager keeping younger siblings alive. - A burned-out food critic, which is ironic and funny. - **Found family:** - A skeptical ex-nurse who worries about infection. - A kid who names the mutants. - A quiet old man who used to forage mushrooms and knows fungus lore. - A dog. - A pragmatic scavenger. - **An outside group:** a militarized compound that burns all fungus and would see the eaters as infected. That's a human antagonist. - **A mutant character:** one bloomer that keeps coming back to their door, gentle and almost familiar. Maybe it was someone they knew. **Setting ideas:** - A converted diner. - A snowed-in lodge in winter, where scarcity is sharpest and the cozy works well. - A seed library. - A greenhouse. - A subway station. Autumn or winter works well for mushrooms, hearths, soup, and wool blankets. **Plot beats over 8 chapters (rough):** 1. Hunger at the shelter. Establish the warmth and the starvation, and the mutants outside, pale and stalk-crowned, humming. 2. A mutant breaches or is killed near the door. The smell of it when it's cut or burned makes everyone's mouth water. Taboo debate. 3. The first meal. Ecstatic, sensory, guilty. Everyone sleeps well for the first time in months. 4. Routine forms: hunting, recipes, preserving (bloomer jerky, broth). Cozy peak. First small oddities: a faint glow in fingernails, dreams of soil, heightened smell. 5. Mutants stop attacking them. Discovery of the immunity or kinship. A trip out that should be fatal isn't. 6. The cost surfaces. Someone is changing faster, perhaps the old forager, who accepts it peacefully. Or the militarized group arrives and sees them as infected. 7. Crisis: the choice between stopping eating (starving, being hunted again) and continuing (becoming something else), or the fight against the humans. 8. Resolution. Bittersweet cozy. They become a new kind of community, half-bloomed, tending a garden, feeding travelers. Or the final image is a meal shared with a mutant at the table. Or the protagonist writes the last recipe as a warning or an invitation. **Motifs:** - Recipes as chapter openers. - The humming of the mutants, which becomes a lullaby. - A cast-iron pan. - Salt as the precious resource. - "Grace" said before meals, which evolves over the story. **Endings:** - Hopeful symbiosis. - A tragic, quiet loss of self. - An ambiguous last line: "It tastes like home now." # Reflection The strongest engine is the idea that deliciousness is the fungus's strategy. It explains the prompt's surprise, it creates an escalating horror, and it lets the cozy elements become the trap itself. The warmth isn't undercut; it's implicated. That's the ideal cozy-horror fusion. It pairs naturally with the "eating makes you kin" survival benefit, which gives chapters 5 and 6 real momentum rather than just repeated meals. Full human cannibalism would sink the cozy side. Making the mutants former humans whose tissue is fully replaced, or an ambiguous mimic organism, keeps the moral itch without revulsion. The ambiguity can itself be a quiet horror beat, such as finding a wedding ring inside one. A cook protagonist makes the sensory writing, which is the heart of the prompt, organic. The first-person voice of a warm, wry former diner cook could carry both the humor ("delicious") and the dread. The forager elder gives lore and a gentle sacrifice. The nurse provides the voice of caution. A kid supplies wonder. I should keep the cast small, four or five, for 8,000 words. A militarized human antagonist risks turning the story into a generic action finale and stealing space from the intimate transformation. It might work better as a brief, offstage threat, or not at all. The real antagonist is hunger and the slow change. An internal choice climax suits cozy horror better than a gunfight. For pacing, chapters 1–2 need genuine starvation to earn the desperation. Chapter 3's meal must be the showpiece. Chapter 4 is the cozy peak with seeds of wrongness. Chapters 5–6 bring revelation and cost. Chapter 7 is the choice. Chapter 8 is a bittersweet, ambiguous ending, perhaps with the mutant visitor finally sitting at the table. A snowbound winter diner or lodge setting concentrates everything. Recipe-card epigraphs are appealing but should stay short, so they don't eat the word budget.

# Intention **Premise:** Eight years after the Bloom, a fungal pandemic, the world is quiet and grey-white. The spore mutants, called "hummers" for the low sound they make, stalk the snow. Their tissue has been almost entirely replaced by mycelium. They were once human, but mostly they aren't now, and the story will keep that "mostly" itching. The central horror conceit is that the hummers are delicious *on purpose*. The fungus wants to be eaten. Eating it makes the survivors kin: first invisible to the hummers, then slowly becoming them. The cozy is the trap, and the story never fully condemns it. **Setting:** Dot's Diner, a roadside diner on a mountain highway, in deep winter. It has a wood stove, a cast-iron griddle, a counter with stools, a jukebox that doesn't work, and a snow-drifted parking lot where hummers wander. **Voice:** First-person past tense, told by **Marguerite "Dot" Okafor-Reyes**, fifties, a former short-order cook who owned the diner. She is warm, wry, bossy, and loving, and she measures life in meals. Her voice carries both halves of the tone: jokes and tenderness, with dread leaking under the door. She is writing this down as a recipe book for whoever comes next, and that framing pays off at the end. **Cast (kept small):** - **Wen**, 11, an orphan Dot took in. Curious, names the hummers, and is the moral barometer. - **Harlan**, 70s, a former mushroom forager. Gentle and knows fungal lore. He changes first and fastest, and accepts it. - **Priya**, 30s, an ex-ER nurse. Skeptical and protective of Wen, she is the voice of caution and keeps a notebook of symptoms. - **The Visitor**, a hummer that returns to the diner window every night. It hums a tune that sounds like an old jukebox song. It was possibly someone Dot knew: her late husband's friend, or a regular. Its identity is never confirmed. **Stylistic choices:** - Each chapter opens with a short recipe-card epigraph of 2–4 lines, handwritten in Dot's voice. They evolve from real pre-apocalypse recipes into hummer recipes, and finally into a recipe for "welcome." - Rich sensory food writing, especially smell and taste. The deliciousness must be convincing enough to seduce the reader too. - The horror stays quiet and bodily: faint gold threads under fingernails, dreams of roots, food losing flavor unless it's hummer, and the hum that starts to sound like words. - Grace before meals is a recurring ritual that shifts as they do. **Aim for:** earned desperation, genuine warmth, a moral grey zone, ambiguity over lore-dumping, and a bittersweet, unsettling final image. **Avoid:** action set-pieces, a militarized human antagonist (at most a distant radio broadcast in one line), gore-for-gore's-sake, explicit cannibalism framing, over-explaining the fungus, and a neatly resolved "cure." # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 – "Last of the Pantry"** *Epigraph:* Dot's actual diner chili recipe, with a note: "We are out of everything in this." The chapter opens on hunger. Dot boils the last of a boot-leather ham bone for the fourth time, and they ration crackers. The chapter establishes the diner, the stove, and each character's warmth and quirks: Wen reads old menus aloud like fairy tales, Harlan whittles, and Priya checks everyone's gums. Outside, hummers drift through the snow, pale with fungal crowns like frilled lamp shades. The Visitor appears at the window, humming, for the first time this winter. Supply runs have failed, and the road is snowed shut. The chapter ends with Dot quietly giving Wen her share and lying that she already ate. **Chapter 2 – "The Smell"** *Epigraph:* "Fat, onion, heat. Every good thing starts the same." A hummer breaks through the storeroom boarding at night. Priya and Harlan kill it with a fire axe and the griddle scraper, a frantic but brief scene. They burn the body in the stove to sterilize it, and the smell that rises is roasted mushrooms, browned butter, and something like Sunday. All four are salivating and ashamed. Harlan quietly mentions that some fungi want to be eaten. Priya refuses outright. Wen asks, "Was it a person?" The question hangs. They leave the second half of the body frozen in the lot. No one sleeps. **Chapter 3 – "Grace"** *Epigraph:* "Hummer, Night One. Sear hard. Don't look at it too long." Two days later, Wen faints. Dot makes the call. She butchers the frozen hummer, whose flesh is layered like oyster mushroom and pale as scallop, and cooks it in the cast iron with the last of the salt. This is the showpiece meal, written with ecstatic sensory detail. Priya holds out, then eats, and cries. They say grace, and Dot doesn't know who they're thanking. Everyone sleeps deeply for the first time in months. Dot dreams of warm soil. At the end of the chapter, the Visitor at the window hums, and it sounds pleased. **Chapter 4 – "Diner Hours"** *Epigraph:* "Hummer broth: bones (they have no bones), simmer 6 hrs, feeds four for a week." This is the cozy peak. They settle into routines: trapping hummers with a snare Harlan designs, curing hummer jerky, and making broth. Dot reopens the diner "for business" as a game, writing the day's specials on the chalkboard. Wen draws menus. Laughter returns, and there are card games by the stove. Seeds of wrongness appear in Priya's notebook: canned peaches taste like nothing now, everyone's smell is sharper, their nail beds show faint gold threads, and Harlan's cough has stopped entirely. Dot notices she can hear the hummers talking in the hum, but she tells no one. **Chapter 5 – "Walking Out"** *Epigraph:* "Travel rations: jerky, thermos of broth, and nerve." The fuel wood runs low, so a trip to the ranger station a mile away is necessary and would once have been fatal. Dot and Harlan go. Hummers surround them in the snow, lean close, sniff, and then turn away, gently parting like a crowd for regulars. The survivors are invisible, or rather, *recognized*. It's wondrous and terrifying at once. At the station, Dot finds a logbook from other survivors who ate hummers. The later entries grow shorter and dreamier, then end mid-sentence. Harlan walks among the hummers smiling. On the way back, Dot sees roots trailing from his boots. **Chapter 6 – "Harlan's Garden"** *Epigraph:* "Some recipes you only make once." Harlan's change accelerates. His skin turns velvet, his voice fills with hum, and a delicate cap begins at his temple. Priya wants to quarantine or stop eating immediately, and there is real conflict and grief. Harlan is calm. He says it doesn't hurt, it feels like "being part of the weather," and he shares forager lore: mycelium networks feed the forest, and nothing is ever really alone in it. A tender final dinner is held in his honor. At dawn he walks into the snow and joins the Visitor at the window. The two hum together. Wen watches, holding Dot's hand. **Chapter 7 – "Stop Eating"** *Epigraph:* A crossed-out recipe. Below it: "No more. Priya's rules." They try abstaining. The hunger returns worse than before, since normal food is ash to them now. On the third night of the fast, the hummers resume circling hungrily. They are no longer seeing kin, only prey. Then the hummers begin testing the boards. Wen is weakening. Priya, holding the notebook, admits her own threads have reached her wrists and that she has dreamed of Harlan saying it's warm down there. There is a quiet, devastating kitchen-table conversation: become something else together, or die as themselves. Dot realizes the choice she is making for Wen, who is barely begun in life. Wen settles it: "Harlan didn't look scared." Dot lights the stove. **Chapter 8 – "Open for Business"** *Epigraph:* "Recipe for Welcome: Leave the door unlocked. Keep the stove lit. Set an extra place." Time jumps forward to spring. The snow melts, and the diner parking lot is carpeted in pale gold mushrooms. Dot, Priya, and Wen are changed but still themselves, mostly. Dot's voice drifts at moments, and her sentences hum. They have rebuilt the diner as a waystation. A radio broadcast, heard in a single line, warns of "infected zones," and they ignore it. Travelers arrive, starving and afraid. Dot sets out the cast iron. The reader realizes the book is this recipe book, left on the counter for the newcomers. The final scene: at dusk, Harlan and the Visitor sit at the counter with the family, humming the jukebox song. Dot pours coffee, looks at the frightened travelers, and smiles. The last line is warm and chilling: something like *"Sit down, honey. You must be starving. Everyone is, at first."*
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
# How a Human Might Approach This A human writer who picked this prompt off a forum would probably start with the joke. The prompt is funny. "Who would have thought the things trying to kill us would be delicious?" has the rhythm of a punchline, and the "cozy-horror" tag signals someone who likes the genre mash for its own sake. A human would likely lean into that: a narrator with a specific, slightly unhinged voice, the pleasure of food writing, a bit of gallows humor. The dread would sneak in sideways rather than being announced. A human would also bring something *personal* and oddly specific. Their grandmother's actual way of rendering fat. A diner they worked at where the fryer oil was changed on Tuesdays. The real, unglamorous texture of hunger: headaches, irritability, thinking about toast constantly. They would include details that serve no thematic purpose but make the world feel lived-in. They'd probably be a bit messy. Some chapters would run long because they were having fun, and some threads would be dropped. They'd care more about a few great moments than about a symmetrical arc. And a human writer working on something like this would probably not know exactly what the story "means" going in. They'd find it. The ending might surprise them. # Telltale LLM Tendencies and How They Threaten This Piece **1. Safety and moral hedging.** LLMs soften taboos. They add "it wasn't really human anymore" disclaimers, have characters voice every objection in balanced debate, and ensure no one does anything unforgivable. This story's core is a taboo, so hedging guts it. The appeal is the guilty pleasure of the meal. If it's pre-absolved, there's no charge. **2. The bow.** LLMs resolve everything: every character gets an arc, every motif returns, the ending lands on a clever final line that restates the theme. Cozy-horror works best when something stays wrong at the end, unresolved and unexplained. **3. Impressive over readable.** There is a pull toward lush, metaphor-dense prose: "the smell unfurled like a memory of Sundays." Each line strains to be quotable. Food writing especially attracts this. Real sensual writing is often plain: "It tasted like the crispy bits at the bottom of the pan. I ate mine standing up." **4. Balanced ensembles and "roles."** LLM casts are built as functions: the Skeptic, the Wise Elder, the Innocent Child, the Mysterious Other. Each gets its beat. Real people are inconsistent, petty, funny at wrong moments, and don't all get equal airtime. **5. Emotional labeling.** Characters say how they feel in articulate full sentences. Grief comes out as speeches. Tender scenes include characters explaining the theme to each other ("nothing is ever really alone"). **6. Symmetry and tidy structure.** Motifs are planted and paid off with mechanical precision: grace, the jukebox song, the recipe book. Every chapter has an epigraph, a turn, and a closing image. That neatness reads as engineered. **7. Earnestness about the premise.** LLMs treat a wry prompt with solemnity and lose the humor. They over-lore the world, with names, eras, and rules. **8. Stock horror and cozy imagery.** Flickering stoves, snow, humming, glowing threads, hand-holding at dawn. These come from the genre's shared database rather than from observation. **9. Predictable escalation.** The shape of discovery, then cozy, then cost, then choice, then bittersweet transformation is the most probable shape. Readers who know the genre will see it coming from chapter 3. # Critique of the Current Intention and Plan **The cast is a role checklist.** Dot (warm narrator), Wen (innocent orphan child who "settles it"), Harlan (wise elder who dies serenely with lore), Priya (skeptic nurse with notebook). This is almost a template. Harlan in particular is the "magical old man who accepts his fate and dispenses wisdom." Wen as moral barometer, and a child who delivers the decisive line, is a trope that makes the kid a device instead of a person. Priya exists to object and then capitulate. **The name "Dot's Diner" plus "Marguerite 'Dot' Okafor-Reyes."** The hyphenated, diversity-signaling name feels assembled rather than grown. That's not a problem because of the heritage, but because nothing in the plan uses it. It reads as a box ticked. The name should come from a specific person. **The moral debate is pre-softened.** "Tissue almost entirely replaced by mycelium... mostly they aren't now." We've built the escape hatch before the story begins. The wedding ring idea from brainstorming was dropped. The single question "Was it a person?" "hangs," which is a very LLM move: raise the question, then decline to engage. **The escalation is highly predictable.** It follows invisibility, logbook with dreamier entries ending mid-sentence (a stock found-document trope), elder transforms first, abstinence fails, family chooses transformation together, then spring with gold mushrooms. Each beat is the most likely next beat. **Too many tidy motifs.** Recipe epigraphs that "evolve," grace that "shifts," a jukebox song that returns, the Visitor, the book-is-the-recipe-book reveal, and "Open for Business" echoing chapter 4's game. It's too symmetric. Some of these should be cut, or allowed to fail. **The ending is a bow wearing a horror costume.** "Sit down, honey. You must be starving. Everyone is, at first." That's a quotable final line with a twist sting. The spring time jump, the rebuilt waystation, the ignored radio broadcast, and Harlan returning to sit at the counter tie everything off. Having the whole family transform together in harmony is comforting. The dread becomes a wink. **Chapter 7 is a staged dilemma.** The kitchen-table talk, "become something else together or die as ourselves," Priya's confession, Dot's realization, and Wen's decisive line all read like a scripted thematic climax. Real choices under starvation are messier, less articulate, and often made by default rather than debate. **Harlan's transformation is aestheticized.** Velvet skin, a delicate cap, "part of the weather," walking into dawn, and humming duets are pretty, safe, and consequence-free. There's no smell, no ugliness, and no one who does it badly. **The Visitor's ambiguity is a coy device.** "Possibly someone Dot knew... identity never confirmed" is deliberate withholding to seem literary. It hasn't been decided what the Visitor means to Dot. **The humor is underplanned.** The intention says "wry," but the chapter plans contain almost no jokes. The prompt's comedic energy, "delicious," is largely missing. **The hunger is generic.** Boiled ham bone and rationed crackers are stock. No detail of what starvation does to people's tempers or bodies has been planned. **The food writing risks purple prose.** The "showpiece meal with ecstatic sensory detail" is exactly where the model will overwrite. **The pacing is even.** There are eight chapters of roughly 1,000 words, each with an epigraph, a turn, and a closing image. There's no variation, no short brutal chapter, and no long languid one. # Brainstorming: Making It More Human **Voice and humor** - Let Dot be funny in a way that sometimes misfires, like joking at a bad time and being told to shut up. She could critique the hummers like a cook: "Tough in the stalk. Best braised." Horror arrives through her cheerfulness being slightly off. - Give her a pet obsession: salt, or the proper way to season cast iron, which she rants about. - Let the epigraphs be inconsistent: some are recipes, some are grocery lists, one is a complaint about Priya, and some chapters have none. **Characters as people, not functions** - Make Harlan not wise. He could be a crank, vain about his foraging, wrong about half his lore, and scared of changing, clawing at it. Or he changes and it's mundane: he just gets quieter, and then one day doesn't come in. - Priya shouldn't just be the skeptic. Maybe she's the one who eats first and most greedily, and hates herself. Or she's secretly relieved by the transformation because she's exhausted. - Wen: a real 11-year-old is sometimes bratty, bored, and cruel. They might name hummers after people they dislike, or find eating them funny, or refuse and have to be force-fed. They should never deliver the thematic line. - Consider cutting the cast to three, or adding one character who's genuinely unlikable, someone the reader doesn't mind seeing change. - Give people conflicts over petty things: who gets the crispy edge, who snores. **Less hedging on the taboo** - Reintroduce a concrete human remnant, like a tattoo, a ring, or a zipper embedded in the flesh. Dot sets it aside and keeps cooking. No speech. - Let someone eat it knowing exactly what it was, and let that sit. - Decide the moral question matters to one character intensely and to others barely at all. **Break predictability** - Maybe the immunity or invisibility isn't universal. It works for some and not others, or wears off. - Perhaps someone doesn't change at all, and that's worse, being left out. - Consider that the hummers aren't gentle once you're kin. They're indifferent, or they want something (to be taken in, to be fed to others). - Drop the logbook, or make it mundane and useless: a guy's list of bird sightings. - Skip the formal "we tried abstaining" chapter. Maybe they just never stop, and the nearest they get to a choice is someone hiding food. **Endings without bows** - End before resolution: mid-meal, strangers at the door, Dot not yet deciding what to serve them. - Leave someone behind, unchanged and gone, or changed badly. - Avoid the quotable final line. End on a small, flat, specific action, like wiping the counter. - Consider no time jump. Keep it in winter. **Sensory writing that stays human** - Plain food language, the diner-cook register: "fond," "a good crust," "tastes like the beef stroganoff at the Moose Lodge." - Include bodily unpleasantness: bad breath, spore dust in sheets, strange stool, cold sweats, food cravings at 3 a.m. - Give the hunger specifics: fights, fantasies about specific brand-name foods, sleeping all day, cold hands. **Structure and pacing** - Vary chapter lengths within budget. One chapter might be a short, frantic night; another a long, slow day. - Don't close every chapter on an image. Some can just stop. - Let one motif fail: the jukebox never works, and no one hums the song. **The Visitor** - Decide who it is to Dot privately, and let that affect behavior without a reveal. Or make it funnier and sadder: it was the regular who always complained about her coffee. - Maybe the Visitor is the one they eat, and its absence afterward is the true horror beat. **Specificity** - Give the world concrete regional texture: the highway name, local brands, the church flyer still on the corkboard, a dead customer's ticket still clipped over the pass. - Let details exist without payoff.

Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **Core promise to the prompt:** The story is about hunger first and horror second. The desperation has to feel real and specific enough that the reader wants the characters to eat. The deliciousness has to be convincing, and it should be a little funny, because the prompt is a little funny. Then the cost comes in quietly, as a consequence of the pleasure. The characters are never punished in a way that neatly absolves anyone. **Setting:** The Blue Spruce Diner on Route 28 in the Adirondacks, the fourth winter after "the Bloom." Nobody uses a grander name for it. The diner has a wood stove the owner's late husband installed against code, a flat-top griddle, a Pepsi cooler used as a pantry, and a corkboard still holding a flyer for the Methodist church's pancake breakfast. There's a laminated menu with prices from before. The parking lot drifts over, and the hummers stand around in it like people waiting for a bus. **The hummers:** They are fungal mutants that were once people and animals. They have pale, gilled growths where faces were, and they make a low sound, like a refrigerator in another room. They kill by grabbing and holding on until you stop moving. I won't build any escape hatch. They were people, and clothes, fillings, and hearing aids turn up. Nobody delivers a speech about it. The story simply doesn't look away. **Voice:** First person, past tense, told by **Joanne "Jo" Kasprzak**, 58. She ran the Blue Spruce for 26 years. She's a short-order cook, not a chef, and she writes in plain diner language: *fond, crust, render, it's done when it's done*. She's funny, bossy, sometimes funny at the wrong moment, and gets told to shut up. She has a running grudge about people who don't salt as they go. Her food writing stays plain and bodily: "I ate mine standing at the flat-top like it was 1998 and I had eleven tickets up." Her humor carries the story. The dread lives in what she stops finding strange. **Cast (four living, one standing in the lot):** - **Jo:** narrator. - **Dana Rourke**, 40s, former LPN at the nursing home in town. She's tired, practical, and not a skeptic. She eats first and eats the most, then gets snappish about it. She keeps no notebook and makes no diagnoses. She has a bad knee and a dirty laugh. - **Marcus**, 11. He wandered in two winters ago and stayed. He's bored, mouthy, and occasionally cruel the way kids are. He names the hummers after teachers he hated. He thinks eating them is gross and hilarious in equal measure and asks for seconds. He never delivers the moral. - **Earl Pelletier**, 70s, a retired snowplow driver and self-taught mushroom forager. He's vain about it and wrong about half of it. He's a crank. He refuses to eat hummer, flatly and permanently. **He is the one who doesn't change.** That inverts the expected "elder transforms first" beat. The kinship protects the eaters, so it's Earl the hummers start coming for. He is left behind in the worst way. - **Gary Pruitt**, a hummer in the lot, and the decided identity of "the Visitor." Gary was a regular who sat at stool four every morning for eleven years and told Jo her coffee tasted burnt every single day. He still wears his Carhartt and a feed-store cap that the growth has fused to. Jo recognized him the first winter. She resents and misses him, and she hasn't told anyone. He stands at the window most nights. Eventually, she cooks him. **Stylistic choices:** - **Epigraphs appear inconsistently.** Some chapters open with a recipe, some with a list, one with a complaint, and some have none. They look like Jo's scraps, not a designed device. - **Chapter lengths and shapes vary** within roughly 1,000 words. One chapter is a short, ugly night. Not every chapter ends on an image. Some just stop. - **Hunger is written specifically:** headaches, cold hands, sleeping till noon, fights over a single Saltine, Marcus describing a Wendy's Frosty in detail until Dana throws a boot at him. - **The changes are written unglamorously:** cellar-smelling breath, grey dust in the bedsheets, canned peaches tasting like the can, sleeping in the walk-in because it's dark and damp and feels right. There is no velvet skin and no glowing threads. - **Some details have no payoff:** the church flyer, a ticket still clipped over the pass for a BLT with no mayo, the jukebox that never works. **Aims:** real guilt and real pleasure at the same table, humor that curdles, characters who are petty and inconsistent, a taboo left uncushioned, and an ending that stops rather than resolves. **Avoid:** - A family debate that settles the moral question - A wise elder dispensing fungal lore about interconnected forests - A child with the decisive line - Found logbooks - Radio broadcasts or militarized antagonists - A time jump to spring - A quotable final line - Purple food prose - Explaining what the hummers "want" # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1: Tuesday, Probably** *Epigraph:* Jo's chili recipe from the old binder, with the note "we have none of this" scrawled across it. The chapter establishes the hunger as texture rather than stakes. Jo boils a ham bone for the fifth time and admits the broth is "hot water that remembers a pig." There's a fight over the last sleeve of Saltines, and Marcus's Frosty monologue ends with the boot. Earl and Jo bicker about his foraging failures, since he swore the chaga off the birches would "keep a man going." The road has been shut since November, and the last supply run to the Agway came back empty. The hummers stand in the lot humming. Jo points out Gary through the window, cap and all, and tells us about the coffee complaints. She keeps it light, and it isn't. The chapter ends flat: Jo slips half her crackers into Marcus's coat pocket and goes to bed early so nobody sees her not eating. **Chapter 2: Storeroom** *No epigraph.* This is a short, frantic chapter. In the middle of the night a hummer pushes through the rotten storeroom boards. It grabs Dana's arm, and Earl and Jo beat it off with a fire axe and the griddle scraper. It is ugly and clumsy, and the thing is heavier than it should be. Earl insists they burn it in the stove because "spores." Half goes in the fire. Then the smell hits: browned butter, mushrooms seared right in a hot pan, the brown bits at the bottom of the roast. All four stand there with their mouths watering. Marcus says, "Oh no, it smells *good*," and laughs until he cries. Dana, cleaning her own arm, licks her thumb without thinking and then goes very still. Earl calls them all ghouls and goes to sleep in the booth by the door. They drag the other half out to the snowbank. Jo doesn't sleep. She lies awake thinking about how she'd cook it, and she hates that she knows. **Chapter 3: Sear Hard, Don't Look** *Epigraph:* "Night one. Hot pan. Salt early. Don't name it." Two days pass. Dana's hands shake too badly to pour water. Nobody makes a decision; Jo just goes out to the snowbank with the carving knife. Butchering it is the horror beat, handled plainly. The flesh is layered and pale, like oyster mushroom crossed with scallop. There's no bone, but there's a hearing aid, a Costco-brand one, which Jo sets on the windowsill and doesn't mention. She cooks it in the cast iron with the last of the good salt. The meal is written in plain diner language, and it's the best thing any of them has ever eaten. Dana eats three pieces before Jo has finished plating. Marcus asks if it has a name, and Jo tells him to shut up and eat. Earl sits at the counter chewing a stick of birch bark out of spite. He does not eat, and Jo doesn't push. They all sleep until noon. Jo dreams of nothing, of damp and dark, and wakes up rested for the first time since the Bloom. The hearing aid is still on the sill. **Chapter 4: Specials** *Epigraph:* A chalkboard specials list: "Hummer Hash, Hummer & Eggs (no eggs), Soup of the Day (hummer)." This is the cozy peak. Jo builds a snare out of plow chain in the lot, over Earl's objection that he's "not helping with that." Marcus names the catches after teachers: "We're having Mrs. Dubicki tonight." It's funny, and it's awful. Jo reopens the diner as a game, with Marcus taking orders on a real ticket pad and Jo yelling "order up." The first laughter in months comes over a game of rummy by the stove. Dana gains weight back and gets mouthy again. The small wrongnesses pile up unremarked: canned peaches taste like the can, the sheets have grey dust in them every morning, and everyone's breath smells like a cellar. Earl gets thinner and meaner. He eats the last of the stale oatmeal alone and doesn't share. Jo notices Gary at the window more often now, and he seems to be looking at her plate. **Chapter 5: Rock Salt** *Epigraph:* "Things we need: salt, lamp oil, Marcus's boots (too small), coffee (dream on)." They're out of salt, and Jo won't cook without it. She and Marcus snowshoe the mile and a half to the Agway, a trip that would have killed them last winter. Hummers drift toward them across the field, lean in close, and then turn away, the way regulars do when you're busy. Jo understands before she lets herself say it. The walk is eerie and oddly beautiful, and Marcus waves at them. At the Agway there's no revelation, only a pallet of water-softener salt, which Jo decides is good enough, and a mouse-eaten wall calendar from the year of the Bloom. On the way back, Gary follows them the whole way at a polite distance, like he used to walk behind her to the door at six a.m. before she'd unlocked it. Back at the diner, Earl has shoved the booths against the storeroom wall. Hummers were at the boards all afternoon, he says, only on his side, only where he sleeps. **Chapter 6: Earl** *No epigraph. The shortest chapter.* It covers one night and the next morning. The hummers press at the boards by Earl's booth, patient and quiet, with no interest in anyone else. Dana tries once, badly, to get him to eat: "one bite, Earl, just so they leave you alone." He says he'd rather be eaten by them than turn into one, and that at least he'll taste like Earl. It's the funniest thing he's ever said, and nobody laughs. At first light he straps on his snowshoes and says he's going to his camp on Stony Creek, which is nine miles off. He calls them what they are. Jo holds out a paper bag of jerky, and he drops it in the snow on the porch. Nobody stops him. She watches from the window as the hummers let him get almost to the tree line, then fold in around him, gently, without hurry. The chapter doesn't describe the rest. Jo goes and gets the jerky out of the snow because it's a waste. **Chapter 7: Burnt** *Epigraph:* "Gary Pruitt. Stool 4. Black, two sugars. Complained." Winter drags. The snare catches less; the lot is thinning out. The changes go on without anyone discussing them. Dana's gums are grey and she doesn't mention it. Marcus starts sleeping in the walk-in cooler because it's "nice in there," and Jo lets him. Jo can hear the hum as almost-words now, and Gary's sounds, unmistakably, like a complaint. There is no meeting and no vote about stopping. Once, Dana hides a slab of jerky under the register. Jo finds it, and neither of them says anything. By the end of February the only hummer that still comes close is Gary. Jo doesn't agonize out loud. She makes a pot of coffee, the real last of the Maxwell House she's been hiding, and pours a cup and sets it at stool four. Then she opens the door. What follows is quick and not pretty. The chapter ends with her cooking him, and it's the best batch yet, which she hates. She tells no one who it was. Dana probably knows. **Chapter 8: Two for Breakfast** *No epigraph.* March brings a false thaw. The lot is slush, with pale mushrooms coming up along the foundation. Jo's coffee tastes like dirt now, like everything that isn't hummer, and she drinks it anyway out of habit. Two strangers walk in off Route 28, a woman and a teenage boy. They're starving, frostbitten, and baffled that the hummers in the field didn't touch the diner. They stare at the chalkboard. Jo looks at them and notices she can smell exactly how hungry they are. She puts them at the counter. There is no decision scene and no explanation of what she'll tell them. She takes a portion out of the cooler and salts the pan early the way she always does. Marcus comes out of the walk-in rubbing his eyes, grey dust in his hair, and takes their order on the ticket pad. Out past the lot, at the tree line, stands a hummer in what might be a red plaid coat. Jo doesn't look long enough to be sure. The story ends on the sound of the pan getting hot and Jo's small, unshowy line, something like "It'll be a few minutes," with no sting and no wink. It ends before we know what she's going to serve them, or what they'll become.

# Joanne "Jo" Kasprzak **Background:** Born in Utica in 1966 to a Polish father who worked at the Oneida silverware plant and a mother who cleaned motel rooms in Old Forge every summer. Jo started working at sixteen, busing tables at the Blue Spruce when it was owned by a man named Stan Hollis, who drank. By twenty-eight she was running the kitchen. By thirty-two she'd bought the place, with a loan her husband Ray co-signed at the bank in Boonville. Ray was a lineman for National Grid, a big quiet man who installed the wood stove himself in 2003 "for when the power goes," and the power went often enough that he got to be right about it for twenty years. He died of a heart attack in 2019, shoveling the diner roof. She found him. She still thinks the roof didn't need shoveling that day. They had no kids. That was a decision early and a sorrow later, and she doesn't talk about it. She has a younger brother, Dennis, in Syracuse, whom she hasn't heard from since the Bloom and assumes is dead. She's made her peace with that, mostly, in the way you make peace with a bad tooth. **Personality:** Bossy in the way of people who've run a kitchen: she gives orders because somebody has to, and she's usually right about small things. Funny, with a mean streak she mostly aims at herself. She processes everything through work. When she's sad, she cleans the flat-top. When she's scared, she makes lists. She is not introspective by nature and distrusts people who are, so the narration keeps skidding away from feelings toward practical detail. That's where her grief shows. She's generous in action and stingy in words. She'll give you her crackers but won't tell you she's worried about you. She holds grudges with real devotion: a food distributor who shorted her in 2011, the county health inspector with the mustache, Gary Pruitt's coffee comments. **Idiosyncrasies:** - She salts as she goes and considers people who salt at the end morally suspect. "You can't fix it at the table. It's got to be in there from the start." - She calls everyone "hon" when she's being kind and by their full name when she's angry. Marcus is "Marcus Anthony" when he's in trouble, though she doesn't know his middle name. She made it up. - She talks to the flat-top. Not out loud much, but she pats it. - She keeps her reading glasses on a beaded chain a customer's granddaughter made her, and she'd rather go blind than lose them. - She rates everything on a diner scale. A good day is "a four-top that tips." A bad one is "a Sunday with the fryer down." - She hums Linda Ronstadt while she cooks, badly, the same three songs. This becomes quietly unnerving later, when humming means something else. - She has a bad right shoulder from thirty years of lifting stockpots and rolls it when she's thinking. **Flaws:** Controlling. She makes decisions for the group and calls it "just getting it done." Proud of her competence to the point of vanity. She'll cook hummer partly because she's good at it and can't stand watching food go to waste, and some part of her likes being needed again. She lies to protect people and doesn't consider it lying. She's capable of real coldness: she'll go get the jerky Earl dropped in the snow. She's the kind of person who's easy to love and hard to argue with, and she knows it. **Physicality:** Five-four, solid, wide in the hips and forearms. She's lost thirty pounds since the Bloom and her skin hangs in ways that surprise her in the mirror, so she avoids mirrors. Grey hair she used to dye auburn, now cut short with kitchen shears. Burn scars up both forearms, a white lattice from decades of oven racks. She moves efficiently, with no wasted steps, because a line cook who wanders gets burned. She wears Ray's old Carhartt vest over two sweaters and men's snow boots two sizes too big stuffed with socks. When she listens she crosses her arms and tilts her head like she's waiting for the punchline. **Motives and relationships:** Jo wants to keep the people in her diner alive. That's the whole of it, and underneath it is a less noble want: she needs something to feed, because if nobody's eating, she isn't anything. The diner is her marriage, her child, her career, and her gravestone all at once. - **Marcus:** She loves him, fiercely and without saying so. She's terrified of being responsible for him and would never admit that she's become his mother because it would mean admitting she's afraid of failing at it. - **Dana:** Friends, in the way two tired women become friends by working side by side. They fight about small things and never about big ones. Jo respects her and occasionally resents that Dana won't let her be in charge of everything. - **Earl:** They've known each other thirty years. He used to plow her lot first, before the Stewart's, as a favor. They bicker like an old married couple, which is all right because neither of them is interested in the other that way. She thinks he's a stubborn old fool. She's right. So is he. - **Gary:** Complicated. See Gary. **Voice:** > "People think hunger's a feeling, like being sad. It isn't. It's a job. You wake up and it's already been at work for hours, and it doesn't take lunch." > "I knew it was Gary the first winter. You don't serve a man eggs over medium eleven years running and not know the shape of him standing in a parking lot. I didn't tell anybody. What was I going to say? That's Gary, he thinks my coffee's burnt?" > "Salt early. That's the one thing I'd tell anybody. You can't fix it at the end." > (internal, Ch. 3) "It had no bones, which I kept waiting for. You get used to a knife finding a joint. This just kept going, pale and layered, like cutting into a stack of wet paper, and then there was the hearing aid." --- # Dana Rourke **Background:** Grew up in Old Forge, the middle of five kids, dad ran a bait shop, mom worked at the Enchanted Forest water park. Got her LPN at Herkimer County Community College and spent nineteen years at Valley View, the nursing home in town, doing night shifts. Divorced twice. The first husband drank and the second was just boring, which she says is worse. She has a daughter, Kayleigh, who was twenty and living in Albany when the Bloom hit. Dana doesn't know if she's alive. She doesn't talk about her except once in a while, sideways: "Kayleigh used to do that," about some small thing Marcus does. She has seen more death than anyone at the diner, handled bodies, changed dressings on people who were already more fungus than skin, and she has lost all squeamishness. That's why she eats first. It isn't greed, or not only. She's the person who's already decided bodies are just bodies. She has a dirty laugh, big and honking, the kind you'd hear across a bar, and it's startling to hear it after months of silence. She swears constantly and creatively. She says she doesn't want to know how it ends; she likes it better this way. - She cuts her own hair with the kitchen scissors and does it badly on purpose so nobody asks her to do theirs. - She calls Marcus "kid" and "you little shit," always with affection. **Flaws:** Snappish and defensive when she feels judged. Not always honest with herself. She tells herself the jerky under the register is for emergencies. She's cynical, sometimes to the point of cruelty. She'll say the true thing at the worst moment, such as telling Earl he's going to die out there, flatly, while he's lacing his boots. She's quick to give up on people, as a defense: she's lost enough of them that she pre-grieves. **Physicality:** Tall, five-ten, rawboned, big hands that have lifted a lot of people. Dirty-blond hair gone mostly grey and chopped to her jaw. She had a tan line from a watch she lost; the line's long gone but she still rubs the spot. Freckled, wind-chapped. She wears scrub pants under snow pants because she has twelve pairs and nothing else fits. Walks with a slight hitch from the knee. Sits with her legs sprawled wide, takes up space. When she eats she hunches over the plate, one arm curled around it like someone might take it. She laughs with her whole body, head back. **Motives and relationships:** Dana wants to stop being tired. She wants to stop being the one who handles the worst parts. Underneath, and she'd never say so, she's a little relieved by what the hummer is doing to them, because it feels like rest, like she might finally get to put something down. That relief scares her more than anything else. - **Jo:** A good friend. Dana lets Jo be in charge because it's easier, and resents it sometimes. Dana's the only one who pushes back on Jo, and Jo listens to her more than she lets on. - **Marcus:** Something between an aunt and an older sister. She teases him relentlessly. He's the thing she watches most carefully, because he's the age Kayleigh was when Dana got her second divorce and wasn't around enough. - **Earl:** She likes him more than she shows. She's the only one who tries to make him eat, and she does it badly, too bluntly, because she can't stand watching another old man die in front of her when she could have done something. - **Gary:** She never knew him. She probably figures it out at the end from Jo's face, and says nothing. **Voice:** > "It's a body, Earl. I've washed four hundred of them. He says it's "Smith," which it isn't. Jo has stopped asking.) **Background:** Eleven, maybe twelve now; he's not sure of his birthday, only that it's in the summer. He doesn't talk about how he got out or how he survived from nine to nearly eleven alone, and when he's asked, he makes jokes. Jo has decided that's the answer. He walked up to the Blue Spruce two winters ago wearing a Buffalo Bills hoodie and one glove, carrying a backpack with a can opener, a butter knife, and eight Pokémon cards. He still has the cards. He's never let anyone touch the holographic Charizard. **Personality:** Mouthy, bored, funny, restless. He names the hummers after teachers he hated, not out of any dark psychology but because it's funny to him, and because he's a kid. He's quick. He picks up on everything adults try to hide and pretends not to notice. He knows Jo gives him her crackers. He knows Dana hides food. He's the least afraid of what's happening, not from wisdom, but because he's eleven and doesn't fully believe anything bad can happen to him specifically, and because so much bad has happened already that this barely registers. **Idiosyncrasies:** - He narrates food in obsessive detail, especially fast food. He's hurt when Marcus mocks him, and doesn't show it. **Voice:** > "Chaga. Off the birches. Keeps a man going.
