There's a stove. I'll be fine." (Everyone knows. He knows they know.) --- # Gary Pruitt (Mostly offstage. Seen through Jo's eyes and memory, never speaking in the present.) **Background:** Sixty-eight at the Bloom. Worked at the Agway feed store in Boonville for thirty years, then retired and did handyman work around Old Forge for cash. Divorced, a long time ago; one son in Florida who didn't call much. Lived alone in a single-wide on Moose River Road with a beagle named Duke. He came into the Blue Spruce every morning at 6:05 a.m. for eleven years, sat at stool four, ordered black coffee with two sugars and eggs over medium with rye toast, and said, every single morning, "Coffee's burnt, Jo." Simmer 3 hrs min. Better next day.* *we have none of this* --- I boiled the ham bone again on what Dana said was Tuesday. Marcus said it was Thursday. Earl said it didn't matter what day it was, which was the first thing he'd been right about since October. It was the fifth time for that bone. The first time you get real broth, gold on top, a little fat you can skim and save. The second time's still decent. By the fourth it's hot water that remembers a pig. By the fifth it's hot water that heard about a pig once, from a friend. I salted it anyway, because you salt as you go, and because we still had salt then, most of a canister of Morton's I'd been treating like it was the last Morton's on earth, which for all I knew it was. I ladled it into the brown mugs, the ones with the chip on the handle that we never gave to customers. Four mugs. Everybody wrapped their hands around them first before they drank. That's the thing about the fourth winter. You stop eating food and start eating warm. "This is good, Jo," Dana said. "It's not." "No," she agreed. "But it's hot." Then there were the Saltines. We had one sleeve left from the box Earl found in a camper back in September, and I'd been doling them out two a day per person like communion. That morning I counted eleven in the sleeve. Eleven doesn't go into four. I've done a lot of math in my life, mostly figuring tips and food cost, and none of it was as hard as eleven into four. Marcus wanted the odd one on the grounds that he was growing. Dana said she was also growing, sideways, in reverse, and she'd take it. Earl said he didn't want any of their crackers and then watched every one of them the whole time like a dog at a picnic. It got loud. I put the odd cracker back in the sleeve and put the sleeve in the Pepsi cooler and closed the lid, and everybody looked at me like I'd shot somebody. "Tomorrow," I said. "It goes to whoever shuts up first." It went quiet for about a minute. Then Marcus started in. "Okay, so a Frosty, right?" "No," Dana said. "You don't use the spoon. That's how you know somebody's never had one right. You get the fries, and they have to be hot, like just-out hot, and you dip one in—" "Marcus Anthony." "—and it's hot and cold at the same time, like your mouth doesn't even know what's happening, and the salt on the fry gets in with the chocolate, and—" Dana's boot hit the wall about a foot over his head and dropped behind the counter. He laughed so hard he slid off the stool. I wanted to yell at him about sitting on the counter, which he'd been doing, but I was laughing too, and it hurt my stomach in the bad way, the hollow way. "You owe me a boot," Dana said. "You threw it!" "You made me." He went and got it for her. He's a good kid under the mouth. --- Earl sat at the end of the counter like he always did, back to the wall, chewing a birch twig. He'd been going out to the trees by the dumpster every couple days with a hatchet and coming back with lumps of black stuff off the birches that looked like somebody had burnt a muffin. "Chaga," he'd said, the first time. "Keeps a man going. The Russians drank it through the whole war." "What war, Earl?" Dana said. "All of 'em." So I'd boiled his chaga. It tasted like a wet stump. Earl drank two mugs and said he felt fine, and then he threw up behind the propane tanks, and now we didn't talk about chaga. The road had been shut since before Thanksgiving. Route 28 is plowed by nobody now, and the drifts come up to the Blue Spruce sign so it looks like we're called BLUE and nothing else. Back at the start of December, Dana and Earl walked out to the Agway in Old Forge on snowshoes. It took them the whole day. They came back with a bag of birdseed that had mice in it and a jug of antifreeze, and Earl's face was grey, and Dana wouldn't say what they'd seen on the way. We ate the birdseed. You pick the mice out. That was the last run. Nobody's said it's the last run. It's just the last one. --- Around four it got dark, which it does up here in January like somebody's pulled a plug. I went to the front window to check the lot, which is a thing I do, the way you check the stove's off even when you know it's off. They were out there. Seven or eight of them, standing around in the snow the way people wait for a bus, not in a line exactly, just spaced out. Pale where their faces used to be, all ruffled and layered, like the underside of the mushrooms Earl brings home and won't let anyone eat. You could hear them through the glass. A low sound, steady, like a refrigerator running in another room. We call them hummers. Nobody decided that. It's just what you'd call them. The one nearest the window had on a brown Carhartt jacket and a red Agway cap. The cap's grown right into him now. There's stuff coming up through the mesh in the back. That's Gary Pruitt. He sat at stool four every morning for eleven years. Black coffee, two sugars, eggs over medium, rye. Every single morning he'd take a sip and say, "Coffee's burnt, Jo." # Chapter 2: Storeroom It was the sound that woke me, and not the humming. I'd gotten used to the humming the way you get used to a freezer compressor. This was wood. A long, slow crack, like somebody leaning on a door they know is going to give. I sleep in the office behind the kitchen, on the cot Ray used to nap on between the breakfast and lunch rush. The storeroom's on the other side of that wall. I lay there for maybe three seconds thinking it was the roof, snow load, and then I thought about Ray on the roof, and then the wall creaked again and something on the other side of it hummed. Close enough that I felt it in the cot frame. Dana was already up. She sleeps on the bench in the kitchen because of her knee, and she was standing in the storeroom doorway in her scrub pants holding the flashlight when I got there, and she said, "Jo," very calm, the way I figure she used to say it at Valley View when somebody's heart stopped. The boards over the back window had been rotten since the fall. I'd meant to fix them. There's a list on the office wall and it was on the list, second after *salt*. One whole board was gone and the second was bowing in, and in the gap there was an arm. I say arm. It had a sleeve on it, a blue fleece, and then where a hand should have been it went pale and soft and branched, like cauliflower if cauliflower moved. It came through the rest of the way while we were looking at it. Not fast. They're never fast. It just kept coming, the way water keeps coming. Dana hit it with the flashlight, which was a waste of a flashlight. It took her by the forearm. That's what they do. They don't bite, they don't tear. They take hold of you and they don't let go until you stop moving, and then I don't know what they do after that, because nobody I've seen get held has told me. She didn't scream. She said "Oh, no, no, no" in a conversational way and sat down hard on a case of empty jars, and it came down with her, onto her, and the humming got very loud. I had the griddle scraper. I don't remember picking it up. I'd have told you it was on the flat-top where it lives, but I had it, and I hit that thing across the back of the head, where the fleece hood was, and it was like hitting a wet bale of hay. I hit it again. Dana was pulling and her arm was turning a color I didn't like even in the flashlight. Then Earl was there with the fire axe off the wall by the door, the one that had never come out of its glass case in twenty-six years. He's seventy-four. He brought it down across the arm, the one holding Dana, right above where the fleece stopped, and it didn't cut clean. It went in and stuck. He had to put his boot on the thing's shoulder and work it loose and do it again. I kept hitting it. I don't know what with, by then. Dana got her arm back and scooted backward across the floor into the canned goods shelf, which was empty, and it rang. It took a long time for it to stop moving. Longer than you'd want. Earl kept going. I think he was past the point where it was about stopping it. When he quit he leaned on the axe handle breathing like a steam engine, and he said, "Heavy," which was a strange thing to say, but he was right. I tried to roll it off the jars afterward and it was like moving a man twice the size. They're dense, all through. Like a wet mattress. "Burn it," Earl said. "Spores. All of it. Tonight." Nobody argued. --- The wood stove in the dining room is a big Vermont Castings Ray put in against code in 2003. It'll take a split log two feet long. It will not take a person, even a person who isn't one anymore. So Earl did the axe work on the storeroom floor, and I held the flashlight, and neither of us said anything, and when he had pieces I carried them. Marcus came out of the back booth in Ray's flannel, rubbing his eyes, and I told him to go back to bed, and he said, "What is that," and I said, "Firewood," and he stayed. Earl put the first piece in and shut the door on it and we all stood there. It hissed, and popped, and then the smell came. I have cooked on a flat-top for forty years. I know what I'm about to say. It smelled like butter going brown in a pan, just at the second before it burns, when it smells like nuts. It smelled like mushrooms you sear in batches because you don't crowd the pan, and they get that crust. It smelled like the bottom of a roasting pan on a Sunday when you pour the wine in and scrape. It smelled like my mother's kitchen and my own and every good thing I ever put in front of anybody. My mouth filled up with water so fast it hurt, under the jaw. I had to swallow twice. Marcus said, "Oh no." We looked at him. "Oh no," he said. "It smells *good*." And he started laughing. He laughed until he had to hold onto the counter, and then he was crying, and it was the same noise, and Dana put her hand on the back of his neck and left it there. Dana's forearm had gone grey and pebbled where it had held her, with a greasy sheen, like the thing had sweated on her. She had the first aid kit open on the counter and she was wiping it down with the last of the alcohol pads. Then she stopped and looked at her thumb, the one she'd been wiping with, and she put it in her mouth. She didn't decide to. I watched her not decide to. Then she took it out and went very still, and looked at the stove, and didn't look at any of us. Earl looked at all of us. "Ghouls," he said. "Every one of you." And he took his hatchet and went and lay down in his booth by the door with his back to the wall. --- We only burned half. The stove couldn't take more than that before morning without smoking us out, and nobody wanted to open a window with that smell pouring out of it into a lot full of them. Dana and I dragged the rest out the back on a tarp and left it in the snowbank past the dumpster, where it's cold enough to keep anything. That was how I thought it. *Cold enough to keep.* I heard myself think it. I didn't sleep. I lay on Ray's cot listening to the stove tick down and the humming out back, and I thought about how it had come apart under the axe, in layers, and I thought about what a hard sear would do to a layer like that, and whether it'd want salt early, and how thin I'd slice it. I knew. That's what kept me up. I already knew exactly how I'd cook it.

# Chapter 3: Sear Hard, Don't Look *Night one. Hot pan. Salt early. Don't name it.* --- Nobody talked about the snowbank for two days. That's not true. Nobody talked about it out loud. But I'd catch Marcus at the back window, the one we'd nailed a door over, with his eye to the gap between the door and the frame. I caught Dana out there once too, standing by the dumpster in her snow pants with her arms crossed, looking at the tarp like it owed her money. She came back in and said she'd been checking the propane. The propane's been empty since Christmas. I didn't go out there. I didn't need to. I knew where it was. We ate the odd cracker, finally. Marcus got it, because on the second morning he didn't say one word through breakfast, which was the broth again, sixth go-round, and I said, "You win," and he said, "Win what," and he'd honestly forgotten. That scared me more than anything. A kid who forgets about a cracker. The second night Dana tried to pour herself water out of the pitcher and couldn't. Her hands were going. Not a tremble, a real shake, like somebody idling a truck in her. The water went on the counter and she stood there looking at it. "Blood sugar," she said. "It's fine. I've seen it a hundred times." "On who?" She wiped the water up with her sleeve. "On people who died, Jo. Mostly." I went and got the carving knife. --- I'd like to say there was a talk. That we all sat down at the counter and said our piece and somebody voted. There wasn't. I got the knife off the magnet strip and the headlamp off the hook and put on Ray's vest, and Dana watched me do it and didn't say anything, and that was the talk. Earl said, "Joanne." Just that. I went out the back anyway. It was maybe ten below. The tarp was frozen stiff and had drifted over, and I had to kick the snow off. It had kept perfectly. It hadn't gone bad or gone soft. It looked the same as it had on the storeroom floor, the blue fleece gone white with frost, and underneath it, where Earl's axe had opened it, you could see inside. No bone. I kept waiting for bone. When you break down a chicken or a pork shoulder, your knife is always looking for the joint, and you find it, and you pop it. This just kept going. Pale, layered, like cutting into a stack of wet paper, except it held its shape. Cream-colored, almost pearly in the headlamp. Like oyster mushroom, if oyster mushroom came in a slab. Like a big sea scallop. It cut clean. It cut beautifully, honest to God. I've never had a knife go through anything like that. About where the chest would've been, the knife hit something hard and small and I stopped. It was a hearing aid. A little tan one, the kind that goes behind the ear. Kirkland brand. You could still read it. It had grown down in there somehow, a couple inches from where an ear would be, like the whole thing had shifted around while it was busy becoming something else. I stood there with it in my glove for a while. Then I put it in the vest pocket and kept cutting. --- I used the ten-inch cast iron, Ray's mother's, the one that's black as a record. Got it screaming hot on the wood stove. Ran it with a little of the lard we'd been saving since fall, which I hadn't told anybody about, and I'm not sorry. I sliced the pieces about half an inch. Patted them dry, because a wet thing won't sear, it steams, and then you've got gray. Then the salt. It was the last of the good Morton's. I tipped the canister and there wasn't much, and I put all of it on. Salt early. You can't fix it at the end. When the first piece went in the pan it made the right noise. Everybody in the diner heard it. Marcus came off the booth and stood right at my elbow, close enough I told him to back up before he got spit on, and he didn't back up. It browned like a dream. Deep gold, crackling at the edges where the layers pulled apart a little. I flipped it and the kitchen filled up with that smell again, the brown-butter smell, and this time nobody laughed or cried. It was quiet in there except for the pan. I didn't get to plate it. Dana took the first piece off the cutting board with her fingers. It was too hot and she ate it anyway, going "hah, hah" with her mouth open, and she took another one and ate that, and she was reaching for the third one before I'd even gotten the next batch in the pan. "Jesus, Mary and Joseph," she said, with her mouth full. "Don't look at me. I'm not talking about it." So I ate one. Standing up at the stove, like it was 1998 and I had eleven tickets up. I'm not going to be fancy about it. It tasted like the crusty bits at the bottom of a pan. It tasted like a good steak and a good mushroom had a baby and the baby had been cooked right. It was rich. It was salty. It was the best thing I have ever eaten in my life, and I've eaten in Montreal. I had to put my hand on the counter. Marcus ate four pieces. Around the third one he said, "Does it have a name?" "Shut up and eat." "Because Mrs. Dubicki—" "Marcus Anthony." He shut up and ate. Earl sat at the end of the counter the whole time, back to the wall, chewing a hunk of birch bark he'd peeled off something outside. He chewed it like it was jerky. He didn't look at the pan and he didn't look at us, and I didn't hand him a plate, and he didn't ask. When we were done he got up and put another log on the stove for us. I don't know what that was. I think it was just Earl. --- We slept until noon. All three of us that ate. I don't remember lying down on the cot. I remember the stove ticking, and being warm, all the way through, in the middle of me, for the first time since the Bloom. I dreamed about nothing. Dark. Damp. Like being down under a pile of leaves in October, where it's warmer than it has any right to be, and quiet, and something is holding you, and you don't mind. I woke up rested. I mean rested. My shoulder didn't hurt. When I went out front Earl was already up, sitting at the counter looking at the window over the sink. I'd put the hearing aid on the sill the night before. I don't remember doing that either. It was just sitting there in the gray light, tan and small, like somebody would be back for it. Neither of us said anything about it. I made the broth.

I didn't quit cooking. I quit pretending it was fine. You can eat a thing without salt. People do. People in hospitals do, and Dana says they hate every minute of it. But I'd stand at the stove with a slab of Ms. Petrakis going gold in the pan and it would smell like heaven and then taste like heaven with the sound off. Flat. Dana and Earl had gone through it in December looking for food and hadn't been looking for salt. Nobody thinks about salt until they're out. Last winter that walk would've killed us. That's the plain truth. You'd get a hundred yards off the porch and they'd start drifting over, slow, from wherever they were standing, and there's nowhere to go on a flat field. Dana and Earl only made it in December because it was forty below and they were slower in the cold, and because they'd run, and because Dana won't talk about what else. So I don't know why I thought I could go. I just knew I was going. Dana couldn't. Her knee had swelled up like a grapefruit after she'd slipped on the porch step, and she was sitting with it up on a stool with snow in a bread bag on top. Earl said he wasn't walking anywhere with me, he'd walked enough, and he looked at me when he said it like he meant something else. Marcus was already putting his boots on. They were too small. He'd cut the toes out of a pair of wool socks to fit over his feet inside them, and he walked like it hurt, and he said it didn't. "No," I said. "You need somebody to carry the sled." "I'll carry the sled." "Your shoulder," he said, and rolled his own shoulder at me, exactly how I do it, and I didn't have anything to say to that. --- We went across the field. It was bright out, one of those January days that looks warm and isn't, the snow so white it hurt. The snowshoes were Ray's and Earl's. Marcus's were too big and he kept stepping on his own frames and going down, and swearing, and I let him swear. We were maybe a quarter of the way across when they started coming. There were five of them out by the tree line, and they turned toward us. Not fast. Just turned, the way people in a waiting room turn when the door opens. They came across the snow at that slow heavy walk, and the humming came with them, and I stopped. Marcus stopped. I had the carving knife in my belt and I remember thinking it was a stupid thing to have brought, like bringing a spoon. I said, "Stay behind me," and he got behind me, and they came right up. The first one was close enough I could have touched it. Tall. Some kind of green jacket, gone gray with frost. It leaned in toward me with that soft layered face, down close to my neck, where you'd smell somebody. The hum went right into my chest. I stood there with my eyes open because I couldn't close them. Then it turned away. Just turned and went on past, off to the left, like I'd been standing in its way at a bus stop. The next one did the same. Leaned in, stopped, turned off. One of them bent toward Marcus and I nearly went for it with the knife and it leaned back and went off and stood in the snow twenty feet away, facing nothing. You know how regulars are when you've got a full counter. They come in and see you've got your hands full and they don't bother you. They nod and go sit down. That's what it was like. I knew what it meant before I let myself say it. Dana would say that's how I do everything. Marcus let out a breath like he'd been holding it since the porch. Then he lifted his mitten and waved at the one in the green jacket. "Why'd you do that?" "I don't know," he said. "It seemed polite." --- The Agway door was still busted from December. Inside it was dark and smelled like mice and cold fertilizer. The food shelves were bare down to the metal. Somebody had pulled the pet food aisle apart a long time ago. No table salt. No kosher. Dana had been right about that, it was all gone. But back by the loading dock there was a pallet of water-softener salt, forty-pound bags, Diamond Crystal, shrink-wrapped and fine. I cut one open and put a pellet on my tongue. It was salt. A little chalky. Good enough. "Is that even food?" Marcus said. "It's salt. Salt's salt." It isn't, entirely. I don't care. We got two bags on the sled. That's eighty pounds and I felt every one. Behind the counter, on the wall, there was a calendar from the Boonville Farm Credit, the mice had gotten most of it, and it was still on the month of the Bloom. A picture of a red barn. Never said anything. Just waited behind me till it was unlocked. He walked all the way back to the lot like that. Then he went and stood by the window at stool four. --- When we came in, the booths had moved. Earl had dragged two of them off their posts and shoved them against the storeroom wall, and stacked the chairs from table six on top, and he was sitting in the one by the door with the hatchet on his knees. None of us did. --- Around midnight Dana got up off her stool, bad knee and all, and went to the cooler and cut a piece off what was left of Ms. Petrakis. She didn't cook it. She put it on a saucer and limped it over to Earl's booth and set it on the table in front of him. "One bite," she said. He looked at it. He didn't look at her. It was nice. I came back out fast. He still hadn't said Earl's name. He sat on stool two now for meals, not the counter. I never did yell at him about the counter again. I'd have liked to. Gary's had a shape. Every night he'd stand at the window by stool four, and his was always the same up and down, short, flat on the end. I'd had it since the first winter, hidden in a box of old invoices behind the filing cabinet. About a third of a can. I'd been saving it for, I don't know what. Something. # Chapter 8: Two for Breakfast The thaw came the second week of March, and it was a liar, like it always is up here. For four days it was forty degrees in the afternoon. The icicles off the porch roof dripped so steady it sounded like rain, and the lot went to slush, brown and gray, with the tops of the wheel stops showing through. Route 28 came up out of the drifts in stripes. You could see the yellow line in places. I stood on the porch and looked at it for a long time, that yellow line. I'd forgotten it was there. Everybody who's lived up here more than a year knows it'll snow again. It always snows again. Ray used to say March is just February wearing a nicer coat. Along the foundation of the diner, where the snow melted back first against the warm wall by the stove, there were mushrooms coming up. Little pale ones, a whole row of them, frilled underneath. They came up overnight. I found them the first morning of the thaw when I went out to shake the sheets. I shook the sheets out right over them, gray dust and all, and I didn't think about it until I was back inside. Earl would've known what they were called. He'd have been wrong, but he'd have known. --- I'd made coffee that morning out of the grounds from the Maxwell House. I'd dried them on a plate on top of the stove and saved them in a jar, because you don't throw out coffee, even the second time. It came out thin and brown. It tasted like dirt. Not bad dirt. I don't know how else to say it. Everything that isn't hummer tastes like something now. The peaches taste like the can. The water tastes like the pipe. The coffee tasted like the ground under the leaves in the woods behind the diner, and I drank it anyway, standing at the counter, because I've had a cup of coffee at a quarter to six every morning since 1982 and I'm not going to quit over a thing like taste. Dana was on the bench with her leg up, reading the same page she's been reading since Christmas. Marcus was still in the walk-in. The humming out in the field was far off and quiet, like a highway you can hear from bed. That's when the door opened. --- I didn't hear them on the porch. That's the thing I keep coming back to. I used to hear a car door in the lot from the back of the kitchen with the fryer going. My ears are different now, but they're different for the humming, not for people. People I've gotten bad at. It was a woman and a boy. She was maybe thirty-five, though it's hard to tell anymore, and he was fourteen or fifteen, tall and skinny with a wool hat pulled down to his eyebrows. They stood in the doorway with the cold coming in around them and they looked at the stove like it was a church. The woman had a hunting rifle she didn't point at anybody. It just hung in her hand. Her lips were split, and there were white patches on her cheekbones where the frostbite had got her, and the boy's jacket was a woman's jacket, too short in the arms. "We saw smoke," she said. "From the road." "Come in," I said. "Shut the door, hon, you're heating the lot." The boy shut it. They stood there. The woman kept looking back at the window like she couldn't make sense of something. "They're all over that field," she said. "They followed us two days. They were right there, at the end of your lot, and they just." She stopped. "They just stopped. They didn't come up." "No," I said. "They don't." Dana had put her book down. She looked at the woman's face, her color, her eyes, the way she was breathing. The first time she'd done that in a month. Then she looked over at me. --- I put them at the counter. The woman at stool three, the boy at stool five. Nobody sat at four, and I didn't say anything about it, and they didn't ask. Standing there, I could smell how hungry they were. I don't know how to put that. It wasn't a smell like sweat. It was more like how you can walk into a kitchen and know somebody's been burning something. It was on them. Sour and thin. I've smelled it on myself, I think, before. I just never could tell before. The boy was reading the chalkboard. His lips moved. I'd never wiped it. *Hummer Hash. Hummer & Eggs (no eggs). Soup of the Day (hummer). Pie (no).* "What's hummer?" he said. The woman didn't say anything. She was looking at the chalkboard too. She'd figured it out faster than he had, I think, or she'd figured out enough to stop asking. I didn't answer him. I want to say I had a reason for that. I don't know what it was. I went to the walk-in instead. Marcus was sitting up on his shelf with the blanket around him. He had gray dust in his hair, in his eyebrows, like he'd been out in a light snow. He looked at me in the dark. "People," I said. "For real?" "Two. Go wash your face." He didn't wash his face. He came out rubbing his eyes, and he looked at the woman and the boy at the counter, and then he went behind the register without a word and got the ticket pad and the pen. He didn't sit on the counter. He stood at the end of it, by stool one, the way a waitress stands, with the pad held up. "What can I get you," he said. --- I took a piece out of the cooler. It was one of the last ones. I don't know which one it was anymore. I got the cast iron down off the hook and set it on the stove to heat. I ground some of the Diamond Crystal in the mortar while I waited. I sliced the piece, half an inch, and I patted it dry with a clean towel, because a wet thing won't sear. Through the front window, past where Gary used to stand, I could see the field going off gray and brown to the tree line. There was one out there, at the edge of the birches. Just one, off by itself. It had on a coat, some kind of coat. Red, maybe. Red and black, maybe, a plaid. I didn't look long enough to be sure. I looked at the pan. Behind me Marcus was writing something in big block capitals and the boy was asking him what it said, and Dana had gotten up off the bench and was limping over with two of the brown mugs, the chipped ones we don't give customers. # Brainstorming **Interpreting the prompt:** "One quickly learns the art of entering a manor through the upper windows." The line reads like a wry aside from a narrator who has had to learn this out of necessity. In a Victorian romance, the obvious reading is a suitor climbing to a lover's window. There are richer options: - **The narrator is the lady herself.** She sneaks *back in* through her own window after secret excursions: to the lecture hall, to the printing press, to a lover, to a medical dissection. She is the climber, not the climbed-to. - **A housebreaker** or gentleman thief who falls for the daughter of the house he is robbing. - **A chimney sweep's apprentice** grown up and now a builder or architect. He knows the house's bones and returns years later. - **A governess** locked out after curfew by a tyrannical housekeeper, who meets a neighbor's son doing the same. - **A secret correspondence.** Two lovers in adjoining townhouses use the upper windows and the leads (rooftops) between them. - **A widow** or poor relation confined to the house by mourning customs. The window is her only escape into life. - **A ghost-story inflection.** Someone keeps entering through the upper window, and the heroine assumes a ghost or thief, but it is someone else. **Character ideas:** - **Heroine options:** - Miss Theodora (Dora) Ashcombe, 24, "on the shelf." She secretly writes sensational serials under a male pseudonym and must deliver manuscripts to her publisher at night. - A botanist's daughter who gathers night-blooming specimens. - A girl illustrating anatomy. - **Hero options:** - A disgraced younger son. - A roof-slater or glazier: a class-crossing romance, and he literally knows windows. - The publisher's editor. - A rival serial writer. - The man her family wants her to marry, secretly also a window-climber. - A policeman investigating a spate of "second-storey" burglaries, who catches her mid-climb. - **Antagonists and obstacles:** - A mother obsessed with Season prospects. - A suspicious housekeeper, Mrs. Pell. - A cousin who wants to inherit. - A real cat burglar working the neighborhood. This makes the heroine a suspect and creates stakes. - **Supporting cast:** - A younger sister who keeps the window latch unfastened. - A lady's maid accomplice. - An ivy-covered wisteria trellis that is slowly failing (a comic running motif). **Plot threads:** 1. Heroine climbs out and in weekly. One night another figure is already on the roof: the hero, who is also sneaking into or out of the neighboring house. 2. The two form a pact to keep each other's secrets. They meet on the rooftops, and trade lessons in climbing, drainpipes, and which slates hold. 3. A burglar strikes the square. Suspicion falls on the hero, or on the "figure seen on the roof." 4. The heroine must choose between revealing her secret (her writing, her independence) and clearing him. 5. A climactic night climb, perhaps during a storm or a ball, to catch the real thief or to retrieve a manuscript. 6. Resolution: a public reveal, and a proposal made at a window, reversing the balcony scene. **Tone options:** - Witty and arch, Austen-meets-Wilkie-Collins. - A first-person confessional voice with epigram-style chapter openings, echoing the prompt ("One quickly learns..."). - Gothic moodiness. - Warm comedic romance with real stakes about women's autonomy. **Structure ideas:** - Each chapter opens with a "lesson" in the art of window entry (e.g., "Lesson the First: Wisteria is a liar"). This builds a playful through-line that doubles as character growth. - Eight chapters of about 1,000 words each allow roughly one major beat per chapter: setup, meeting, pact, deepening, complication, crisis, climax, resolution. **Possible beats:** 1. Dora returns from her publisher, and the climb goes wrong. 2. She meets a stranger on the leads: Mr. Julian Marsh, a new neighbor. 3. They make a bargain of mutual secrecy. 4. Rooftop meetings deepen into romance. He reveals why he climbs: he visits his sick illegitimate sibling? He is an astronomer? He works as a journalist? 5. A burglary happens, and the police are involved. 6. Her mother arranges an engagement, and Julian is arrested. 7. Dora climbs to prove him innocent, and publicly confesses her authorship. 8. Resolution with a window proposal. The final line inverts the prompt. # Reflection Making the heroine the climber is the strongest choice. It subverts the Romeo trope and gives the prompt's line a knowing, first-person irony. The climbing also becomes a metaphor for female autonomy under Victorian constraints. That gives the romance thematic weight without heaviness. The secret authorship of sensation novels fits the period well, since sensation fiction was scandalous in the 1860s. It also gives her a concrete, recurring reason to climb. The "lessons" framing at each chapter opening is charming and keeps the prompt central. It risks becoming gimmicky if the lessons don't evolve. They should turn emotional by the end ("One learns, too, that a window opens both ways"). For the hero, the policeman idea creates immediate tension but makes him an authority figure, which undercuts equality. A fellow climber is better, because the pact of mutual secrets creates intimacy. His secret must be sympathetic but also a liability. The astronomer idea is lovely but low-stakes. The journalist idea connects to her writing and could create rivalry or betrayal risk. A secret visit to someone needy works emotionally but may feel sentimental. A blend could work: he writes for a radical paper, or he investigates the burglaries himself, so they overlap. The burglar subplot supplies necessary external stakes for chapters 5–7. Without it, eight chapters of rooftop flirting would sag. It must stay lean at 1,000 words per chapter. There should be a limited suspect pool, perhaps the cousin or a charming guest. Pacing concerns: - The meeting must happen by chapter 1's end or chapter 2's start. - The romance needs to be earned through quieter rooftop scenes around chapters 3–4. - The climax should use a climb that tests everything she has "learned." The gothic tone feels less fitting than wit with sincere undercurrents. The failing wisteria is a good comic device that can pay off at the climax, when it finally gives way. The ending proposal at *her* window, with him climbing up at last, would neatly reverse the roles.
