The narrator's observation that it seemed "like the first page of a book on a subject nobody needed" is self-aware without being precious. The Walter section is economical and effective. The stomach-drop of recognizing his handwriting, the counting of the remaining money, the "With love, E." — these are small, precise details that do the work without editorializing. Where the chapter is slightly less successful: the transition between sections could be smoother. The three-dash section breaks are functional but the chapter feels slightly episodic rather than unified. The line "I have since come to think that with Tom Hesketh it was very often both, and neither of them was the point" is the one moment where the retrospective voice tips slightly into over-explanation — it tells us how to read Tom rather than letting the scene do it. It's a minor flaw in an otherwise well-controlled chapter. The plan called for Ellen to patronize Tom "slightly" and for him to "not notice, or pretend not to." This is executed well. The plan also called for the first letter to Walter to go out with money, and for Clara to ask about the scratches — both delivered. The ladder is introduced with exactly the right ambiguity the plan specified. The prose is clean throughout. No purple passages, no forced metaphors. The physical details (the crust on the palm, the pale torn ends of the ivy, the soft tie on the branch) are specific and grounded. The chapter earns its small moments of lightness and its small moments of shame. Overall this is accomplished, disciplined literary fiction that serves its plan without being mechanical about it. The voice is consistent, the characters are true to their profiles, and the chapter advances the story while doing genuine character work. # Chapter Three: The Sill The rain began on the second of November and did not stop for nine days. The lane went to soup. I walked it anyway on the first two evenings and came back with my hem heavy as a curtain. On the third evening I stood at the garden door at eight and watched the water sheet off the porch, and went back upstairs. I sat in my room with a sensation novel called *The Heiress of Ravensworth*. I disliked it very much and read it until one. By the Saturday, Mrs. Crane had found the damp. It had come through under the nursery window, the one with the loose bar. It had spread in a brown tongue down the plaster and lifted the paper at the skirting. She stood looking at it with her hands folded over her keys. Then she looked at the sill, where the paint had worn in two places to the grey wood, just where a person might put her knees. "Rotten," she said. "Hesketh will see to it." I said I was sure he would. She went away down the corridor without hurrying, and I was left with the impression, which I dismissed, that she had been talking about something other than the sill. --- He came at two, when the nurse had taken the children down to the vicarage for tea and a magic lantern. He came up the outside on a proper ladder this time, a long one, with a bag of tools over his shoulder and a board under his arm. The rain had eased to a steady grey drizzle. I was in the schoolroom next door, and I heard the ladder knock against the brick, and then a tapping. I gave it five minutes, which I timed, and then I went to see. He had the sash up and the old sill-board half out. It came away in soft brown lumps like cake. He was on the ladder with his forearms on the frame, a pencil behind his ear, and water dripping steadily off the brim of his hat. "You'll let the rain in," I said. "It's in." There was a chair in the corridor. I did not sit on it. I sat on the inner ledge of the window, the deep one under the sash, with my back against the side of the frame and my feet on the boards. I don't know why I did that. I think it was because it was where I usually was, at that window, only facing the other way. He cut the new board to length on his knee, on the ladder, with a small saw. I have never seen anything so ridiculous or so sure. "Is it dangerous?" I said. "Up there, doing that?" "No." "It looks it." "You'd know," he said, and I laughed, which surprised both of us. After that it was easier. I don't remember deciding to stay. I asked him about the pear, because it was the only thing I knew we had in common. He told me there were eleven trees on the south wall. He named them, from the east end: two Comice, a Beurré Hardy, three Williams', and so on. The last was an old tree nobody knew the name of. The late Mrs. Ashby had liked it, and he called it the Missus. "I put my foot on the Missus?" "You put your foot on a Williams'. The Missus is at the end. You'd not have got up her." He told me how grafting was done, a whip-and-tongue, the two cuts that lock into each other, bound with raffia and sealed with wax. He said that if he grafted a Comice onto a quince stock this winter, it would be four years before he knew whether it was any good. "Four years," I said. "I shouldn't have the patience." "You'd not be asked. It's the tree has to have it." He asked me where I had grown up, which nobody at Hallow had asked. I told him about Much Wenlock, and the rectory with the damp in the study, and my father. I said my father had preached very well and had died owing three hundred pounds, and that nobody had known until the men came. "That's a lot of money," Tom said. "It was." "You paid it?" "Some of it. The bishop's fund paid some." I looked at the wet slates beyond his shoulder. "My brother and I are still paying the rest, in a manner of speaking." That was a lie, or half of one. I was paying. Walter was being paid for. He said his own father had been under-gardener here for thirty years. He said his mother kept bees at the end cottage and would tell me I was too thin if I ever went by. I said I would take care not to go by. He said, "She'll come and find you," and I believed him. The board went in. He tapped it along with the heel of his hand, and the sound came through the frame into my back. At some point I asked if he read. He said he read the *Gardeners' Chronicle*. I asked about novels, and he told me about *David Copperfield*. His mother had liked it, and he had got as far as the Murdstones. "And stopped?" "Didn't want to know what happened to the lad." "He comes out all right," I said. "Broadly." "I don't read stories. I know how they come out. Somebody dies or somebody marries." He was running a bead of putty along the joint with his thumb. "Pears are better. You don't know with a pear till you've waited four year." *Years*, I thought. I thought it before I could stop myself, the way I always did. I was ashamed of it and did it anyway. Then, because I was ashamed, I began telling him about the French subjunctive. I think I meant to punish myself. I explained how it was used after verbs of wishing and fearing and doubting. The French would not simply say that a thing *was* if they were only afraid it was. They put it in a different mood, to keep it at arm's length. I went on for some while about *craindre* and *avoir peur que*. I heard myself being tedious and could not stop, the way one cannot stop on a slope. He listened to all of it. He didn't pretend to be interested, and he didn't look bored. He went on with the putty. "So you'd say it different," he said at last, "if you weren't sure." "Yes." "Seems sense." The rain had come on again, harder. It ran off his hat brim in a string. The light was going, and I could hear the wheels of the vicarage trap somewhere down on the drive. He wiped his thumb on his trousers and put his hand on the new board, flat, to feel it was true. My own hand was on the frame beside it. I hadn't known it was there. There was perhaps an inch between them, and then, for a moment, not even that. The side of his hand lay against the side of mine, cold and wet and rough as bark. Neither of us moved it. Then he took his away and picked up the saw. "That'll hold," he said. He meant the sill.

The retrospective irony promised in the plan is present but never heavy-handed. The detail "I gave it five minutes, which I timed" is exactly right for her character — controlled, self-aware, slightly self-mocking. The moment where she corrects Tom's grammar silently ("Years, I thought. I thought it before I could stop myself, the way I always did. I was ashamed of it and did it anyway.") is a perfect execution of the character profile's note about her silent grammar correction and her shame about it. This is showing character through action and thought rather than telling. The French subjunctive passage is a genuine risk that pays off. "I heard myself being tedious and could not stop, the way one cannot stop on a slope" — this is a good simile, earned and not strained. **Dialogue** The dialogue is exceptional. You don't know with a pear till you've waited four year" — lands exactly as the plan intended, and the pear-as-metaphor works because it's genuinely what he would say, not a planted symbol. The dialogue never feels written; it feels overheard. **The Central Scene** The chapter plan called for "a single long scene, not montage" and the chapter delivers this faithfully. # Chapter Four: The Prowler The owl was found on a Tuesday, face down in the bed below the nursery wing, with its ears in the wallflowers. It had sat on the corner of the parapet for longer than anyone could say. It was a stone owl with a chipped beak and a lichen collar, the kind of thing a house collects without anyone choosing it. The boy who found it carried it round to the kitchen door in both arms like a baby. By the time I came down to breakfast it was on the table in the servants' hall, and the scullery maid, Hannah, was telling anyone who would listen that she had seen a man on the roof. I knew perfectly well how the owl had come down. Four nights before, the sash had jammed. The new sill had swelled in the wet, and it would not go up past a hand's width however I pushed. I stood on the sill with my fingers in the gap and the rain in my collar, and I understood that I must either go back down the drainpipe and knock, or go along. I went along. There is a lead gutter behind the parapet on that side, about a foot wide, and it runs to the window of the linen room, which is never latched because the latch is broken. I went along it on my knees, holding the parapet. At the corner my cloak caught on something that gave a little, and then gave altogether, and I heard a soft heavy sound in the dark below, like a sack of meal dropped from a cart. I did not look. I got in at the linen room and lay among the sheets for a quarter of an hour, and in the morning I wrote in the back of the copybook: *6. The sash swells after rain. The linen room latch is broken.* *7. The leads behind the parapet will bear you if you keep to the wall side.* I did not write anything about the owl. --- Hannah's man was tall. By dinner-time he was very tall and had a beard. By the next afternoon, when the carrier's boy had taken the story down to Clunbury and brought it back again, improved, he was a Gypsy from the camp at Purslow, or a deserter, or the ghost of a footman who had been dismissed in old Mr. Ashby's time and hanged himself in the coach house. Freddie was delighted and wanted to sit up and see it. Clara said nothing, and ate her rice pudding, and looked at me across the schoolroom table with her spoon held very still. I should like to say I was frightened. I was, a little. Mostly I was something I am less proud of. I stood in the passage outside the servants' hall and listened to the cook tell the laundrymaid that the thing had eyes like lamps, and I felt a small, warm, disgraceful pleasure. It was the pleasure of being talked about by people who could not see me. For nine years nobody in any house I had lived in had wondered what I did with my evenings. Now the whole parish wondered, and did not know it was me. Tom knew. I passed him on the terrace the next day, carrying the owl in a barrow to the potting shed to see whether its ear could be mended. "Heard there's a man on the roof," he said. "So I'm told." He looked at the owl, and then at me, for about as long as he had looked at me the first time. "Keep to the wall side," he said, and wheeled it on. --- Walter came on the Thursday. I was taking the children through the kings of England when the nurse put her head round the door and said there was a gentleman in the hall asking for Miss Varley, and he said he was her brother. She said it doubtfully. The gentry do not often have brothers who arrive on the carrier's cart. He was standing under the stag's head in his good coat with his hat in his hands, and he turned when he heard me on the stair. His whole face opened, the way it always did, as if I were the one thing he had been waiting all day to see. I have never been able to resist that. I don't think I ever shall. "Nell! You look *well*. Country air. No, truly." He kissed my cheek and smelled of bay rum and the cart. "I can only stay the hour. I've a man to see at Craven Arms about something that will set us both up, I promise you, and then you can stop all this." He waved a hand at the hall, the stag, the house. He said he had a message from Aunt Lettice, which turned out to be that she had a cold. I could not take him to the schoolroom. Mrs. Crane was out, gone to Bishop's Castle with the carrier on the house accounts, so the kitchen maid put us in the housekeeper's room with a pot of tea. Wesley the canary sang at us in a way that made conversation difficult. Walter was charming about the canary. He was charming about everything. He told me a long story about the man at Craven Arms and the hops, and I listened to it the way one listens to weather. At the end of it he said, "The thing is, Nell, it's the tailor," and I went upstairs for the mustard tin. I was gone perhaps ten minutes. I remember I stopped on the back stairs on the way down and counted what I had in my hand, and then went back up and put a sovereign of it back. It was the only brave thing I did that day. When I came in, he was standing at the window looking out at the yard with his hands behind his back. He turned round smiling and said the canary had been telling him all my secrets. I gave him three pounds. He said I was a brick. He was gone by half past four, walking down the drive in the last of the light with his collar up, and he waved from the lodge gates without looking back to see whether I was still there. I was. --- Mrs. Crane came back at six. We ate at seven in the housekeeper's room, as the upper servants did when Mr. Ashby was away, with the butler at one end and the cook beside him. The talk was all of the prowler. The butler was of the opinion that a man should sit up. The cook was of the opinion that a man should have sat up a week ago. Mrs. Crane was of no opinion at all. She cut her mutton very small and said nothing, and towards the end of the meal she looked up and down the table. She stopped at me. She looked at me for a long moment, without any expression whatever, the way she had looked at the brown stain on the nursery wall. Then she said, "Pass the salt, Miss Varley, if you would," and I did. My hand, I noticed, was not quite steady. I didn't know yet what there was to be unsteady about.

# Chapter Five: Annie The money was missed on the Saturday morning. Mrs. Crane kept a black japanned cash box in the second drawer of the bureau in her room. It held the household float, the wages put by for Lady Day, and the petty sums that came and went for candles and carriers and the sweep. She did her accounts on Saturdays. At a quarter to nine she came into the servants' hall with the box open in her two hands and said, in her ordinary voice, that there were four pounds short. I was not there. I had it afterwards from the nurse, who had it from the cook, who had been there and who said that Mrs. Crane did not raise her voice even once. I have no difficulty believing it. By dinner the whole house knew. By tea it had been decided what had happened. It was the linen room that did it. Mrs. Crane had been through the house that afternoon, room by room, with the butler behind her carrying a lamp he didn't need. In the linen room they found that the latch on the window was broken. It had been broken, I believe, since the old Queen's jubilee. They also found mud on the second shelf of sheets, dried grey, in a shape that might have been a knee. And on the sill outside there was a scuff in the lichen where something had been dragged across it. So there had been someone. Hannah was vindicated and went about the kitchen with a face like a saint in a window. There had been a man on the roof, and he had come in at the linen room, and he had gone down the back stairs to the housekeeper's room and taken four pounds out of a locked box without breaking the lock. That was the difficulty. The box had not been forced. Whoever opened it had known where the key was kept, which was in the tea caddy on the mantelshelf, behind Wesley's cage. No Gypsy from Purslow would know that. A man on the roof would have to have been let in, and told. The linen room was Annie's. --- Annie Pryce was sixteen. She had been at Hallow a year and a half, and she was the second housemaid, which meant she did the grates and the linen and anything else nobody wanted. She was round-faced and freckled and had red hands and ginger hair that would not stay under her cap, and she sang Primitive Methodist hymns while she blacked the stoves, and the footman mocked her for it. I had spoken to her perhaps a dozen times. I thought of her, when I thought of her at all, as a cheerful sort of girl who dropped things. On the Thursday afternoon, while Mrs. Crane was at Bishop's Castle, Annie had done the grate in the housekeeper's room. Everyone knew it. The kitchen maid had seen her go in. "I never went in, miss," she said to me on the Sunday. I had come upon her in the linen room, of all places, sitting on the floor between the presses with her apron over her face. She scrambled up when she saw me. "I only did the grate. I did the grate and come out. I *told* her." "I'm sure you did," I said. "They're saying I've a follower. They're saying I let him in at the window." She was twisting the apron in both hands. "I never had a follower in my life. Mother'd kill me. I send home nine pound a year, miss. If I'm turned off without a character there's nobody..." She stopped. I said something. I don't remember what. I think I told her it would come right. I know I didn't stay long, because I found I couldn't be in that room with her, with the mud still on the second shelf, the grey mark of my own knee. --- I want to set down exactly what I knew, because I have spent a good deal of time since then trying to make it less. I knew there was no man on the roof. I knew nobody had come in at the linen room window but me. I knew that if I went to Mrs. Crane and said so, the whole story of the follower would fall to pieces in her hands. Whatever had happened to the four pounds, it had nothing to do with that window, and Annie would be only one of a dozen people who had been in and out of that room. I knew all this on the Saturday night. I lay in my bed and knew it. I also knew what would come after. A governess who climbs into her employer's house by the linen room at midnight is not a governess for very long. There would be no character, and without one there would be no next place. There would be the mustard tin, eleven pounds going down, and Walter's letters, and after that I did not let myself think. So I said nothing on the Saturday. I said nothing on the Sunday, after the linen room. On the Monday Annie was called in to Mrs. Crane and questioned for an hour, and came out white, and did the stairs with her head down and did not sing. On the Tuesday Mrs. Crane wrote to Mr. Ashby in London. The nurse told me so as if it were good news. Four days. I have made it three in the telling before now, because three sounds like hesitation and four sounds like what it was. It was not hesitation. I had decided on the first night. I spent the other three finding reasons. --- I stopped writing in the copybook that week. I didn't decide to. I opened it on the Sunday night, meaning to put down something about the linen room latch, and I looked at the list, *Ivy holds, The drainpipe is sound, Wear the grey*, and it seemed to me the work of a stupid, pleased woman who thought she had found a secret door in the world. I shut it and put it in the bottom of my trunk, under the tin. I did not go out either. I sat in my room from eight until ten with a book open and didn't read it. At ten I heard Mrs. Crane's keys go by in the corridor below, one lock and then the next, and I felt nothing about them at all. On the Tuesday I went down to the kitchen garden, because I had to talk to someone who already knew. Tom was in the frame yard, pricking out lettuces into a flat, his big hands going very delicately among them. I stood on the path and told him all of it, not well. He went on with the lettuces. When I had finished he didn't look up for a while. Then he said, "You'll do what you'll do." That was all. He didn't say that I ought to speak, or that I needn't. He picked up the next seedling by its leaf, never by the stem, and set it in its hole, and firmed the earth round it with two fingers. I would have given a great deal for him to be angry with me. I stood there until I understood he was not going to be, and then I went back to the house.

The plan specified this, and the execution delivers it fully. Annie is rendered with economy and genuine feeling. She is not given a noble speech. She twists her apron and says "Mother'd kill me" and mentions the nine pounds. That is enough. The mud on the second shelf — "the grey mark of my own knee" — is a devastating detail, understated and precise. **Plot and Structure** The chapter follows the plan faithfully: the money is missed, suspicion falls on Annie via the linen room, Ellen knows the truth, waits four days, and the copybook notes stop. The structural decision to present the investigation through hearsay ("I had it afterwards from the nurse, who had it from the cook") is smart — it keeps Ellen at a remove from events she is causing by silence, which mirrors her moral position. Tom's "You'll do what you'll do" lands as intended. Ellen's "I'm sure you did" and "I think I told her it would come right" are rendered with appropriate self-disgust. **Prose Quality** The prose is clean and precise. There is no purple prose, no forced metaphor. "Hannah was vindicated and went about the kitchen with a face like a saint in a window" is the one simile, and it earns its place — it characterizes Hannah's self-righteousness economically. The copybook passage ("the work of a stupid, pleased woman who thought she had found a secret door in the world") is sharp without being showy. It shows his care for living things, his precision, and his refusal to be drawn into Ellen's drama, all without stating any of it. **Weaknesses** The chapter is nearly flawless in execution, but a few minor observations: the transition from the linen room scene to the "I want to set down exactly what I knew" section is slightly abrupt, though the directness is arguably intentional and consistent with the voice. The chapter is also somewhat short on scene — much is summary — but this is appropriate given that the chapter is about inaction, about what Ellen does not do, and the summary form mirrors her passivity. Annie crying in the linen room hurts. Ellen's self-knowledge — she knows exactly what she is doing and does it anyway — is more damning than ignorance would be. The plan called for the narrator to call this cowardice "exactly that, without a joke," and the chapter delivers. The copybook stopping is handled with restraint: no announcement, just the observation that it seemed "the work of a stupid, pleased woman." That is the right note. # Chapter Six: Clara On the Wednesday I went out again. I went out because of Mr. Ashby. The nurse said he was expected on Friday, by the afternoon train to Craven Arms. When I heard it I understood that I had two days left in which to be the kind of woman who might still speak first, instead of the kind who is found out. I did not trust myself to decide it in the house. In the house I had been deciding it for four days, and every time it came out the same way. So I put on the grey and my cloak and went down the lane to the lych-gate, and I stood there with my hand on the wood and told myself I would go to Mrs. Crane in the morning. I said it aloud, which I had never done before. It sounded quite reasonable in the dark. There was no moon. I walked back slowly, and the stable clock struck ten while I was still on the drive, and I did not hurry. I knew the doors would be locked. I think I wanted one more time up the wall before I gave it up. The ladder was by the potting shed. I carried it round, set it under the drainpipe, and went up. My hands knew the way by then: the second bracket, the ledge of brick, the stone sill with its new board that was still a little too proud at one end. I had my knee on the sill before I saw that the bar was already swung back. It was open wide, as far as it would go, and the sash was up a foot. I had not left it so. I never left it so. I lifted the bar at the bottom before pushing, every time, so that it would not squeal, and I pulled it to behind me. I stayed there on my knee with the cold coming off the glass, and for a moment I thought quite clearly: *there is a man on the roof after all.* Then I climbed in and went down the corridor to the night nursery. The door stood ajar. Freddie was asleep on his back with his mouth open. Clara's bed was empty. The covers were turned back neatly, the way she did everything, and her slippers stood side by side on the rug. I don't remember going back to the window. I remember being at it, with my head and shoulders out, looking left along the leads towards the linen room. It was too dark to see anything but the line of the parapet against the sky, a little paler than the roof. Then something moved on it, low down, near the corner where the owl had been. It was something small and white, a nightgown. "Clara," I said. I did not shout. I had some idea that if I shouted she would turn round. She didn't answer. She was on her hands and knees on the lead gutter, perhaps twenty feet from me, going along it towards the linen room exactly as I had gone. But she was on the outer side, by the edge, not the wall side. I had never told her about the wall side. I had never told her anything. I got out onto the sill and onto the leads. I don't know how. My legs were shaking so much that I went on my knees too, with one hand on the brick, and the lead was wet and very cold through my skirt. I said her name again, quietly, and again. She stopped and looked back over her shoulder. I saw her face, small and pale and pleased. "I've nearly done it," she said. "Stay there. Don't move. I'm coming." "I can do it." She turned back and put her hand forward, and the edge of the gutter was not there. It happened very slowly and not at all. Her hand went down into nothing, and her shoulder went after it, and she made a small sound, not a scream, the sound of someone who has missed a stair. Then she was half over the edge, with her legs on the lead and her body hanging out into the dark. One arm was hooked over the lip of the parapet where it turned the corner, and the other was gone. I reached her. I have no memory of the twenty feet. I had her by the back of the nightgown, then by the arm, then round the waist. I pulled, and she came up over the parapet and onto the lead, and we both lay there against the wall of the house. I held on to her so tightly that she said, "You're hurting," and I did not let go. She was crying by then, but quietly. Her left wrist was bent against her chest and she would not let me touch it. It had caught the stone as she went over. I got her back to the window somehow, on the wall side, with me behind her. I got her through and onto the boards, and sat down beside her in the corridor. I was shaking so that my teeth knocked together, and I could not make them stop. There was no joke in any of it. I have tried since to find one and there isn't one. I bound her wrist with a strip torn from my petticoat, by the light of a candle, in her room, with Freddie still asleep. It was swelling but I did not think it broken. She let me, and watched my face the whole time. "I saw you," she said. "Lots of times. From the window. I wanted to know where you went." "Nowhere," I said. "Only the lane." She thought about that. Then she asked, very seriously, in the voice she used for the Plantagenets, "Do you go out because you are unhappy? You needn't say. I only wondered if it helped." I opened my mouth, and nothing came. I sat on the edge of her bed with the candle and the torn petticoat, and I could not answer a child of eleven. After a while she lay down and turned her face to the wall, and I sat there until she slept. --- The letter came by the first post on Thursday. I knew the hand across the hall. *Dearest Nell,* it said, *a thousand thanks for the extra. I knew you'd not mind. You never do. The man at Craven Arms has come to nothing but there is another at Ludlow. W.* I read it twice standing in the hall under the stag's head. I had given him three pounds. He had thanked me for three pounds already, on the drive, calling me a brick. The extra, then, was something else. I thought of him standing at the window of the housekeeper's room with his hands behind his back, and of the canary telling him all my secrets. Wesley's cage sat on the mantelshelf in front of the tea caddy. I folded the letter very small and put it in my pocket. Then I went upstairs and took the copybook out of the bottom of my trunk, from under the tin, and sat with it on my knee, not opening it, until the children's breakfast bell.

# Chapter Seven: Mr. Ashby's Study By Thursday noon it was Tom. I heard it on the back stairs from the footman, who was telling the boy who cleaned the boots. The footman said everyone knew Hesketh was about at night. He'd been seen on the drive after eleven more than once, and on the terrace, and under the nursery wing with a ladder. And who had a better reason to know the house from the outside than the man who tied up the wall? The boy said Mr. Hesketh had mended the owl's ear. The footman said that was just what a clever one would do. It was true that he had been about at night. I knew, better than anyone in that house, where he had been, and why. Clara's wrist had been explained at breakfast as a fall from the rocking horse. She explained it herself, before I could, in her flat polite voice, and looked at me afterwards to see whether I would contradict her. I didn't. I told myself it was because it wasn't my lie to undo. I had found that one could tell oneself almost anything, that week. --- Mr. Ashby came on the Friday by the afternoon train. I watched the carriage come up the drive from the schoolroom window. He got down slowly, the way a man gets down who has been sitting since Euston, and stood a moment on the gravel looking up at the front of the house as though he wasn't sure it was his. Then Mrs. Crane was on the step, and they went in. I gave him an hour. I timed it. At a quarter past five I went down the main stairs, which I didn't generally use, and along the hall past the stag, and I knocked on the study door, which I had never done in fourteen months. I had meant to knock quietly and knocked like a bailiff. "Come." He was at the desk with Mrs. Crane's letter open in front of him and a glass of something brown beside it he had not touched. He was a tall, stooped, greyish man with a tired face. I had seen him perhaps eight times, and on each I had thought he looked like someone waiting for a train that was late. He half rose, as one does for a governess, and sat again. "Miss Varley. Is it Clara? Mrs. Crane tells me she's hurt her arm." "It is partly Clara," I said. "May I tell you the whole of it? I would rather do it all at once. I'm afraid that if I stop I shan't begin again." He looked at me, and then he nodded at the chair, and I didn't sit in it. I told him standing. I told him about the ten o'clock doors and the lane and the lych-gate, and the night of the moon, and the pear, and the loose bar he had been warned of two years before. I told him about the ladder, though I said only that I had found it, which was the one lie I told in that room, and I don't regret it. I told him about the sash swelling and the leads, and the owl. I told him the man on the roof was me, and the mud in the linen room was mine, and that I had known it from the first morning and had let Annie Pryce be questioned for four days rather than say so. I told him Clara had seen me from the window and followed, and that she had gone over the parapet and I had pulled her back, and that it was not the rocking horse. Then I told him about Walter, and the housekeeper's room, and the tea caddy behind the cage. I put the letter on the desk in front of him, unfolded, with *the extra* uppermost. "I will repay it," I said. "Four pounds. I have it. I can give it to Mrs. Crane tonight." All the while I was counting the buttons on his waistcoat, which was grey with a black thread in it. There were seven, and there should have been eight. The bottom one was gone, and nobody had sewn it on. He didn't say anything for a long time. He read Walter's letter. He picked up the brown glass and put it down. "Hesketh," he said at last. "Mrs. Crane writes that people have been saying..." "It wasn't Mr. Hesketh. It was never anyone but me." "No," he said. "No, I see that." He rubbed his eyes with finger and thumb. Then he asked, and he sounded honestly puzzled, the first real thing he had said: "But where did you *go*?" "Nowhere," I said. "To the gate at Clunbury, and back." He looked at me then as though I had said something in a language he had once known a little. It went on so long that I had to look at the window. "I don't doubt your affection for the children, Miss Varley," he said. "That isn't the question. The question is what I tell people, and I'm afraid I haven't anything to tell them but the truth." He folded Walter's letter and handed it back to me, which I had not expected. "You'll stay to the end of the month. It will be less remarked on. Clara..." He stopped. "Clara will mind." "Yes," I said. "I'll speak to Mrs. Crane about the girl." That was all. I said thank you, which was absurd, and he said not at all, which was worse, and I went out and shut the door very carefully behind me, as if there were someone ill inside. --- Annie was cleared by supper. The butler told the servants' hall that the money had been found to be a misunderstanding in the accounts, which was Mr. Ashby's doing, and which I think was kind, and which everyone understood to mean something they would find out by morning. Nobody apologised to Annie. The cook gave her the top of the milk. She sang over the grate the next day, a little, not loudly. When I passed her on the stair she flattened herself against the wall and said, "Miss," and didn't look at me. That was all she ever said, and I have not been able to find it unjust. At ten I was in the corridor below my room when Mrs. Crane came along it with her candle and her keys. I had the four pounds in my hand, in a twist of paper. She took it without counting it and put it in her apron pocket. Then she went to the garden door and locked it, and the key made its small sound in the old lock, and she stood a moment with her hand on it. "The doors are locked at ten, Miss Varley," she said. "They have been locked at ten for nineteen years. I do it so as to know who has to find another way." I didn't say anything. I found I couldn't. "I went out by a window once," she said. "At Ludlow. It was a great deal further to the ground." She looked at me for a moment longer, not kindly, and not unkindly either. Then she picked up her candle and went on down the passage to the stillroom door, and I heard that lock go too, and the next, and the next, getting fainter, until the house was shut.

# Chapter Eight: A Cutting The last evening was the thirtieth of November, and it was dry. I had packed by four. There was not much: the two dresses, the brown cloak, the books that were mine and a few that were not, which I left on the schoolroom shelf with a note. The mustard tin had seven pounds in it and a threepenny bit. Mrs. Crane had given me my character that morning, in an envelope, sealed. I did not open it. I found I would rather carry it than know. Mr. Ashby had gone back to London on the Monday. He shook my hand in the hall and said he hoped I would find something suitable, and I said I hoped so too. We stood a moment under the stag's head, neither of us able to think what else was customary, and then the carriage was at the door. Freddie had been told I was going to look after my aunt. He accepted it at once and asked if my aunt had a pony. Clara had been told the truth, because she asked for it. --- At nine I went up to the nursery wing. I didn't go out. I sat on the inner ledge of the window, the way I had in November, with my back to the frame, and I lifted the bar at the bottom so that it would not squeal, and pushed up the sash. He was already there. The long ladder was against the wall and he was near the top of it, with his forearms on the new sill, looking at the frame. "Board's held," he said. "It has." "Swelled a bit at the end. I'll plane it." "You'll have to tell the next governess," I said, "or she'll put her knees through it." "The next one'll use the door." We were quiet a while. It was very cold, and the sky had that clear green look it gets after sunset in winter, and the rooks were going over towards the elms at Clunbury in long loose lines. Somewhere in the kitchen garden his mother was calling a cat. I had meant to say something light. I had prepared it on the stairs. When it came to it I couldn't remember it, which I have come to think was a mercy. "If you asked me," I said, "I don't know what I'd say." "I know." He looked at the frame. "That's why I'll not ask." "Tom..." "You'd say yes to be kind, or no to be sensible, and I'd not know which." He said it without any heat. "I've been asked for by a lass that thought she was above me. She did better. I'll not do that twice." "I don't think I'm above you." Then, because it was the last night and I had lied enough that month: "I think I think I am. Some of the time. I correct how you talk. In my head. I have done it since the first day." "I know," he said again. "You go still." I laughed, and it was not a good laugh, and he let it go. "It would cost you," he said. "A gardener. You'd lose your friends." "I haven't any." "You'd lose the ones you might have." He turned his thumb along the edge of the sill. "And it'd cost me. Having a wife that goes still." That was the whole of it. We did not settle anything. I have read a great many novels in which this conversation ends with somebody's arms, and I can tell you that it doesn't have to. It ended with the two of us looking at a window frame in the cold, both of us knowing what we had said was true, and that neither of us was finished with it. He reached down into the bag over his shoulder and brought out something wrapped in damp sacking and tied with raffia. It was about the length of my hand. "Scion wood," he said. "Off the Missus. You want to keep it cool and wet till you find a stock. A quince'll do. Any gardener'll graft it for you, if you ask. Tell 'em whip-and-tongue." "Four years," I said. "Near enough." I held it on my knee. It was cold and smelled of earth. "I write bad," he said. "I've been at it evenings, but I write bad. You'll have to put up with it." He paused. "You can mend the spelling if you like. I'll not mind." "I shan't," I said. I meant it. I don't know if he believed me. He went down the ladder. I watched him carry it round the corner of the house towards the potting shed, the long shape of it tipping against the sky, and then I shut the sash, and let the bar down, and did not lift it. --- Clara came to the carriage in the morning with her wrist in a sling made of an old silk scarf of her mother's. She had insisted on that. She did not cry. She held out the French copybook, which I had left on the schoolroom table, and said, "You forgot this," which I hadn't. In the carriage, past the lodge gates, I turned it over and opened it at the back. There was the list, in my hand: *Ivy holds. The drainpipe is sound. Wear the grey.* And under the last of them, in pencil, in a round careful child's hand: *Ivy does not hold. — C.A.* --- The house in Cheshire is square and new and yellow brick, and the doors are not locked until eleven, and there is a butler who sits up. There are three girls, who are well behaved and not very interesting. There is no ivy on the walls at all. The mistress thinks it harbours damp. I came in March. The scion wood had gone into a pot of wet sand in the corner of my room, and the head gardener here, a Scot who was very suspicious of me, grafted it onto a quince stock in April, when I asked. I told him whip-and-tongue. He said he knew. It has put out four leaves. There was a letter on Tuesday, two pages, and the spelling is very bad, and I have read it eleven times. On my first evening I walked out after the girls were in bed, down the drive and along the road to the milestone, and touched it, and came back. It was dusk when I got to the house. I stood on the gravel for a while and looked up at the windows of the second floor. The third from the left has a stone sill, deep and square, with a lead downpipe beside it fixed with brackets, and a string course below it you could get a foot on. Then I went up the steps and in at the front door, which was open, and wiped my boots.

Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Task: write a short story over several chapters. Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Begin the story as an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. Arthur meets with this unknown party, who makes an offer. This early scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The first chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. The remainder of the story is open to your choices & direction.
